#3560. How the Newly Elected Congress Can Save the Smithsonian

This is the November 6, 2026 edition of True Colors, a look inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

It’s True Colors. The Democrats have flipped the House and the Senate, which could usher in a new era of funding at the Smithsonian—or, at the very least, a vibe shift in DC. There are a ton of gallery shows opening around New York, and on the West Coast, LACMA Art+Film Gala goes down tomorrow night. We got the rare chance to sit down with one of the night’s honorees, Vija Celmins.

Mentioned in this issue: Donald Trump, Lonnie Bunch, Alma Allen, Tilman Fertitta, Yoshitomo Nara, Loïc Gouzer, Vija Celmins, Matthew Marks, Leonardo DiCaprio, Eva Chow, Denis Villeneuve, Gary Hume, Jacqueline Tran, Michael Govan, Katherine Ross, James Turrell, Riko Mizuno, Matthew Barney, Roni Horn, Meshell Ndegeocello, Steve McQueen, Matthieu Blazy, Rosemarie Trockel, Carrie Mae Weems, Marina Abramović, Wade Guyton, Christopher Wool, Rashid Johnson, Felix Rödder, Calvin Marcus, James Ensor.

Trump has spent the last two years attacking Washington’s cultural hub with executive orders and legally dubious firings issued via fiat. But the Smithsonian gets its funding through Congress—what if Congress actually acted on that authority?

Sure, Congress has more pressing issues to address once the deeply blue House and Senate get sworn in early next year. But here at True Colors I think it’s fair to ask the question: Will lawmakers wind back the years of impact the Trump administration has had on the Smithsonian Institution?

Although Congress has authority over the cultural behemoth, the White House has in just the last two years issued executive orders, been extremely hands-on in its public signage, and mounted pressure campaigns to fire directors and censor artworks. Congress could have stopped all of this, but didn't. Republicans naturally didn’t want to cross Trump and support the beleaguered arts mecca. But Democrats have every reason to—after the new Congress is sworn in they’ll have the power to appropriate massive amounts of funding to each Smithsonian museum—or even create new museums. Plus, that can impact how the whole institution is run on a day-to-day basis, as Congress has the power to shake up the Smithsonian’s board of regents. That governing body will choose the next Smithsonian secretary, after Lonnie Bunch resigned earlier this year.

I’m particularly interested in who takes over as the director of the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden. Melissa Chiu, who held the position for 12 years, stepped down earlier this year to be the director of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and rumors are swirling about who will succeed her in the post. The prospect of a culture-living Congress—and, who knows...a Democratic president come 2029?—could make the Smithsonian seem like a swell place to be long term.

Add in the prospect of a new crop of congressional staffers and the attendant cottage industries of consultants and lobbyists all flocking to Washington, and I could see the Hirshhorn getting caught up in the vibe shift, pronto. There’s expected to be a sea change of DC residents in town, and there’s every reason to believe they’ll make the (free! always free!) contemporary art museum a constant stop on the rotation. Plus, the long-gestating renovation of the Sculpture Garden literally just opened this past weekend. I don’t have any inside intel on who’s in the running for the job —but it’s looking like a pretty great gig these days.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

Meanwhile, the artworks that filled the American Pavilion at the Venice Biennale, made by State Department–tapped artist Alma Allen, might be stuck in Italy for the foreseeable future. Funding has run out, and there’s nothing in the budget for moving the works. I wonder how that can be resolved. Seems like a job for an art-loving, restaurant-owning Italian ambassador, Tilman Fertitta!

The massive two-location Yoshitomo Nara show opened at David Zwirner last night, truly one of the great gallery moments here in New York this season. Don’t miss the pop-up one-painting exhibition of Nara’s In the Milky Lake / Thinking One, which will be sold by Loïc Gouzer’s one-lot auction business, Fair Warning. It’s on view at 534 W. 22nd Street. The lot opens for live bidding November 19 and is expected to sell for the eye-popping sum of $10 million to $15 million.

You can also see Nara’s work in Washington, DC, where the aforementioned Hirshhorn just opened a grand survey of the artist timed to the inauguration of its sculpture garden. And if you want to check out some of Nara’s artworks in a very unexpected place, head to the Avenue A dive bar Niagara, where Nara drunkenly created a masterwork on the walls late one night after an opening at Pace. The bar wisely conserved the artwork behind glass, and it remains there nearly two decades later.

It’s not usually worth reporting on the toasts given at gala dinners here in the prized real estate that is this newspaper’s Table Hopping section, but the Dia Fall Night had some good honorary toast content! On Monday, Matthew Barney proved himself to be a very deep Roni Horn fan with his toast. Then Meshell Ndegeocello went super outside the box, honoring Steve McQueen by stepping in front of the podium and leading a band around the gala. The whole evening was like that. Chanel wasn’t just a sponsor—the brand’s creative director Matthieu Blazy, a true contemporary art head, chaired the whole thing alongside artists Rosemarie Trockel and Carrie Mae Weems. Marina Abramović was at my table; she told me she reads Vanity Fair every time she’s on a plane and appreciates how thick the issues have been lately. Marina, it’s an honor. Thank you for reading.

Matthew Marks hosted a party on Wednesday night for Wade Guyton’s excellent new show at Bridges, the best restaurant on Chatham Square. Fun fact: Christopher Wool’s old studio was right next to the restaurant some decades back.

On Election Day, as the results started coming in, Rashid Johnson opened a show of new work at Hauser & Wirth’s Wooster Street gallery, which has recently become my favorite of the mega-gallery’s dozen or so global outposts. It’s a throwback of sorts, a small space in the neighborhood that was once the city’s gallery nexus, with an excellent track record of great shows. The dinner was at the gallery’s restaurant, Manuela, right around the corner on Prince Street. There was caviar, and while it was served to celebrate Johnson, it happened to come out right as the news networks indicated the Democrats were going to flip a Senate seat in South Carolina. Spirits were high.

If you’re making your way to The Met to see “Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous,” do stop by Rodder, the gallery founded by Felix Rödder, to see one of the most inspired artist pairings in the city right now. Calvin Marcus, the fanatically talented and free-wheeling Los Angeles painter, has new and recent paintings, drawings, and ceramics installed alongside work by the great Belgian weirdo James Ensor. The chemistry between these two artists from different centuries and continents is uncanny. The dinner for the show was held somewhere unusual: House of the Redeemer, the Episcopalian Church in a former Italian Renaissance Revival townhouse once owned by a Vanderbilt heiress.

#3559. John Goodman Thinks He Shouldn't Have Starred In George Clooney's 2014 Critical Flop

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

George Clooney enjoys a heightened status in Hollywood. He is one of the most handsome and charismatic movie stars in the history of the medium, and he relishes the opportunity to make a total fool out of himself (especially if he's working for Joel and Ethan Coen). For a moment, his instincts were unerring. On the strength of "Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" and "Good Night, and Good Luck," those instincts seemed to extend to directing. His next two directorial efforts, "Leatherheads" and "The Ides of March," were solid, but they lacked the snap of his early work. Then he just up and lost it.

Clooney's last five movies — "The Monuments Men," "Suburbicon," "The Midnight Sky," "The Tender Bar" and "The Boys in the Boat" — are bizarrely inert. I revere Clooney as an actor (I wrote a book about him), and, via interviews with people who know him well, believe that he cares deeply about his art. But there's no passion in those aforementioned movies. They're smart, considered, compassionate works, but they've got a blasé point of view. Clooney admirably promotes a humanistic point of view, but there's no technical or intellectual rigor behind his efforts. It's like watching LeBron James make layups.

I hate writing this stuff because I know Clooney has it in him to make great films. But when I run into a series of comments from a serious actor like John Goodman about how he spent months working on "The Monuments Men" with Clooney, only to walk away wishing he hadn't made the movie, I wonder where it all went wrong. While Goodman admittedly had a good time making the film, he also confessed, "It was one of those movies ... I probably shouldn't have done."

During a recent SAG-AFTRA Foundation Q&A, Goodman dished on two films that, in his estimation, he shouldn't have done. One was John Landis' reviled "Saturday Night Live" movie sequel "Blues Brothers 2000," which at least gave the rhythm and blues aficionado the opportunity to work with music legends like Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett, and B.B. King. He didn't mention Landis' involvement in the deaths of Vic Morrow, Myca Dinh Le, and Renee Shin-Ye Lee on the set of "Twilight Zone: The Movie," but people were still making films with the director at the time.

The other was "The Monuments Men" with Clooney. According to Goodman, "George loves movies and he loves stories and he's such a great storyteller himself, and I think he's a great director. I had fun with him. 'Monuments Men.' We were over in Germany for six months. And England."

But the film about art experts being dropped into Europe during World War II to save the continent's cultural treasures was DOA critically and commercially. It's a handsomely mounted would-be epic, but the theme is clearly stated early on, which leaves Clooney nowhere to go narratively. Protecting art, reinforcing its importance in the middle of a war that threatens to end civilization, is a wildly worthwhile premise. Especially now. I just wish Clooney and co-screenwriter Grant Heslov hadn't taken a softball approach to this subject. We need a guy like Clooney hurling heat.

#3558. Five Hacks Every Suunto Race 3S User Should Know

Suunto's new Race 3S is a lightweight, premium racing watch—but at a retail price of $599, it's a steep climb from the Race S, which is regularly on sale for $299. Still, there are certainly some major upgrades: The battery holds 46% more than the Race S's, and it's good for up to 38 hours of dual-band GPS; storage is double the Race S's, at 64GB. And as always, with the SuuntoPlus store, you can download apps and integrations so your watch can do more than just the default features. After all, the best way to justify the price is to really make use of everything the watch can do. Here are five ways to get more out of your Suunto Race 3S.

(Suunto Race 3S users should also check out these Suunto Run hacks).

There are several ways you can explore new hikes, straight from your watch or app, and all from the comfort of your home. First up, make sure you download offline maps at home. The Race 3S offers free worldwide offline maps with contour lines and place names, and you pay no subscription. Download your regions over wifi before you leave, so you aren't relying on a phone signal at the trailhead. The 64GB of storage leaves room for several regions, so grab the places you actually run, plus anywhere you're traveling. Menu paths can shift with firmware updates, so check the Suunto app if the layout has changed.

From there, build a library of points of interest. A POI is any spot worth returning to, such as a trailhead, water source, campsite, or viewpoint—and with Suunto specifically, you get a broad definition of “POI,” including spots for hunting, fishing, foraging, or wildlife watching. There are built-in POI types for noting where a deer seemed to have rubbed its antlers, where you've seen marine mammals, or where you've spotted mushrooms. And with the Race 3S, you can store up to 250 of them on the watch.

You can create them on the map in the Suunto app without even being there in person, or when you do stumble upon one, you can save your current location from the watch mid-run. You just have to plug in the POI as a Navigation Target under the options for your trail run or other activity. There's also a navigation app, accessible from the bottom of the widget list (select All Apps), and you can navigate without having an activity running. Organize them by area before a hiking trip, and you can navigate to a trailhead or a spring with a few taps, with the map showing the terrain around you.

For all the hikers out there, you can use Climb Guidance to preview the climbs. When you load a route, Climb Guidance splits it into flat, uphill, downhill, climb and descent sections, and shows remaining ascent. Use it to decide where to push and where to hold back. It doesn't set your pace for you, but it lets you pace by terrain.

Suunto’s Race line includes a storm alarm that watches for rapid pressure drops, a warning sign that weather is turning. It only helps if the barometer reading is trustworthy, so set your altitude to a known reference (a trailhead sign or a verified elevation) before you head up. To turn on storm alerts, go into Settings > System notifications > Alerts > Storm. (This is also where you can set up sunrise and sunset notifications.)

Just remember to recalibrate your barometer every time you start from a new elevation. Also under the Settings menu, you can select Alti & Baro, and then you have the option to either Set altitude or Auto adjust altitude. The auto-adjustment uses a GPS reading to make sure the altimeter is calibrated. But if you know your current altitude from a map, you can set it manually.

Training by heart rate is a great idea, but the default zones on your watch are based on broad formulas and guesses. With the SuuntoPlus app store, you can select Anaerobic Threshold and follow the instructions to find the heart rate where effort turns hard, so your zones reflect your body.

Be prepared: A threshold test is a tough workout. After a warm-up, you’ll be asked to run as fast as you can for 30 minutes. At the end, the app will tell you the heart rate that seems to correspond with your lactate threshold.

Now here’s the cool part: On your watch, go into Settings, then Training, then Intensity zones. Choose either the Default HR zones for all sports (what I’d recommend if you aren’t sure) or choose a sport under the advanced setting. Here, you can set the boundaries between your zones. The boundary at the bottom of zone 5 (and thus the top of zone 4) should be set to the number you got from the threshold test. If you’d like to tweak the other zones, Suunto has more information on how to calculate numbers for the other zone boundaries.

And for any threshold test, where precision matters most, I recommend pairing with a chest strap.

SuuntoPlus apps run on the watch and show extra data during activities, and these two are worth setting up during your training:

Cadence Coach shows live cadence and stride length so you can work on running form and, in Suunto's words, avoid injuries. Run a few easy sessions with it, find the cadence that feels smooth, and use it as a target.

Sprint automatically records your strides and sprints, using wrist acceleration. Instead of tapping laps during strides or hill sprints, just run, and review the efforts afterward.

Activate both in the Suunto app's SuuntoPlus store before starting an exercise, and watch your running economy start to improve.

My favorite time-saving shortcut is to pin the timer widget. Widgets are reachable from the watch face by swiping up or turning the crown, and you can choose which ones to show and in what order in the Suunto app. Move the timer to the top, and pin it so a crown press opens it. Then the upper button starts and stops the stopwatch, and the lower button resets it. It's ideal for intervals, cooking, and race-day warm-ups, and you never have to start a full workout for a quick timing job. The timer remembers whether you last used the stopwatch or the countdown.

Finally, I’m keeping my eye on the launch of the Race Planner feature. It's meant to build a pacing plan from your route, weather, and goal time, and then guide your pace on race day. Suunto hasn't announced a date yet, so I wouldn’t exactly buy the watch for it.

I'm old enough to remember when Netflix mailing DVDs to my house felt like we’d finally made it to "The Future." These days, with the 2026 Netflix streaming schedule packed with original movies and shows, I'm watching the streamer rediscover something considerably older: movie theaters. After years of Netflix treating theatrical releases like an inconvenience, I'm genuinely happy to hear that KPop Demon Hunters 2 and Greta Gerwig's Narnia are getting proper shots at the big screen.

According to Deadline, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos discussed plans for longer theatrical engagements during Bloomberg's Screentime event. The biggest surprise was his confirmation that the eventual sequel to the animated phenomenon KPop Demon Hunters won't be confined to a quick promotional screening. As he put it:

We’re going to do a big wide release for Narnia next year, and then we’ll do a big wide release for Charlie vs. the Chocolate Factory at the end of the year. We think they’ll do great, and when the KPop Demon Hunters sequel comes, you can expect a very broad theatrical release.

Gerwig's upcoming page-to-screen adaptation of The Chronicles of Narnia, Narnia: The Magician's Nephew, is pushing things even further with a theatrical run. The fantasy film opens in theaters on Feb. 12, 2027, following IMAX previews on Feb. 10, and won't arrive on Netflix until April 2. That's a 49-day exclusive theatrical window. Considering the film's reported blockbuster-sized budget, it makes sense to question why Netflix wouldn't give it a proper theatrical push.

Netflix's relationship with exhibitors hasn't exactly been friendly. The company has historically favored streaming premieres, with limited theatrical runs for awards consideration or special events. Even Glass Onion got only a week in roughly 600 theaters back in 2022, despite a star-studded cast and a built-in audience. Imagine how much further that run could have gone if given the opportunity. However, theaters understandably haven't loved booking films that audiences can stream almost immediately, and big chains have sometimes refused to play them at all.

The streamer isn't promising a nationwide theatrical release for every original movie, though. Sarandos is clearly talking about choosing the right approach for each film. According to him, specific movies will player better than others:

On one end of the spectrum is La Bola Negra, Train Dreams last year that could have played in the theaters for six months and it wouldn’t have impacted, it would have done net positive on Netflix... Those kind of art house films play like that. And then the other end is the kind of four-quad family rewatch movie, so we said let’s take those two and treat them different.

The KPop sequel doesn't have an announced theatrical window yet, but a promise of a wide release is something fans of original blockbuster movies and event films can look forward to, while smaller projects can still thrive on streaming. It’s the best of both worlds.

I love being able to throw on a movie with my streaming subscriptions, but I also love sitting in a packed theater when everybody reacts to the same moment. If Netflix can make room for both experiences, I'll happily buy a ticket before pressing play at home.

Narnia: The Magician's Nephew hits the 2027 movie calendar on February 12, 2027, before landing on streaming in April. Also, stay tuned for updates on the highly anticipated KPop Demon Hunters sequel.

#3556. Walter Koenig Wanted A Star Trek: The Next Generation Role That Wasn't Pavel Chekov

While "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is set 100 years after "Star Trek: The Original Series," some "TOS" cast members appeared on the show. In the pilot, "Encounter at Farpoint," a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) visits the Enterprise-D and gives Data (Brent Spiner) some sound advice: "You treat her like a lady, she'll always bring you home."

Later, in the Season 3 episode "Sarek," Mark Lenard guest-starred as the eponymous Vulcan ambassador, also known for being Spock's (Leonard Nimoy) father. Spock himself then appeared in the Season 5 two-parter "Reunification," where it's revealed he's moved to Romulus to try and bring the Vulcans and Romulans together again as one. After that, the former Enterprise Chief Engineer Scotty (James Doohan) appeared in the "Next Generation" Season 6 Episode "Relics," having spent several decades trapped in a Dyson sphere. Finally, Captain Kirk (William Shatner) teamed up with Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) in the 1994 spin-off film "Star Trek Generations."

That lineup leaves out George Takei (Sulu), Nichelle Nichols (Uhura), and Walter Koenig (Chekov), who died this past October right before Stewart did. The closest Koenig came to appearing on "The Next Generation" was in "Star Trek: Generations." In a scene set in 2294, Captain Kirk, Scotty, and Chekov attend the maiden voyage of the Enterprise-B. But Koenig had a pitch to appear on "Next Generation," which he shared in the October 1989 issue of "Starlog" magazine:

"I don't want to do a walk-on. I have an idea for an opening moment. Somebody has just come aboard the ship. They're talking about him in general. He turns around and it's [my] face. They say, 'Well, Commander Chekov.' 'No,' I say, 'Lt. Commander Chekov, Pavel Chekov's son.' It's a great opening."

"Star Trek" is no stranger at all to reusing the same actors to play different roles, including across series. Majel Barrett (wife of "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry), who played Nurse Chapel on the original series, also had a recurring part on "Next Generation" as Ambassador Lwaxana Troi, mother of Counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

It's worth noting that Walter Koenig specifically wanted a part worth playing — "Not a walk-on" as he put it. Joining "Star Trek" in Season 2, Chekov was invariably the most overlooked member of the cast. One of his biggest parts in the "Trek" movies was in "Wrath of Khan," and that whole role is built on a continuity error: Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán) and Chekov know each other even though Koenig wasn't part of the "Star Trek" cast during Khan's first appearance, "Space Seed." Koenig later claimed he caught the error but, tellingly, stayed silent to protect his screentime.

Koenig often said he preferred his role on "Babylon 5," a different sci-fi series where he played the sinister psychic Alfred Bester, over playing Chekov because Bester was a much more substantive role. Note that "Starlog" interview was in 1989, years before "Babylon 5," so it's no surprise he was hungry for meaty roles.

"Star Trek: Picard" Season 3 eventually used Koenig's idea to give him a voiceover cameo as Anton Chekov, son of Pavel and the Federation's president. ("Anton" doubles as a homage to the late Anton Yelchin, who played Chekov in the 2009 "Star Trek" film and its sequels.) Sadly, though, that sort of Easter Egg cameo is exactly the kind of appearance Koenig had said he didn't want to settle for back in 1989.

#3555. How Elizabeth Taylor’s Childhood and Career Were Defined by Her Overbearing Mother

Elizabeth Taylor, like many other actors of her time, experienced the demands of Hollywood from a very young age. Her parents could never have imagined on February 27, 1932, just how much their newborn baby would achieve artistically. Sooner rather than later, however, they recognized her potential. Although she spent most of her life in Southern California in the heart of the movie industry, Taylor was born in Hampstead, England, to an American family consisting of her father, Francis Lenn Taylor, her mother, Sara Sothern, and their son, Howard, the movie star’s brother with whom she was close. They didn’t remain in Great Britain long, returning to the United States in 1939, shortly before World War II.

Sara Sothern with her children, Elizabeth and Howard Taylor.

The family sailed from London to New York and then settled in Los Angeles. By then, Taylor already had some experience in the performing arts, as she had been taking ballet lessons since she was just three years old. She made her debut in a recital that same year. Once in California, the father of the violet-eyed legend opened an art gallery featuring works imported from the UK. This would turn out to be an important step that brought the Taylors into the world of Hollywood. As biographer Alexander Walker would recount in Elizabeth: The Life of Elizabeth Taylor (Grove Press), the space “opened many doors for the Taylors, leading them directly into the society of money and prestige.”

Despite their differences, mother and daughter grew closer as they matured.

Sothern, the mother of this acting prodigy, saw her daughter as the perfect excuse to live the dream she didn’t fulfill because she was focused on caring for her family. If she couldn’t pursue an acting career, her daughter would. Seeing the effect that Taylor’s beauty had on others, Sothern set out to introduce her to people in the film industry. “Elizabeth Taylor probably wouldn’t have been an actress if it hadn’t been for her mother,” notes actor George Hamilton in the BBC documentary Elizabeth Taylor: Rebel Superstar. In this same documentary, Liz herself can be heard saying in an old recording: “My mother was an actress, but then she married my father, and he didn’t want her to be one, so she gave it up. I think she lived her life through me.”

Kate Andersen Brower, author of Elizabeth Taylor: The Grit and Glamour of an Icon (Harper Collins), explains that Sothern was behind the scenes trying to control every aspect of her daughter’s life in order to make her famous. This included sending Taylor to the same schools as the children of movie studio executives. Soon, thanks to a meeting with the fiancée of a high-ranking Universal Pictures exec who visited the gallery run by Taylor’s father, Elizabeth made her big-screen debut. Her early Hollywood years were propelled by connections her mother painstakingly built.

In 1949, Elizabeth Taylor and Sara Sothern pose at their home in Beverly Hills.

Taylor’s first movie was There’s One Born Every Minute, filmed when she was only 10 years old. Also starring Carl Switzer, who played Alfalfa in Our Gang, it was not a success, and Universal chose not to extend her option. Andersen Brower quotes the studio’s casting director: “The kid has nothing. Her eyes are too old; she doesn’t have the face of a kid.” Sara persisted, however, and through her husband, she met Sam Marx, a producer working on an MGM film, Lassie Come Home. Taylor would be cast in a small role.

Elizabeth Taylor and her mother in a 1948 photo taken in London.

Its success paved the way for another milestone in Taylor’s early career. At age 12, she landed the role of Velvet Brown in National Velvet, alongside Mickey Rooney and Angela Lansbury. Released in December 1944, it grossed almost $6 million worldwide, making it one of MGM’s top films of that period. Taylor signed a new contract with the studio, though she later complained about how she was treated by its head, Louis B. Mayer.

Elizabeth Taylor helps her mother prepare hot dogs and hamburgers at their home in Los Angeles in 1947.

At the same time, her father was both astonished by and jealous of his teenage daughter’s success. An alcoholic and physically abusive, on one occasion he punched her in the jaw, and for the rest of her life, she suffered from TMJ, or lockjaw. Andersen Brower writes, “She explained it away—as she always had—saying that her father was embarrassed that Taylor was the breadwinner of the family and that he felt emasculated.”

Sothern was a practicing Christian (though she was also interested in Judaism, which may have contributed to Taylor’s decision to convert to that religion so that she could marry Eddie Fisher, her fourth husband), and she taught her daughter from an early age that she could not sleep with any man until she was married to him. It’s a view that Taylor appears to have adopted: “Nothing comes off until the ring goes on,” she told gossip columnist Louella Parsons. Sothern, however, had her doubts. Before Taylor married Conrad “Nicky” Hilton in 1950, when she was just 18 years old, Sothern paid a doctor to confirm that her daughter was still a virgin and also to open her hymen to spare her pain during the first time she had sex.

Years later, Taylor would admit that her early years in the film industry were not easy. Her parents spent practically all the money she earned as a child actor. In a 1997 interview with Barbara Walters on 20/20, she described her childhood as “lonely.” She once confided to her close friend George Hamilton that she just wanted “to be a little girl again,” to relive those years that she never got to enjoy.

Originally published by Vanity Fair Spain.

#3554. The Kindle Click Is the One Accessory Readers Have Been Waiting For

The Kindle is the world's most ubiquitous e-reader, but that's not the same as being the best. Don't get me wrong: Amazon deserves a large share of the credit for bringing e-books into the mainstream, and over the years, the Kindle has consistently offered a top-tier user experience, thanks to both generally good hardware and its integration into the retailer's ecosystem (for better or worse). But the company also rarely innovates in the space, waiting until other players like Barnes & Noble and Boox have tested out new features (like temperature-adjustable lighting and color screens, respectively) before adopting them itself. It's also not shy about dictating to customers what they can and can't do with their Kindles, from removing the ability to directly download copies of their e-books to limiting support for third-party accessories.

One such accessory has been maddeningly absent from the Kindle for years, despite the device having the technology in place to support it: a Bluetooth remote control (all Kindles released since 2018 support Bluetooth for connecting wireless headphones, but only wireless headphones).

A few years ago, third-party e-reader remotes became a big thing on BookTok, prompting competitors like Kobo and Boox to release their own versions of the peripherals. But with the Kindle's Bluetooth protocol locked down, Kindle owners were mostly out of luck; their only option a third-party clip-on accessory that attaches to the side of the device and manually taps the display at the press of a remote button—far from ideal, as they can only turn pages in one direction and block a portion of the screen.But finally, Amazon has seen the light and made its own Bluetooth remote, which it has dubbed the Kindle Click. More importantly, it has opened up the Bluetooth protocol within the Kindle firmware so it can connect to the accessory in the first place—though it will only work on Kindles from 2024 or later. (It pairs well with the new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, no pun intended.)

If you've never used one before, it can be a bit confusing to consider why someone would want a remote for their Kindle—why bother fussing with an extra device when you can just tap the screen or press a button? But for certain scenarios, it really does make sense.

Most practically, a remote can allow you to turn pages in circumstances where holding the e-reader itself is less than convenient, as when you're exercising: Holding a Kindle in your hands is tough when you're on an elliptical, and the words can bounce around too much if you're trying to use a spin bike while gulping down a few chapters of Yesteryear. But if you can prop the e-reader onto the machine's handlebars or a nearby surface, you can turn pages easily without missing a step.

Then there's the coziness factor: Reading under a big blanket in winter is one of the coziest activities I can imagine, but if you have to keep your arms outside of the blanket to turn pages on your Kindle, well, that's going to have an impact on how cozy you feel. (This is a real problem!) But what if you could comfortably arrange the device within your line of sight and turn pages while keeping your hands ensconced within your weighted throw? Some readers are willing to spend multiple tens of dollars to achieve this level of coziness.

How many dollars? In the case of the Kindle Click, around 35 of them (plus tax). Though that may seem like kind of a lot for a simple little remote with two basic functions and four buttons, it's just $5 more than the admittedly much cuter Boox Tappy. Speaking of which, while the new firmware update will also allow the Kindle to support cheaper third-party alternatives, there's no guarantee they will work as well.

So how does the Kindle Click work? Pretty seamlessly: You press and hold one button on the remote to put it in pairing mode. You open up the Settings menu on your 2024 or later Kindle and tap Accessories (you may need to perform a software update, if you aren't seeing that option). You tap Kindle Click in the resulting list to pair it. Once paired, the remote seems to connect to the Kindle automatically if the two devices are nearby and both powered up, provided you keep the latter's Bluetooth functionality turned on; you don't have to manually pair them every time.

That's pretty much it: Once you've opened a book, you can now turn pages with a button press (you can map which of the big grey buttons moves pages forward or back to suit your preferences). The volume-like buttons on the side can be used to adjust the brightness of the front light. You can't use the remote to navigate around the device or open a different book, so choose your reading material carefully before you enter your cocoon.

While the Click definitely works as advertised, Amazon could have been a bit more creative with its functionality. The Boox Tappy, for example, can switch between modes so it can be used to jump backward and forward between tracks in an audiobook or scroll pages in a web browser. While the Kindle can't display websites, it definitely supports audiobooks, but you can't use the Click to jump between chapters or adjust the volume while listening to an Audible book; these both seem like no-brainers to me.And while being able to turn the brightness up or down is nice, why not let the remote control the warmth settings as well, either through enabling different modes (like the Tappy) or via a combination of button presses? I'm not an engineer, so I don't know how complicated it would be to get that to work, but Amazon employs a lot of them, and I bet they could figure it out.

#3553. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Reveals The Two Beloved Scenes He Wanted To Cut From The Movie [Exclusive]

It's no surprise that "Project Hail Mary" became such a box office success in 2026. There's so much to like about Chris Lord and Phil Miller's adaptation of Andy Weir's 2021 novel, from the performances and humor to the stunning visuals. It turns out, however, that one of the most breathtaking shots in the entire movie was deemed unnecessary by Weir himself, who also suggested cutting a scene in which we get an insight into the headspace of Sandra Hüller's Eva Stratt.

The first cut of "Project Hail Mary" was four hours long and received brutal feedback. Thankfully Lord and Miller were ultimately able to prune the film to a more lean (but still considerable) 2 hours and 36 minutes. But it seems they didn't get there by listening to Weir. The author spoke to /Film about his involvement in the editing process, which seems to have consisted of attempting to cut scenes which went on to become some viewers' favorite moments in the entire film. Thankfully, Weir seems to be aware of his questionable directing judgement.

"What I've learned from the process of 'PHM' is that I belong writing novels and I should never be a director," he said. "Because there were scenes in the movie that I argued we should cut that are people's favorite scenes." When asked for examples, the writer pointed to the moment Ryan Gosling's Ryland Grace carries out a space walk as the Hail Mary passes through the Petrova Line. In this moment the music swells and suddenly Grace is surrounded by a glowing pink dust in one of the movie's most spectacular scenes. Turns out, Weir wanted it gone.

Given the original cut was unwieldy to say the least, Phil Lord and Chris Miller ended up with a bunch of "Project Hail Mary" deleted scenes. Thankfully, one of them wasn't the moment in which Ryland Grace finds himself immersed in a cloud of astrophage, the fictional light-absorbing alien microbe that threatens to destroy Earth's sun. The scene in question is a beautiful sequence, and one that played particularly well on the big screen. For Andy Weir, however, it was sort of pointless in terms of the overall narrative.

The author told /Film that he suggested cutting the entire thing: "First off, the [scene] where [Grace is] having a moment and you can see all the astrophage around him and there's beautiful music playing. I'm like, 'Yeah, cool, but we should cut it because it doesn't advance the plot.'" That's technically true, but there's so much more to the scene that makes it worthwhile. At first, however, Weir couldn't see that, and had a scientific reason as to why the entire sequence didn't make any sense. "It's like he's just sitting out there and he wouldn't be able to see that anyway," he continued. "He can't see infrared. So this doesn't even make sense. This is dumb. We should get rid of it."

Predictably, this gorgeous shot — which as revealed in an IMAX Instagram account video was mostly captured in camera using actual infrared lights and some ingenious on-set contraptions — quickly became a fan-favorite moment. "So many people are like, 'What a beautiful scene. I love this scene,'" added Weir. "So that's why I don't belong as a director, and I should be kept away from any editing bays."

Andy Weir wasn't only convinced the astrophage sequence should be cut from "Project Hail Mary." He also didn't see the point in the scene wherein Sandra Hüller's Eva Stratt, head of the Petrova Taskforce and director of Project Hail Mary, sings karaoke. "I wanted to get rid of the karaoke scene," said Weir. "[...] again, I'm like, 'Guys, we're running long. This is a long movie, and we're just going to have Stratt singing karaoke, which seems a little iffy for the character of Stratt that I had in mind anyway. Let's cut it.'" According to the writer, he immediately faced pushback. "They're like, 'Hell no, we're not cutting it. This is awesome,'" he continued. "Everyone who watched the movie agrees it's awesome. So I mean, this is a recurring pattern for me."

Interestingly enough, this now popular "Project Hail Mary" scene wasn't originally in the movie, but the directors found a way to add it. That's a good thing, as it serves as a succinct way to sum up Stratt's inner turmoil over sending a man to certain death in order to save the world.

Interestingly enough, it seems this wasn't the first time Weir has been proved wrong when it comes to his initial take on movie adaptations of his novels. The author revealed that when he first saw the cover art for the 2015's adaptation of his book "The Martian" he wasn't impressed. "I'm like, 'I don't like it,'" he recalled. "Then it won awards for the astronaut falling backwards in the red dust. It was [...] evocative, everybody agreed, 'What an amazing cover. They did such a great job.' So I should just not be put in charge of anything that's visual."

Following Patrick Stewart's death, I'm still wrestling with the fact that the beloved actor is no longer with us. At the same time, though, I've also been enjoying the sweet and interesting anecdotes shared by those who've worked with him. With that, I was shocked to read a recently resurfaced story about Wil Wheaton apologizing to Stewart. It turned out the former child actor had some guilt about his behavior on the set of Star Trek: The Next Generation, and I'm not at all surprised to hear how Stewart responded.

The apology apparently came shortly after the end of production on 2002's Star Trek: Nemesis, which Wheaton was originally in before getting cut from the movie. Wheaton wrote in his book Just A Geek that he apologized to Stewart for his cocky behavior on the set of The Next Generation. After admitting he'd "been a dick" during filming, Wheaton wrote that the Picard actor said the following (via Star Trek Fan Group):

Wil, my dear, you were a teenager. We all understood… I wasn't thrilled about working with a child, but working with you was a great pleasure.

It's worth remembering that when Star Trek: The Next Generation first started, Wheaton was the biggest star of the bunch. The majority of audiences knew him through Rob Reiner's 1986 coming-of-age drama, Stand By Me, while Stewart and others were relative unknowns. This, paired with alleged emotional abuse at home, led Wheaton to have an arrogant attitude on set.

Wil Wheaton wouldn't open up about any of that until long after his time working on The Next Generation, and at this point, he's spoken about it at length. As Wheaton previously explained, the TNG cast was there for him when he felt his parents weren't, and he also saw Patrick Stewart as a father figure.

Stewart wrote about Wheaton on the set of TNG in his own memoir, Making It So. While the actor admitted feeling some annoyance at the young actor having such bravado, he ultimately realized it stemmed from his own insecurities as a lead in his breakout television role:

To me, he initially came off as cocky. But as I examined my feelings, I realized that they were not really about Wil or some notion that he should know his place as a juvenile actor — they reflected my own vulnerability. In those first weeks, I wished I had Wil’s confidence.

Wheaton shared a sweet throwback photo of him and Patrick Stewart shortly after news of the latter's death broke. It's great to know that, despite feeling like a "dick" for how he acted, Wheaton has such fond memories of that time and holds such a deep reverence for all of his cast members.

Stewart's death feels like a capstone on a year in which Star Trek's 60th anniversary has felt like a bittersweet celebration. His passing came just on the heels of fans mourning Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original series.

Take those two massive losses and the fact that there are no Star Trek shows in active development, and it's been a bit of a downer year. However, there is a movie in development as well as growing optimism that while Trek is in a valley, it may peak once again in the future. At present, though, I'm content with honoring Patrick Stewart for his contributions to Trek and for his character as human being.

Readers needing Star Trek in their lives can always stream the series on Paramount+, or for free over on Pluto TV. I've been streaming TNG in the wake of Stewart's death and have had a blast watching him in action.

#3551. 10 Hacks Every Fitbit Edge User Should Know

The Fitbit Edge really hits a sweet spot for anyone who wants a minimalist fitness tracker but still wants a screen to tell the time and display workout data. Here are my tips on how to get the most out of it, including hidden features and surprising ways to use the device.

It’s not very obvious from the watch or the app, but you can switch watch faces—and if you use the app on your phone, you can change color schemes and sometimes even complications.

On the watch, long-press the middle of the watch face. This brings up a carousel of the faces you’ve selected in the app. The last screen in the carousel gives you a button to bring up the watch face library on your phone. This is the quickest way to open it, but you can also go to your device settings in the app.

From here, tap All Clocks and browse the available faces. Once you’ve installed a face you like, tap Customize to choose a color scheme and select which complications appear (like your steps for the day, or the weather). Sadly, the share button doesn’t seem to work—it sends a broken link to the old Fitbit website—but it’s a nice idea.

The Fitbit Edge is built with the assumption that you’ll want the side button on the right. But if you wear other jewelry or watches with it, or if you wear it low on your wrist and find that flexing your hand pushes the button, you can change this.

Just go into your device settings in the Google Health app, tap Device preferences, and then change Tracker orientation to put the button on the left instead of the right. This turns the display upside down, so take off your watch and turn it around so you can see it properly again.

The AI-powered Health Coach is both the best and the worst thing about the Google Health app. Fortunately, you can turn it off. What’s better, Google added a feature that lets you turn off the unprompted insights while still having the AI available when you need it.

Tap your profile picture in the app, then Google Health Settings, then Coaching, and select No Coach Insights. The chatty summaries (and notifications) will stop popping up throughout the day, but you can always hit the Ask Coach button if you have a question or if you want to use AI-powered food logging or workout logging.

The workout app on the Fitbit Edge is pretty minimal and can’t be customized, but it is possible to get more information during your workouts. Swipe down from the top of your Fitbit Edge screen, and tap the icon that looks like a wifi heart. This turns on heart-rate broadcasting.

Then go into the Strava app, hit Record to start a workout, and swipe up from the bottom of the screen to see workout options. Select the Fitbit Edge as your heart rate sensor, and now your phone can track your workout using heart rate data from the Fitbit. The Strava app gives you a lap button and can show you the time for your previous laps; it also shows you a map of where you are and where you’ve been.

Fitbit devices have always been a little over-enthusiastic about counting steps compared to other wearables, and they know it. Hand and arm movements can mistakenly contribute to your step count, but there’s a way to adjust the device’s sensitivity. If you wear the device on your dominant hand (say, on your right hand if you’re right-handed), go into Device preferences on the phone app and set your Wrist preference to dominant.

If you already wear the device on your non-dominant hand, you may still want to use this hack. Wear it on your left hand (if you’re right-handed) and still change your preference to dominant. This will tell the Fitbit to slightly undercount your steps.

The Fitbit Edge can use its own built-in GPS, or it can use the GPS that is built into your phone. By default, it will switch sources automatically based on what it thinks the best option will be.

But you can change this. Go into Device preferences again, and choose GPS settings. If you always carry your phone with you, and you’d prefer to save battery on your Fitbit, tell the device to always use your phone's GPS. On the other hand, if you want the Fitbit to handle its own GPS without piggybacking on your phone all the time, tell it to use the built-in GPS instead.

If your phone is an older one, switching to the built-in GPS will probably give you more accurate distance and pace than using the default switching. If your phone is newer, choose based on which device you want to preserve battery.

At the same time as the Fitbit Edge came out, Google made it so that the app can work with multiple Fitbits. If you sometimes like to have a screen on your wrist, but sometimes you don’t, you can swap seamlessly back and forth between the Edge and the Air (and a Pixel watch, should you happen to have one of those as well). No extra steps are necessary—just set up both of them, and wear whichever you feel like at any given moment.

Small screens can mean less visibility, but there is a setting that helps. In Device preferences, select Magnification and toggle it on. Now, triple-tapping the screen (three quick taps with one finger) enlarges what you’re looking at. You can use your finger to move the image around the screen to see different parts—for example, to get a better look at the number under the step count complication on some watch faces.

In this part of the app, you can also choose whether the magnification gesture gives you a 2x or a 3x zoom. To zoom out, just triple-tap the screen again.

The charger for the Fitbit Edge (like that for the Pixel Watch) is incredibly fast. If your watch is running low on charge and you don't have time to wait for it to charge, just put it on the charger for five minutes. Google says this gives it enough juice for a full day, and that matches my experience. Just now, three minutes of charging brought the device from 31% up to 41%.

If your Fitbit Edge tends to last about a week, you'll need about 15% to get through a full day. I like to use the always-on display (AOD), so I only get about three days per charge. If you're using the five-minute trick because you're low on battery, turn off the AOD if you have it enabled, and you'll get through the rest of the day. But if you always have the AOD enabled, you may be able to get into the habit of charging your Fitbit for about five minutes every day—maybe 10 every now and then—and never have to walk away from it for an hour like you would with most wearables.

I don’t follow the workouts the AI coach gives me, but it can be nice to have a record of what I did. So I’ll take a screenshot of my workout in Hevy, or a photo of my training journal, and show it to the Coach.

You can do this from the Ask Coach button in the bottom right corner of the app. Tell it which workout it should attach the exercises to (for example, “log this for my strength training session from last night”), and it will fill in the exercises in that workout summary. You can view past workouts in the Fitness tab.

#3550. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3549. Gene Roddenberry Wrote An Unmade Pilot For A Non-Sci-Fi Show About A Classic Hero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

In David Alexander's book "Star Trek Creator: The Authorized Biography of Gene Roddenberry," it was revealed that back in 1967, Roddenberry wrote a pilot episode for a Robin Hood TV series called — what else? — "Robin Hood."

1967 was when the second season of "Star Trek" was airing, and it's worth remembering that the show wasn't a crackerjack hit at the time. "Star Trek" didn't find mass audiences until after it had been canceled in 1969 and began appearing regularly in syndication. As such, Roddenberry was likely working on other projects constantly, not necessarily putting all his eggs in the USS Enterprise, so to speak. We've actually ranked all of Gene Roddenberry's non-"Star Trek" projects, from the military drama "A.P.O. 923" to posthumous projects like "Earth: Final Conflict" and "Andromeda." Roddenberry is known today as the "Star Trek" guy, but back in the '60s, he was eager to explore many different kinds of shows and genres.

Little is known about his "Robin Hood" pilot, although Alexander's biography does contain a letter that Roddenberry wrote to "a friend" about the script he was working on. Roddenberry wanted to make a revisionist version of Robin Hood, adding a modern edge to the character. He wanted to rid Robin Hood of his traditional corniness and fresh-faced heroism, as one might see in Michael Curtiz's legendary 1938 feature film "The Adventures of Robin Hood." Several decades after Curtiz's movie, Roddenberry wanted to make an updated Robin Hood wherein he was meant to be something of an antihero.

The writer was seemingly taking the "dark and gritty" path, decades before that became trendy in Hollywood. As for things like casting, direction, and individual stories, we can only speculate.

In the letter mentioned above, Gene Roddenberry was clearly still hammering out his "Robin Hood" script, and was asking for some input. He wrote:

"By a strange coincidence, your letter came at a time in which I was preparing a pilot in the 'Robin Hood' area, and was at the moment wrestling with the problem of hero and antihero. I realized that Robin Hood could not succeed in today's market if he were the wimpy 'St. George and England!'-type hero and yet how far could I go in the other direction without completely destroying the value of the legendary figure? I think I have the problem solved, but it would be fun if you were here so I could sit down over coffee and discuss the questions involved."

These seem like the kinds of questions that many makers of modern reboots might ask themselves, as we live in an entertainment marketplace that is lousy with pop figures that are many decades old. Superman and Batman, both created in the 1930s, are still being refreshed and rebooted to this day, for instance. Heck, even "Star Trek" itself, now 60 years old, is also constantly undergoing changes and reboots, with the most recent season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" coming out in 2026.

Sadly, the above passage seems to be all the information the world has about Gene Roddenberry's "Robin Hood." The script is not readily available online (as far as I was able to find), and there are seemingly no outlines or treatments around, either.

"Star Trek" and Robin Hood did eventually cross over, albeit in an oblique way, and it happened early enough in "Star Trek" history that Gene Roddenberry was able to see it before his death in October of 1991.

In the "Star Trek: The Next Generation" episode "QPid," the impish trickster deity Q (John de Lancie) witnesses that Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) is experiencing a pinched relationship with Vash (Jennifer Hetrick), a woman he hooked up with on his last vacation. To give Picard an opportunity to express some old-fashioned chivalry, Q magically teleports Picard and his senior staff into a living, breathing version of Sherwood Forest, with Picard playing the role of Robin Hood. Q becomes the Sheriff of Nottingham, and Vash becomes the imprisoned Maid Marian whom Robin Hood must rescue.

It's one of the most whimsical episodes of "Next Generation," and is often pointed to by Trekkies as an example of how silly the franchise can sometimes become. (That's a gentler way of saying that some fans have written missives with titles like "QPid is the stupidest episode in human history.") Personally, I think the humor works, as it's a good contrast with the ordinarily stern and serious "Next Generation" characters who typically endeavor to remain professional at all times. The comedy episodes of "Star Trek" are great, but the franchise can occasionally go overboard.

The script for "QPid" is credited to Ira Steven Behr and Randee Russell, so it's unlikely that Roddenberry contributed to it in any significant way. But one can hope that it was the final realization of Roddenberry's Robin Hood fantasies that begun 24 years earlier.

#3548. 10 Hacks Every iCloud User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you accidentally delete or overwrite a file or contact that's synced to iCloud, you can restore it from the Recovery portal on iCloud.com. This feature works across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Contacts, Mail, Photos, Notes, and Reminders, as well as Drive, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote. When you restore an old version of your data, the current version is archived so you can revert back if you change your mind. Deleted files can be recovered within 30 days.

One benefit of an iCloud+ subscription is Apple's Hide My Email, which allows you to create unique, random aliases to keep your real email address private. These addresses forward to your primary inbox, and replies appear to come from the alias rather than your personal email. There's no limit on how many Hide My Email addresses you can generate, so you can use them for newsletter sign-ups, online shopping, and any other credential you may want to deactivate if you start getting spammed. Hide My Email is compatible with Safari, Mail, Apple Pay, and some third-party apps.

Apple supports legacy contacts for Apple Accounts, meaning you can designate someone to receive access to your data—including photos, files, messages, and backups—after your death. This allows you to use iCloud as a digital vault for storing documents and other important information that can be securely passed down. (Note that legacy contacts will not receive iCloud Keychain data like passwords and passkeys, so you'll need another way to share this information if desired.) To designate a legacy contact, go to Settings > [Your Name] > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact and follow the prompts. That person will need the access key you generate and your death certificate to take over your accounts.

Apple's Family Sharing allows up to six users to share a single iCloud+ subscription while maintaining separate Apple Accounts. This means that each user has their own private vault for photos, documents, and backups while gaining access to premium features and a lot more storage overall. iCloud+ offers plans from 50 GB to 12 TB of storage. Family Sharing likely makes the most sense if you can fill most or all of the seats and/or already pay for or plan to use close to the limit of one of the higher-cost plans (compared to each individual paying for their own subscription).

Sorting through photos and adding them to a shared album after a vacation can feel like a huge project—but iCloud can do this work for you in real time if your friends and family have iPhones with Bluetooth enabled and are logged into their Apple Accounts. Set up an iCloud Shared Photo Library in the Photos app under Collections > [Your account] > Shared Library and add up to five participants. Then, from Shared Library, tap Sharing from Camera > Share Automatically. If you take photos when other album participants are nearby, they will be uploaded to the shared album.

If you want to text a large photo or video to someone who doesn't have an Apple Account and access to iCloud photos without compressing the file, you can create a temporary link that gives them access to view and download the file for 30 days. This also allows you to share multiple files with a single link rather than sending them individually, and you can revoke access whenever you'd like. To create an iCloud link, open an image, tap Share, and select Copy iCloud Link.

Note that as of iOS 27 and macOS 27, Apple now supports adding Windows and Android users to iCloud Shared Albums. However, temporary links are still a good solution if you don't want to share whole albums.

iCloud's backup feature will automatically back up your iPhone periodically so you can restore your data if your device is lost or stolen. This includes information that isn't regularly synced to iCloud storage, like settings and app organization. You can disable cellular backups to restrict backups to wifi only—or you can turn on low data mode, which will allow for backing up over your cellular connection except when speeds are low, or your data is capped. Low data mode could also save battery by not straining a slow connection. You can enable low data mode for cellular via Settings > Cellular > Cellular Data Options > Data Mode.

If your Apple device is backing up to iCloud, you could regularly bump up against your storage limit, especially if you aren't paying for a large amount of space. One way to mitigate this is to cut down what gets backed up, which you can do at the app level. If you have apps you don't use regularly or don't need data from, you can disable them from your iCloud backups. Go to your Apple account in the Settings app and tap iCloud > Storage > Backups > [This iPhone] to manage app backups.

If you sync tons of photos and files to iCloud along with device backups, you may find yourself hitting the storage cap. But you don't necessarily have to buy more storage space, nor are you stuck manually deleting items one by one. Instead, go to Settings > [Your Account] > iCloud > Recommended For You to find suggestions for freeing up storage space. This may include deleting inactive backups or reviewing your files or photos and videos, which are categorized by duplicates, screenshots, and videos (the content you're most likely to be able to offload). If you don't see these options under Recommended For You, go back to iCloud > Storage and select the app you want to clean up. Finally, check what's included in your device backups, and disable any apps you don't need under iCloud > Storage > Backups.

While the 1976 film Rocky tells the story of an underdog fighter, the biopic about the making of Rocky reveals the equally fascinating underdog story behind the Oscar-winning film's development. Through Peter Farrelly's I Play Rocky, audiences see see the inspirational story chronicling young Sylvester Stallone's aim to play the lead boxer in the film (which he wrote). As for the real Stallone's thoughts on the film, he admitted to having been ready to be “hypercritical” of it. However, that changed after he saw the film.

In I Play Rocky, Anthony Ippolito plays young Sylvester Stallone, and he's the spitting image of the Rocky icon. Based on the trailers alone, Ippolito completely nails the Rambo actor’s voice and swagger. Still, I'd imagine that the biggest stamp of approval would come from Stallone himself. After the Cobra actor saw the biopic, he admitted to CBS Mornings that he was somewhat reluctant about the 2026 movie release, but even he eventually gave into it:

It was very surreal because at first I was gonna be hypercritical, like that's me. I don't walk like that. But I did walk like that. I did talk like that. I'm realizing this guy did a magnificent job, and I actually forgot I was me, and I sat back and watched the movie like the audience.

I can understand Stallone's natural inclination to be “hypercritical,” especially given this is his story being told. It must be trippy for him to see another actor channel his voice and mannerisms and emulate his role as Rocky Balboa. However, it’s a relief that the Expendables star has high praise for the biopic and Ippolito himself. I know I keep harping on it, but seriously, it's hard to deny how accurately Ippolito takes on Stallone's baritone voice and rugged physical presence.

The Tulsa King star isn’t the only one loving I Play Rocky. Early reviews were quick to give praise, with many saying Ippolito fully absorbed Stallone so much that someone could forget it was a performance. Ryan Gosling also gave his stamp of approval, telling lead female actress Annasophia Robb how much he loved it. With all of these rave reviews, I’d say Stallone is right on the mark.

During his CBS Mornings interview, Stallone also said that if Ippolito didn’t endure a concussion during his I Play Rocky training, then he “didn’t try hard enough” with the role. Well, Ippolito said -- after being shown the footage of Stallone's chat -- that he may not have gotten a concussion, but he did get “a little banged up” training at the historic Gleason’s Gym. So, we can’t say the Offer actor didn’t put in the grunt work like Stallone did when he first played “The Italian Stallion.”

It's not small feat for an actor to play such a recognizable star like Sylvester Stallone, so Anthony Ippolito deserves some serious credit. And, if Stallone felt like he was watching himself while watching the movie, I have a feeling audiences will also be engaged.

Right now, I Play Rocky is playing in limited release, but the film will open nationwide on November 20. Also, fans can also relive Balboa's exploits by streaming the Rocky movies with a Paramount+ subscription.

#3546. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3544. Sarah Michelle Gellar Passed On A Martin Scorsese Movie Because Of Buffy The Vampire Slayer

Martin Scorsese's filmography is filled with films that took decades to get off the ground. By the 21st Century, Scorsese had settled into a statesman of cinema stature, and (to the joy of cinephiles everywhere) he's cashed in decades of chits and clout to deliver passion projects like 2016's "Silence," 2019's "The Irishman," and 2002's "Gangs of New York."

The latter draws on a 1928 nonfiction book, "The Gangs of New York" by Herbert Ashbury, that tracked the history of New York's organized crime from the 19th to 20th Century. As the book and movie show, that tale is intertwined with how Irish and Italian immigrants settled in New York went from spat-upon outsiders to true Americans.

Scorsese read "The Gangs of New York" in 1970 and acquired the rights to make a movie out of it in 1979, but development took over 20 years. It's no surprise that in that time, Scorsese's plans for "Gangs of New York" evolved. The final film — set mostly in the 1860s — is an epic revenge narrative starring Leonardo DiCaprio as the fictional Amsterdam Vallon and Daniel Day-Lewis as a fictionalized version of real New York gang leader Bill the Butcher (named William Cutting in the film, but William Poole in real life).

One change close to the finish line was the casting of female lead Jenny, Amsterdam's love interest and a thief in Bill's organization. Sarah Michelle Gellar, a star thanks to her role on the then contemporary TV series "Buffy the Vampire Slayer," was considered for the part. However, her commitments to "Buffy" (which was in its fifth season when "Gangs of New York" shot from December 2000 to March 2001) meant she couldn't sign on. Jenny went on to be played by Cameron Diaz instead.

Now, Cameron Diaz wasn't Martin Scorsese's first choice understudy for Jenny. He was also interested in casting Sarah Polley, but now-disgraced producer Harvey Weinstein insisted on a bigger name. (Weinstein was the reason Scorsese made sure the film debuted as his director's cut, too.) So, Diaz, a comedy starlet after 1998's "There's Something About Mary," won the part. Her turn as Jenny has since been called one of the worst performances in any Scorsese movie.

Now, Jenny is a pretty thankless role (she's a fairly typical love interest character), but Diaz is still out of her depth. She can't keep her Irish accent down, and like Leonardo DiCaprio as Amsterdam, her wooden performance stands out all the more next to Daniel Day-Lewis' show-stopping turn as Bill the Butcher. Granted, most actors will have trouble outshining Day-Lewis (his latest film "Anemone" at least gives him a worthy scene partner in Sean Bean), but in "Gangs of New York," it's not even a competition.

That's what makes it sting to know that Sarah Michelle Gellar turned down the role. She's a great actor who carried seven seasons of "Buffy the Vampire Slayer" on her back. She might've still not stolen the show from Day-Lewis, but I feel confident saying she'd probably out-charisma DiCaprio's stilted Amsterdam and make Jenny a livelier character. Moreover, you can't help but wonder if Gellar's career could've soared even higher if she had a Scorsese movie on her resume.

But Gellar doesn't regret it. In 2023, she told The Guardian that she doesn't worry about the projects she missed out on due to her commitments to "Buffy," not even "Gangs of New York." This "Buffy" and Scorsese fan, though, is always going to feel a little differently.

Some new insider reporting has shed new light on the future of Assassin's Creed

Some new reports regarding the Assassin's Creed series emerged last week, giving us a better idea of what to expect from Ubisoft's flagship series for the rest of the decade. While we learned about two Assassin's Creed titles for the first time, it has also been reported that the development of Assassin's Creed Hexe is taking longer than expected.

On Nov. 6, Ubisoft insider j0nathan posted a YouTube video in which he teased two new Assassin's Creed games. One is codenamed Mars and is reportedly a traditional Assassin's Creed game set in Ancient Rome, the same era in which the show's upcoming Netflix adaptation is set. The other is Assassin's Creed Pocket, a mobile game inspired by Valhalla's Mastery Challenges that will be set in Jerusalem.

It then revealed some more verified information about Assassin's Creed Hexe: While it was expected to be released in 2027, it has internally been pushed back to 2028.

Assassin's Creed Hexe was first teased by Ubisoft in 2022, and is supposed to have a more magical edge and be set in the Holy Roman Empire during the 17th century. While Ubisoft has promised to reveal more about the game next year, we've yet to actually see the game in action. According to Insider Gaming, Hexe's development has "had issues," with several high-level developers exiting Ubisoft during its development.

Insider Gaming now does not expect Hexe to launch until 2028; in turn, it also reports that Mars likely wouldn't be released, or even revealed, until 2029 or 2030 at the earliest. For now, we'll just have to stick to playing Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced.

November 7 actually marked his first official day as co-anchor of Today Saturday alongside Laura Jarrett. Fans had hoped Daly might land the gig, and they seem excited now that he has. They’re not the only ones, as Today shared a video in which Green, Shelton, Kelly Clarkson and Adam Levine all congratulated Daly. Check it out:

It’s so sweet that the Voice coaches would take time to send such supportive messages to Daly, who’s been hosting the reality competition series since its debut in 2011. What’s even funnier to me is that each comment feels on brand for the person sharing it. For instance, I’m not surprised that Clarkson would share such bubbly sentiments:

Carson Daly, congratulations on getting Saturday on Today! People love you. They just want your face all the time. I do.

Of course, Shelton and Daly have long had a friendly rivalry filled with occasional trolling. So, while Shelton’s message to his longtime pal and former co-star is sweet, it also features a couple of funny jabs:

Man, just wanted to drop a line here and say congratulations on the Saturday Today Show. I think you’re going to do an incredible job. I’m not too worried about it, because I know Saturday’s like any other day of the week for you. You’ll be drinking. And I know you’ll do a great job, you’ll feel natural. Maybe because it’s the weekend show, it’ll be more entertainment, not as much breaking news, which is good for you, because I don’t think people take you that seriously anyway. Anyway, buddy, good luck. Love you.

All of these warm thoughts come on the heels of rumors regarding Daly possibly leaving The Voice, on which he also serves as an executive producer. The Daly speculation proved to be correct and incorrect, as he did return for Season 30 but was confirmed to not be hosting Season 31. That latter season is subtitled Celebrity and will not only bring a new format to the franchise but will also see Keke Palmer take over hosting duties from Daly.

Considering Palmer’s presence and the potential for Carson Daly’s role on The Today Show to grow with this new job, it’s hard not to wonder whether he might step away from The Voice for good. Daly himself hasn’t given any indication that he plans to leave, as of this writing. Fans will just have to wait and see how that all plays out but, for now, let’s take a page out of the Voice coaches’ book and congratulate Daly on his new position!
