#3519. All 10 Sauron Forms In The Lord Of The Rings Explained

The great villain of The Lord of the Rings, Sauron has taken many forms over the millennia. Most viewers envision Sauron as a towering presence, with the Eye of Sauron gazing out across Middle-earth. But, of course, Sauron was originally far more than just an eye; in fact, he was a shapeshifter, and that was one of the reasons Sauron endured where other evils like his master Morgoth were defeated. The Rings of Power has exploited this, using Sauron's shapeshifting to surprise viewers (especially in season 1).

J.R.R. Tolkien was, of course, strongly influenced by Christian tradition and his Catholic faith. That meant the Dark Lord was basically a Satan archetype, and the Devil is famously said to appear "as an angel of light" when he wants to. Unsurprisingly, then, Tolkien's villain manifests some shocking guises; here are all the ones you need to knw about.

J.R.R. Tolkien was a devout Catholic, and there are many Biblical themes that filter through into his work. The story of Sauron is rife with Biblical imagery, as his story parallels that of Lucifer Morningstar, the fallen Angel who became Satan, in many ways. This is most evidenced when analyzing Sauron's first form — Mairon, the Maiar. Before Sauron was ever a Dark Lord and embodiment of wickedness, his original form was a Maiar associated with Aule the Smith.

Like the rest of the almost-angelic Maiar, Mairon was created by Ilúvatar as a force for goodness, peace, and order in the world that would eventually become Middle-earth. Prior to his betrayal, downfall, and becoming Sauron, Mairon was fair and handsome, with a preference for order and symmetry. However, it was his inherent disdain for chaos and anything out of place would shape his future and subsequent service to Morgoth, whom he felt shared the same perspective. Sauron would later take similar forms to Mairon during his wanderings in Middle-earth, particularly to gain the confidence and trust of Elves.

After becoming Morgoth's servant, Sauron could no longer appear as Mairon or any truly pure form, and instead resembled Tolkien's description as larger than a man "but not gigantic." Sauron and Morgoth were both powerful but at this time, Sauron's ability to shapeshift was constricted, and while his eyes burned and his presence radiated malice, there was no misconstruing his evil intent to subject Middle-earth to Morgoth's sense of order.

At this point, Tolkien doesn't provide an extensive description of Sauron as an individual, but more as a manifestation of malevolence. He'd already started transcending into the force of Evil that would eventually become the Eye of Mordor. However, it's likely he could still take a physical form of sorts, and this body probably wasn't too dissimilar to the version of Sauron seen in the opening of The Fellowship Of The Ring.

Mairon was forever transformed when he entered the service of Morgoth and betrayed Ilúvatar, though the power he gained came with challenges. He wasn't yet able to maintain a physical presence in the traditional sense as he eventually would, and what's more, his moral downfall meant he could never become Mairon again (at least not outside of visions planted in the eyes of others). While he might not have been able to make himself fair again, Sauron could transform himself into a terrifying werewolf.

Before forging the One Ring and taking the fearsome physical form seen in the war at the end of the Second Age, Sauron could still make himself dangerous in combat. In his earlier years, he often turned into a giant, snarling wolf. Only the High Elves and the Dwarves had the courage to face him when he appeared in this form, and the fortitude to try to best him in combat. As a last line of defense, the Valar used their own wolf to best Sauron — Huan, the wolfhound of Oromë the Hunter.

Judging from J.R.R Tolkien's writings on the earliest centuries of Sauron after entering Morgoth's service (detailed in books like The Silmarillion), Sauron's favored form for direct confrontation was that of the wolf. However, this wasn't the only animal form Sauron could take. The future Great Evil was cunning, and his physical form was malleable. He knew that keeping his enemies on their toes would sew confusion and discord – powerful weapons in a prolonged conflict — and having a variety of different forms was one of many ways he achieved this.

During the many conflicts between Morgoth and the united armies of Men, Elves, and even the Valar, Sauron began to change his appearance to win battles. The wolf may have been the most common shape taken by Sauron and the one the first Elves and Dwarves to resist him saw most, but he became other nightmarishly large animals too. Prior to Morgoth's defeat during the First Age, one of the many other forms Sauron took was a giant serpent.

Sauron is not a vampire, of course. He took the form of one on multiple occasions, but the Lord of Mordor was merely imitating their shape, and at no point in the history of Middle-earth did was he a bloodsucking creature of the night. Vampires do exist in J.R.R Tolkien's mythos, but not in the same sense as Dracula, Nosferatu, or other vampires from pop culture.

In Tolkien's Middle-earth, vampires are large bat-like creatures in service to Morgoth and Sauron, with one in particular, Thuringwethil, being referenced in the annals of Arda. During the travels of Beren and Lúthien recorded in The Silmarillion, it's said that Sauron himself took the form of a vampire on at least one important occasion. However, despite Sauron's propensity to engage in psychological warfare with his foes, his vampire form wasn't to strike fear but to flee Huan.

Sauron was an incredibly dangerous presence on the battlefield, though this wasn't the only reason he became so feared or rose to power so quickly. There are many reasons he earned the moniker Sauron the Deceiver, and this is most evidenced by him taking the form of the human King named Halbrand, or (depending on the occasion) the Elf named Annatar. In order to gain the trust of Celebrimbor in the City of the Elven Smiths and trick him into forging the Rings of Power, Sauron needed a disguise that would not only fool others but be pleasing to the eye.

To do this, he became Annatar "Lord of Gifts". The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power changes the timeline slightly when it comes to this form, and instead has Sauron take the form of Halbrand (played by Charlie Vickers) and pose as a displaced King of the Southlands and deceive Galadriel and the Numenoreans in season 1. By giving the Elves the "gift" of how to bind mithril with other ore, he convinces them to aid their own impending doom.

Sauron's physical form that emerged towards the end of the Second Age of Middle-earth was the first glimpse cinema audiences got of the character in The Lord of the Ring: The Fellowship of the Ring. It's somewhat surprising for many to learn that, of all Sauron's forms, this is one of the shapes taken by the Deceiver that J.R.R Tolkien wrote about the least (and, considering he's an author who famously wrote at least a page describing a single tree on one occasions, this says a lot).

Tolkien doesn't go into great depth about what Sauron looked like underneath his armor after he destroyed Númenor. However, LotR director Peter Jackson gave a visual shape to this form of Sauron. Visually, Jackson wanted Sauron to look impressive and intimidating, and his fearsome appearance seen on the battlefield in front of Mount Doom has made him an iconic cinematic villain. At this point, Sauron's physical form resembled pure evil and darkness beneath the intimidating armour he wore into battle when he was defeated in the Last Alliance of Elves and Men, when Isildur was able to cut the One Ring from his finger.

The Necromancer is one of the most intriguing forms of Sauron, as J.R.R Tolkien didn't initially envision the primary antagonist of The Hobbit to be the same villain that had plagued Middle-earth since the First Age. It wasn't until writing The Lord of the Rings trilogy and integrating The Hobbit with his wider mythos that Tolkien weaved The Necromancer into the canon as a form of Sauron the Deceiver.

After laying dormant for years, Sauron began his restoration in the Third Age, taking a form simply known as The Necromancer. Gandalf began to suspect that the Dark Lord had taken up residency in Dol Guldur, known to many as the Hill of Dark Sorcery but the White Council didn't listen to him about Sauron's return and the sudden concentration of dark energy. This stronghold was not only Sauron's base of operations but Gandalf's eventual prison, and not even Galadriel, Elrond, and Saruman could weaken The Necromancer enough to prevent him from becoming more powerful.

When Sauron is partially restored in the Third Age, he doesn't appear in the sharp, jagged armor from the beginning of Jackson's films, and sends emissaries like the Mouth of Sauron to speak for him. It's easy to presume that, at this point, Sauron is only capable of manifesting in Middle-earth as the Great Eye that sits atop Barad-dûr. However, this isn't technically the case. Sauron could still take a physical form when he needed to during this time, but seems to choose not to.

He is only described briefly by those who have interacted with him, such as when he personally tortured Gollum in 3017, who stated that "he has only four [fingers] on the Black Hand, but they are enough." Sauron was significantly weakened after being defeated by Isildur, so it's entirely possible that he would be vulnerable in a physical body without possession of The One Ring by the time Frodo came to possess it. It's suggested in The Return of the King novel that Sauron would have appeared to claim victory after the War of the Ring had he triumphed, implying that at some point, the Great Eye could have taken a more corporeal form.

Of all the forms of Sauron, it is the Great Eye that most viewers are familiar with due to its iconic presence in The Lord of the Rings movie trilogy. For most of Jackson's Lord of the Rings movies, Sauron appeared as the great lidless, fiery eye whose gaze could penetrate every inch of the ashen volcanic fields of Morder and see far beyond their borders too. Known as the Eye of Sauron, this form of Sauron sat above Barad-dûr, the stronghold of Mordor, tracking the movements of anyone who crossed the shadowlands.

Samwise and Frodo had to be particularly careful moving through Mordor on their way to Mt. Doom because the closer they got to the Eye of Sauron, the more it could sense their presence, and if Frodo ever used the ring that close to the Dark Lord, he would send his Nazgûl after them and, in their weakened state, they would not have survived. Sauron took many forms prior to the events of The Lord of the Rings, but his final one remains the most iconic.

The Lord of the Rings is a multimedia franchise consisting of several movies and a TV show released by Amazon titled The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. The franchise is based on J.R.R. Tolkien's book series that began in 1954 with The Fellowship of the Ring. The Lord of the Rings saw mainstream popularity with Peter Jackson's The Lord of the Rings and The Hobbit trilogies.

#3518. These Sony ANC Headphones Are on Sale for $128 Right Now

It's hard to convince yourself to spend nearly half a grand on premium headphones, like the Sony WH-1000XM6, even if you consider yourself an audiophile. Not everyone can afford those prices, which is why the budget, mid-tier, and premium tiers exist. While the premium 1000XM6 headphones are over three times the price of the mid-tier Sony WH-CH730N, they're not three times as good. The Sony WH-CH730N are $128 (originally $179) right now, the lowest price they've ever been according to price-tracking tools, and they offer an amazing value for your money.

It's pretty impressive what $128 in headphones gets you in 2026. The CH730N uses the same Sony Connect app as the premium headphones; as a result, you get a 10-band slider on the EQ menu, a battery care feature that extends the longevity of your battery life, 50 hours of juice, ANC, Ambient Sound (transparency mode), Multipoint to connect to two devices at once, and Bluetooth 6.0. The Adaptive Sound Control feature can detect your activity (walking, sitting down, loud environment, etc.) and automatically switch the level of ANC and transparency to make your experience as comfortable and seamless as possible.

The microphones are decent and use a feature to isolate your voice in noisy environments. I love that there's an AUX connection to give you the option, which seems to be coming back with newer headphones. The design is light and will feel like plastic, but they are comfortable to wear for long sessions. If you're looking to maximize the quality of headphones you can get for your money, the Sony WH-CH730N offer a pretty compelling option at $128.

#3517. Before Ghost Rider, Nicolas Cage Nearly Played A Very Different Marvel Superhero

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Nicolas Cage is an absolute legend. Along with his Oscar-winning turn in "Leaving Las Vegas" and roles in hits like "National Treasure," he's also played some superheroes in his day. Perhaps most notably, he played Ghost Rider in a pair of films released in 2007 and 2012. This came about years after Cage's "Superman Lives" was canceled. But before he suited up as Johnny Blaze, he almost portrayed another, very different hero from the pages of Marvel Comics.

In a 1997 report from Variety going over the "mania" surrounding Marvel movies in development at that time, it was revealed that Cage was still "firmly" attached to star as "his favorite "Marvel hero," Iron Man. Indeed, more than a decade before Robert Downey Jr. would take on the role as Tony Stark, it was Cage who was being eyed to bring the Marvel Comics hero to life. "Iron Man" became the unlikely superhero that changed Hollywood forever, so Cage taking on the role could have literally rewritten this chapter in cinema history.

At the time, the "Iron man" script was being written by Jeff Vintar ("Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within"), with "Cops" creator John Langley on board to produce alongside Elie Cohn and Stephen Chao. It's unclear who was being eyed to direct or where the project was being set up, but this was just one of many, many Marvel movies in development at the time that never saw the light of day.

As just one example, "Black Panther" was almost made in the '90s with Wesley Snipes, even though he also starred in 1998's "Blade." Mind you, this was ages before the idea of a cinematic universe even existed. That '97 article even mentions a "Hulk" film directed by Joe Johnston ("The Rocketeer") and a "Sliver Surfer" movie, among others.

This was also around the time that director James Cameron was trying to get his "Spider-Man" movie adaptation off the ground. Cameron later called his unmade "Spider-Man" film "the greatest movie I never made."

The point is, there were a lot of superhero films swirling back then that would ultimately never be made. Nicolas Cage was part of that, as his and Tim Burton's "Superman Lives" remains one of the most curious, unrealized pieces of comic book cinema ever conceived. But Cage has been a vocal comic book fan for a very long time and, at least according to Variety at the time, Iron Man was his favorite hero.

It's worth remembering that, back then, Iron Man was far from an A-lister. It wasn't until "Iron Man" director Jon Favreau used a sneaky trick to cast Robert Downey Jr. as Tony Stark, and their ensuing movie became a surprise hit, that he ascended to the A-list. When Cage was eyeing the role, it was for the love of the game, in the hopes of perhaps elevating a character he adored. It didn't pan out. Had it panned out? It could have reshaped Marvel's entire future cinematically.

Instead, Cage's "Ghost Rider" flopped its way to a franchise, with the first movie performing well enough on home media to justify a lower-rent, badly-regarded sequel several years later. It's a shame that Cage didn't get to try his hand at something more befitting his talents in the 2010s, but his unrealized turn as Tony Stark is always going to exist as a curious bit of "What if?" alternate cinema history.

You can grab "Ghost Rider" and "Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance" on DVD from Amazon.

When I was watching Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, a project on the 2026 movie schedule that features a lot of talk about death, I couldn’t help but think about how often some of its stars have died on screen. Specifically, Steve Buscemi has famously kicked the bucket in a ton of projects, and Sam Rockwell has had his fair share of deaths (and kills) too. So, I asked them about all this, and I was shocked that they had very different takes on the matter.

While Steve Buscemi is on the record saying that the on-screen death that amused him most was his death in The Big Lebowski, I asked him who he was most excited to be killed by. He had a pretty great answer too, as he said:

I mean, Tony Soprano. That was a good one. Coen Brothers have done their best, too.

Listen, to die in such a classic TV show like The Sopranos (which you can watch with an HBO Max subscription), and at the hands of Tony Soprano himself, is pretty epic. Plus, as Buscemi mentioned, the Coen Brothers sure have done their best to creatively kill him too. Honestly, it’d be an honor to die on screen at the hands of any of these guys.

However, despite all this, and the fact that Buscemi has died in movies and TV shows what feels like countless times, he’s actually not a huge fan of watching that kind of thing. He brought that up in our conversation when I asked him to reveal something surprising about himself:

I'm pretty squeamish. I don't like watching violence, including my own death scenes. But you know, it's an occupational hazard for me.

Well, while it’s an occupational hazard for him, his Wild Horse Nine co-star, Sam Rockwell, has a totally different take on what it’s like to die on screen.

**Now, beyond this point there are major, and I mean MAJOR, spoilers for Wild Horse Nine. Please continue reading with caution, and go see the movie in theaters. **

Now, ironically, in the critically acclaimed Wild Horse Nine, Sam Rockwell’s character, Lee, is responsible for multiple deaths, including MJ’s, who Steve Buscemi plays, and Chris’ (John Malkovich). However, while the Oscar winner survived this film, he’s died in plenty of other projects, so I asked him about his favorite way he’s died and his favorite person he’s killed. Here’s what he had to say:

Whoa, favorite person I've killed, and favorite movie I've died? I died in Seven Psychopaths. That was pretty fun. Favorite person I've killed is probably John.

Well, notably, while Buscemi called dying on screen an “occupational hazard,” Rockwell was throwing around “fun” as his primary adjective. However, his death in Martin McDonagh’s Seven Psychopaths is objectively “pretty fun”. I mean, it involves a standoff, Rockwell’s Billy getting shot by Woody Harrelson’s Charlie, and one very memorable moment with a Shih Tzu.

Moving on from that, though, he said his favorite person to kill on screen was John Malkovich, which happens in Wild Horse Nine at the very end of the movie. While it’s by no means a fun scene, it is a very meaningful one, and when I asked Malkovich what it was like to be killed by Rockwell, he said:

Well, there you have it, sometimes dying on screen is fun, sometimes it’s great, and other times it's hard to watch. However, no matter how they react to it, all these guys are remarkable actors who are very good at being both alive and dead in the movies.

So, if you’d like to see them do all that, you can catch Wild Horse Nine in theaters now.

#3515. Speedrunners Already Breaking The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Remake

The addition of jumping to The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has enabled a new speedrunning trick

Speedrunners have had their hands on the Nintendo Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for a couple of days now, and some funky tricks have already been discovered. In particular, the remake's addition of a jumping mechanic has enabled new speedrunning tactics that just weren't possible in the Nintendo 64 original or its 3DS remake.

Videos from YouTubers like Kethaldo and Knightpohtayto, as well as Bluesky user Mircacle, show how actor jumping is essentially a glitched super jump that players can do with certain aimable tools in Ocarina of Time. To perform the trick, players have to find a movable object, or "actor," in the game's environments, like a chest or movable tombstone. When standing on it, players then have to shoot, press the lock-on button (ZL by default) before it's done being used, and then jump as soon as the animation ends.

By doing this, Link can jump much higher than he is supposed to. When used at certain parts of Ocarina of Time's levels, it's possible to jump even higher and skip massive swaths of the game. Right now, it's easiest to pull off when using the hookshot, so actor jumps are worth attempting once you get it.

Nintendo has yet to patch this trick out of the remake, so the speedrunning community is avidly taking advantage of it less than a week after the game's launch. Compared to some other speedrunning tricks in the remake, action jumps are very easy to perform, too.

When Nintendo decided to add jumping to Ocarina of Time, I'm not sure this is quite what it had in mind. Regardless, it will be very entertaining to see what new speedrunning tricks emerge and how Nintendo responds to or attempts to fix them, as speedrunners spend even more time playing and breaking the remake.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3513. Steven Spielberg Made Changes To One Of His Sci-Fi Movies Decades After Its Release

Movies are an artform with a uniquely long lifespan. A film can connect with viewers decades later just as much as it did when it was new, perhaps even more so. Cinema is a great cultural time capsule, but it's also evergreen with its heady mixture of thoughts and emotions. The danger, however, lies in feeling that the power of cinema's reach should exceed its grasp.

That's precisely what legendary filmmaker Steven Spielberg learned when revisiting his 1982 smash "E.T. The Extra Terrestrial" for its 20th anniversary in 2002. The opportunity arose at a perfect nexus point between movie culture and visual effects capabilities. By the early '00s, it was clear that home video (or at least home viewing) was here to stay, and many ordinary families as well as cinephiles were building personal film libraries thanks to the popularity of VHS and the then-new DVD format.

Part of the attraction of a new release of a classic film was getting bonus material or even a new cut, something that auteurs like James Cameron indulged in. Spielberg's colleague George Lucas went one further with his theatrical release of the "Star Wars" trilogy special editions in 1997, debuting versions which were intended to fully replace the original releases (which they still have done ... for now). Spielberg then seized upon the chance to make some changes to "E.T." to try and update its sensibilities to the modern era. While these alterations seemed prudent in an immediate post-9/11 world, a more sober Spielberg later admitted his error in trying to mess with cultural history too much.

After George Lucas' "Star Wars" trilogy special editions were released and Lucas made a point of taking the original cuts out of circulation, many fans and cinema preservationists alike cried foul. In addition to the blow against preservation, folks were less than pleased with some of the egregious and very obvious changes Lucas decided to make. When the news broke that Steven Spielberg would essentially be making an "E.T" special edition, producer Kathleen Kennedy told the Los Angeles Times that "there's no comparison" between the two, given that the changes to "Star Wars" were extensive while "E.T." would only be getting "a wide variety of subtle changes."

Those changes may have been subtle, but they were impactful all the same. In addition to cosmetic alterations like making digital adjustments to the 1982 E.T. animatronic, Spielberg elected to change the guns brandished by government officials in the film to walkie-talkies. In fairness to the filmmaker, he'd been vocalizing his wish to do so since at least 1995, where he explained his reasoning:

"I regret that a gun was used as a threat to stop children on bicycles [...] And if I ever reissue the picture, I'll use the digital miracle of, you know, CGI to take the guns out of the cops' hands. [...] I think those were, you know, distasteful moments to me."

While that change was already in the works before 9/11, the choice to delete a flippant off-screen line of dialogue involving a character trying to dress as a terrorist for Halloween was made as a response to the then very recent tragedy. Though understandable, these changes had a cumulative effect of making "E.T." feel significantly different altogether.

Despite making these changes to "E.T.," Steven Spielberg deserves a lot of credit for not making the same mistakes that George Lucas or some other filmmakers have made when tinkering with their work long after the fact. For one thing, Spielberg did have the original 1982 cut of "E.T." included on the film's DVD release in 2002. More than that, however, is Spielberg's retraction of the 2002 edition years later. Around the time of the release of "The Fablemans" in 2023, Spielberg gave a masterclass at the Time 100 summit, and expressed his regrets at ever having made the alterations to "E.T." in the first place:

"That was a mistake. I never should have done that. 'E.T.' is a product of its era. No film should be revised based on the lenses we now are, either voluntarily, or being forced to peer through. [...] Years went by and I changed my own views. I should have never messed with the archives of my own work, and I don't recommend anyone do that. All our movies are a kind of a signpost of where we were when we made them, what the world was like and what the world was receiving when we got those stories out there. So I really regret having that out there."

Spielberg, being the wise and observant person he is, came to the Ian Malcolm-esque realization that just because he could change things doesn't mean he should. While the temptation to alter or "fix" a movie is natural, a revision can only work in addition to the original, and cannot replace it. Only by observing our past can we understand our present and, hopefully, build a better future. Film is forever.

#3512. 63 Years Marvel Comics Gives Fans The Perfect Superhero Roster

The Marvel Comics event Avengers: Armageddon is the perfect example of how to never judge a series until it’s over. The miniseries began with Earth’s Mightiest Heroes, The Fantastic Four, and a few others going to stop Red Hulk from taking over a Symkaria. This is despite the United Nations telling the heroes to stand down.

As the story continues, the former Captain America, David Colton, threw all of the world’s nukes into the sun. Except he missed the ones Russia was hiding, and how they turned the Red Hulk into a bomb. The result was the world losing faith in humanity and the U.N. funding S.H.I.E.L.D. to protect non-powered people. Things continue to get worse after that.

Sam Wilson quit after Bucky's apparent death, Iron Man left New York, and Captain America doesn’t have part of his soul. To top it all off, Nick Fury Jr. is preparing for a war against the superpowered community. Luckily, no matter how bad things are, the best won’t leave the world unprotected, and this new Avengers team is exactly what the world needs.

Steve Rogers always believed that the Avengers roster wasn’t selected. Destiny brings them together. First, it was Loki’s mischief that caused Earth's Mightiest Heroes to come into existence. Decades later, a breakout on the raft created a new roster. Now, Mephisto's deals ending early have brought angels to Earth. This assembled the newest group of Earth’s Mightiest Heroes: Spider-Man, Luke Cage, Captain Marvel, Daredevil, Miracleman, and Wolverine.

Fans of Marvel Comics’ Avengers may recognize this team from the Brian Michael Bendis days. What made that team special was that they were all heroes with a major connection to regular people. Obviously, Spider-Man, Daredevil, Luke Cage, and Logan are all known for being more down-to-earth than other Avengers. But Carol Danvers is too. Don’t forget, before she was flying through space, she was a military woman who was also a detective. And Miracleman may be a god, but he’s also someone who understands the plight of regular people.

What makes this team perfect is that they’re closer to the people who now fear them. Obviously, Spider-Man, Daredevil, Luke Cage, and Logan are all known for being more down-to-earth than other Avengers, like Thor or T’Challa. But Carol Danvers is too. Don’t forget, before she flew through space, she was a military officer and a journalist. And Miracleman may be god-like, but he’s also someone who understands the plight of regular people.

Now that the world is scared of or dislikes heroes, a new team needs to assemble, and they must be trusted. This team has that in spades.

“They can fear us. They can hate us. It doesn’t matter. Because we’ll always help. We’ll always fight back.”

Spider-Man may be the most loved hero in New York, and this is despite what the Daily Bugle used to print. Luke Cage was a mayor that people trusted long before he worked in the government. Daredevil is known as the protector of Hell’s Kitchen. Carol Danvers is a recognized Avenger. Lastly, while many people are slightly scared of Wolverine, he’s looked at more fondly thanks to his time in New Orleans with the X-Men.

When the Red Hulk exploded in Russia, Carol Danvers tried to absorb all of the blast's energy. She saved as many as she could, but thousands still died. Not only is that weighing heavily on her conscience, but absorbing the blast de-powered her by 90%. She can’t fly, and while bullets bounce off her, she says it hurts.

Seeing Captain Marvel adjust to her lack of powers will be great for readers. For years, she’s been looked at as overpowered and kind of stuck up (the latter being far from true). Now, the non-believers will see what many have known for years. Carol Danvers’ powers don’t make her a great character. Writers like Kelly Thompson and Kelly Sue Deconnick did that.

Finally, the time has come to bring up the most important part of Chip Zdarsky’s Avengers, and that's Spider-Man being team leader.

Peter has been on the front lines of battles before, but this is different. He will be the one leading Earth’s Mightiest Heroes. It’s even more important because it comes at a time similar to Marvel Comics' Civil War, when the superheroes’ approval rating was at an all-time low.

Now that Peter is in charge, he will have the team moving differently within this series and Amazing Spider-Man​​​​​​. Luckily, he has the respect of everyone on his team. They know that he’s stood among their best for years, and trust Spidey enough to follow him into Hell. Since it looks like Hell came to Earth, this happened right on time.

#3511. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. His Merlin is all wild hair and rock band T-shirts, possessed of an essential kindness that makes him a valued mentor, and one deserving of his character's poignant farewell at the film's conclusion.Stream The Kid Who Would Be King on Disney+ and Prime Video.

#3510. 25 Best Directors Of All Time, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Ranking the best directors of all time is a formidable task. How do you weigh a director's output against their influence? Ultimately, the question is who has left the most lasting impression on film culture, and why.

Making a list like this also means confronting the industry's realities. You'll notice a dismal underrepresentation of directors of color, women, and queer filmmakers compared to the overwhelming majority of entries: white men.

Hollywood, and the filmmaking industry writ large, have historically diminished the voices of marginalized filmmakers, limiting their opportunities to create, distribute, and receive recognition for their work. When those opportunities have disproportionately gone to the same insular group, it's no surprise their work has come to dominate the cinematic canon. Hopefully, future renditions of this list will reflect a greater appreciation of historically overlooked filmmakers and the continued emergence of exciting, diverse voices pushing the medium forward.

For now, the directors on this list reflect film history's achievements and the inequities that have shaped it. Here are the 25 best directors of all time, ranked.

John Carpenter may not watch his own movies, but for the rest of us, he's left an indelible mark on genre cinema. He made "Halloween" in 1978 for a reported $325,000, scoring one of horror's most recognizable piano themes in three days and drafting a slasher blueprint: the ominous quiet of suburbia shattered by violence, all in gorgeous Scope framing. That's just one of his essential films, as "Assault on Precinct 13," "Escape From New York," and "The Thing" have helped cement his legacy.

Hollywood never quite knew what to do with Carpenter, not that he cared. "Big Trouble in Little China" flopped before becoming a respected cult object. "They Live" screamed its anti-consumerist messaging to the rafters inside a winking sci-fi B-movie, featuring one of the longest and goofiest fight scenes ever filmed. Few filmmakers have maintained such an unmistakable sensibility as Carpenter's stylish, innovative takes on horror and pulp.

Billy Wilder fled terror in Europe and arrived in Hollywood with limited English, eventually becoming one of the town's sharpest writers. As a director, he constantly hopped genres without a hitch. "Double Indemnity," co-written with Raymond Chandler, helped define film noir; "The Lost Weekend" won Best Picture and Best Director at the Academy Awards for its unflinching look at alcoholism; the Gothic Hollywood nightmare of "Sunset Boulevard" scandalized the industry and aged into one of the most essential showbiz movies ever.

"Some Like It Hot," starring Marilyn Monroe, was named the greatest American comedy by the AFI. "The Apartment" threaded office-politics farce through a funny, emotional, deeply bittersweet story of loneliness, heartbreak, and workplace exploitation, going on to take home Best Picture. Wilder's films were often cynical, funny, and deeply humane all at once. If you need a place to start, we ranked 14 of his best movies.

Christopher Nolan's legacy is already set in stone as a modern-day showman, and he's perhaps the last director who can conjure blockbuster events based on his name alone. His modest breakout "Memento" hinted at his cerebral ambitions. "The Dark Knight" elevated the gritty, tactile superhero movie into a new blockbuster standard, and "Inception" cemented his reputation as a purveyor of brainy yet crowd-pleasing big-budget spectacle. Of course, he is also the movie theater's loudest and most ardent evangelist, championing IMAX cameras, real film stock, and practical stunts.

His overwhelming ambition has never insulated him from criticism though, as detractors harp on cold characters, muddy sound mixes, and an unholy amount of exposition. But to see "Interstellar," "Dunkirk," or "The Odyssey" in a true IMAX presentation is to immerse yourself in the palpable vision of a man who knows exactly how to stage a set-piece. To watch "Oppenheimer" is to be amazed at how he can turn a three-hour biopic of men talking in rooms into something as high-octane as his thrillers. Nolan is in a league all his own, so we had a hard time ranking his movies.

Nobody captures the sensorial experience of longing quite like Wong Kar-wai. The Hong Kong auteur, often working with cinematographer Christopher Doyle, built a visual language of romantic yearning from neon smears, slow-motion blurs, and step-printing warps of time and motion. Countless filmmakers have chased the ineffable quality he summons in his films about the aches and desires of the human experience, especially his standout film "Chungking Express," anchored by Tony Leung's exquisite features. The film helped make him an international name, with a boost from Quentin Tarantino, whose short-lived Rolling Thunder Pictures label brought it to American theaters, and "Happy Together" earned him Best Director at Cannes in 1997.

But it's "In the Mood for Love" that gave him legendary status. Pairing Tony Leung with Maggie Cheung as neighbors in 1962 Hong Kong who discover their spouses are having an affair, he turns it into a romance of pure, repressed feeling. It's the epitome of the entire Wong Kar-wai project, and it's the movie that has cemented his legacy. It also landed at #5 in Sight & Sound's 2022 critics' poll.

Robert Altman wasn't one to conform to Hollywood's tidy, controlled storytelling. A former bomber pilot who cut his teeth on industrial films and television, he broke through with "M*A*S*H," a profane, anti-authoritarian war comedy that won the top prize at Cannes in 1970. He developed a signature style built on overlapping dialogue, wandering zoom lenses, and enormous ensemble casts, often capturing multiple conversations simultaneously and extracting moments of clarity from the chaos. He adapted this style across the gamut of genres: "McCabe & Mrs. Miller" envisioned the Western as a hazy character study; "The Long Goodbye" subverted the noir by turning it into a shaggy, meandering ramble; and "Nashville" makes a compelling case for being the great American movie of the 1970s.

After the troubled "Popeye" in 1980, he spent years on the margins, working in theater and low-budget stage adaptations, before roaring back with "The Player," his biting Hollywood satire, followed by "Short Cuts" and "Gosford Park." He was nominated for Best Director five times, never won, but finally received an honorary Oscar in 2006, months before his death at 81. Altman may not have spent much time analyzing his own films, but a wealth of genius remains.

Before becoming an architect of cinematic epics, David Lean worked his way up from studio cutting rooms to become one of British film's finest editors. The training shows in the precision of everything he would go on to shoot. After co-directing "In Which We Serve" with Noël Coward, he made "Brief Encounter," a beautifully felt railway-station romance of aching restraint, whose DNA is evident in beloved movies such as "Before Sunset" and "The Bridges of Madison County."

It was later that he would prove his gift for scale. "The Bridge on the River Kwai" won Best Picture and Best Director, but, of course, it's "Lawrence of Arabia" that turned his name into shorthand for grandeur — a movie with a rare perfect Metacritic score. That film alone earns him a spot here, even without his other wonderfully helmed features, which all reveal a filmmaker attuned to the most crucial tenets of storytelling.

Not just one of the most influential comedy stars in history, and one of the most famous entertainers to ever work in Hollywood, many of Charles "Charlie" Chaplin's greatest successes were helmed by the man himself. From London poverty and the music-hall stage, he began experimenting with directing at Keystone in 1914 with "Twenty Minutes of Love." "Caught in the Rain" followed, his first film with sole directing responsibility. From there, he spent his career proving how his formal prowess complemented his physical dexterity.

His silent and early sound masterpieces include "The Kid," "The Gold Rush," "City Lights," "Modern Times," and "The Great Dictator," his first full talkie, in which he lampooned Hitler while the United States was still neutral. Such boldness had consequences: While sailing for London in 1952, amid the Red Scare, the government revoked his re-entry permit, and he settled in Switzerland, later returning for an honorary Oscar in 1972.

Howard Hawks left enduring imprints across seemingly limitless genres. He helped define the violent gangster picture with "Scarface." He directed two of the best screwball comedies of all time, "Bringing Up Baby" and "His Girl Friday." He made the tough-minded adventure "Only Angels Have Wings." He paired Humphrey Bogart with Lauren Bacall twice, in "To Have and Have Not" and "The Big Sleep," creating one of the most seductive cinematic pairings ever seen on screen. "Red River" and "Rio Bravo" can both claim a place among Hollywood's most essential Westerns.

Hawks did it all. He accentuates the material with an invisible style: eye-level camerawork, unfussy staging, and a preoccupation with professionals who earn each other's respect, including strong-willed women who demand to be treated as equals. He was the kind of Hollywood workman who made masterpieces by simply showing up and understanding the job.

Federico Fellini began as a cartoonist and gag writer, then he co-wrote for Roberto Rossellini on "Rome, Open City" and "Paisan," foundational works of Italian neorealism, before broadening his scope. "La Strada" and "Nights of Cabiria," fables of the poor and discarded, announced his talent, but it was "La Dolce Vita" that cemented his international reputation and became one of the greatest Italian films ever made — it was also Roger Ebert's favorite movie of all time. The Palme d'Or winner follows Marcello Mastroianni through Rome's decadent nightlife, capturing the estranged emotional perspective of a hollow, meaningless pursuit of glamour.

From there, he turned inward. "8½" is perhaps his most famous film, the definitive movie about a director paralyzed by his own creative crisis, blending memory, fantasy, and self-doubt in a way self-reflective directors have tried to imitate in Fellini's wake. Later came the carnivalesque "Fellini Satyricon," "Roma," and the nostalgic "Amarcord," another Oscar winner. His singular vision earned him a word of his own: "Felliniesque."

In a decade, Francis Ford Coppola made a run of films that may be the greatest in history. He fought a studio that didn't want Marlon Brando or Al Pacino in what would be his seminal, culture-shattering "The Godfather." He followed that up with two masterpieces in 1974: "The Conversation," which took home the top prize at Cannes, and "The Godfather Part II," the rare sequel that exceeded its predecessor and became the first sequel to win Best Picture. "Apocalypse Now" followed, after a legendarily disastrous shoot in the Philippines so troubled it inspired its own documentary, "Hearts of Darkness."

That run alone earns Coppola his place among the greats, even if all that risk-taking nearly broke him. The expensive flop "One from the Heart" crippled his Zoetrope studio, and he spent years making movies to pay off debts. Even so, he kept swinging, from "Rumble Fish" to the operatic "Bram Stoker's Dracula," and bankrolled the truly zany "Megalopolis" himself, reportedly with money from his wine business. Whatever you make of it, few directors have been this ambitious for this long.

Spike Lee, for all his prolificacy, can be an uneven director — there's a reason we were able to list his eight best and seven worst movies — but he's responsible for some of the most important American movies ever made, particularly in his exploration of Black American life. Arriving with "She's Gotta Have It," he would soon follow with his critically acclaimed drama "Do the Right Thing," a loving yet raging cultural firestorm of fractured societal relationships that refuses to placate its audience.

His refusal to back down from his beliefs comes through in a brash, flashy style that is instantly recognizable, particularly in his signature "double dolly" shot. But he can be flexible too. "Malcolm X" showed his epic reach, "Inside Man" his mainstream chops, and "BlacKkKlansman" his insight into how yesterday's politics collide with today's. Consistency be damned, he's an essential component of American filmmaking.

Agnès Varda came to cinema as a still photographer with almost no film training, and she made her debut, "La Pointe Courte," in 1955, years before the French New Wave she's often credited with anticipating. She was one of the few women in a scene dominated by cinephile men, and she stood out by making her sensibility entirely her own: curious, playful, and warmly attentive to ordinary people. "Cléo from 5 to 7" is a luminous examination of a pop singer drifting through Paris as she awaits medical test results, while "Vagabond," which won the Golden Lion at Venice, is an unsentimental portrait of a young drifter found dead in a ditch.

Varda also slipped freely between fiction and documentary, often blending the two. "The Gleaners and I" found poetry in scavengers and discarded produce, while "Faces Places," co-directed with the artist JR, earned her a Best Documentary Feature nomination at the 90th Academy Awards in 2018, making the 89-year-old Varda the oldest Oscar nominee in Academy history at the time. She kept working until her death in 2019 and made waves with critics throughout her career, including being among the highest-rated female-directed movies on Metacritic.

Hayao Miyazaki is animation's most devoted craftsman, introducing generations of children internationally to the detailed artistry of Japanese animation while also exposing them to challenging, scary, and profound ideas that have helped prepare them for adulthood. He co-founded Studio Ghibli (whose films we've ranked) in 1985 with Isao Takahata and Toshio Suzuki, and made a run of films that treated childhood as serious business: the gentle fable "My Neighbor Totoro," the coming-of-age story of a young witch discovering her purpose in "Kiki's Delivery Service," and the ecological fantasy epic "Princess Mononoke."

Then came "Spirited Away," which won the Golden Bear in Berlin and the Oscar for Best Animated Feature, and it was Japan's highest-grossing film for nearly two decades. The free-wheeling, wafting nature of Miyazaki's films comes from his unconventional process: He storyboards without a finished script, discovering the heart of the films as he draws. After returning from retirement to make "The Boy and the Heron," which earned him another Oscar for Best Animated Feature, Miyazaki remains creatively active well into his eighties. His extraordinary animation is a legacy any filmmaker could only dream of.

Andrei Tarkovsky made only seven features, each with seismic influence across generations. He once called filmmaking "sculpting in time," and that idea shapes his often abstruse yet spiritually profound work. As Ingmar Bergman once said, he invented a new language for film. Watching a Tarkovsky movie means being enraptured by its emotional depth, hidden within its mysteries.

His major works are must-sees. These include "Solaris," which turns Stanisław Lem's novel into a fractured meditation on memory and guilt; "Mirror," which weaves Tarkovsky's own childhood, newsreel footage, and his father Arseny's poetry into a chimerical collage; and "Stalker," one of the most influential and widely imitated sci-fi films ever made. Along with works such as "Andrei Rublev" and "Ivan's Childhood," Tarkovsky left behind a slim yet crucial filmography that helped define Soviet cinema and continues to influence filmmakers worldwide.

Sidney Lumet was a child actor on stage before becoming one of television's most active directors, and the discipline of working quickly and efficiently for television remained in his DNA. He put his TV work to good use with "12 Angry Men," his iconic pressure-cooker juror drama, which now stands as one of the best film debuts ever. He favored complex characters and sharp commentary on the modern world, as seen in movies like "Serpico," "Dog Day Afternoon," "Prince of the City," and "Network."

Lumet loved actors, rehearsing them like a stage company, and many of his stars delivered some of their best performances under his direction, from Al Pacino's sweaty bank robber in "Dog Day Afternoon" to Paul Newman's washed-up lawyer in "The Verdict." He made great movies until the end of his career, releasing "Before the Devil Knows You're Dead" at age 83, before his death in 2011.

Alfred Hitchcock earned the nickname "The Master of Suspense" for a reason. After honing his craft on British silent films and thrillers like "The 39 Steps" and "The Lady Vanishes," he crossed the Atlantic to work with producer David O. Selznick and made "Rebecca," which won Best Picture. However, since Best Picture statues go to a film's producers, Hitchcock would ultimately go 0-for-5 in the Best Director category.

Hitchcock's legacy has rested less on awards than on his ability to shock audiences. He made archetypal horror and thriller masterpieces, including "Rear Window," "North by Northwest," "Psycho," and "Vertigo," which would later topple "Citizen Kane" from the top of Sight & Sound's critics' poll in 2012, ending a 50-year reign. His genius endures to this day, and his films feel just as thrilling and transgressive as ever, which is fitting for the director with the most perfect movies, according to Metacritic.

It's often said that Joel and Ethan Coen are a directing duo who share a single brain, each completely in tune with the other's dry, morbid, gleefully caustic sense of humor and irony in their portrayals of people whose downfalls are their own making. They distilled the sensibility of their entire career in their debut neo-noir "Blood Simple" and kept that same mordant sensibility across genres and decades. From the screwball kidnapping farce "Raising Arizona" to the surrealistic Hollywood allegory "Barton Fink" to the breakout Minnesota nice-crime story "Fargo," which won a screenplay Oscar and Best Actress for Frances McDormand, nearly all of the Coens' films share a harmonious blend of dark comedy and drama.

Their mid-career run was just as strong: "No Country for Old Men" is one of the best neo-Westerns ever, while movies like "A Serious Man," "True Grit," and "Inside Llewyn Davis" continued to prove the success of their strange amalgamations of tenderness, humor, and bleak perceptions of reality. The Coens also pull career-best performances from their actors, so good that we had to rank the best of them. Their decision to pursue separate projects in recent years has only accentuated the miraculous consistency of their work together — and with the brothers now expressing plans to reunite behind the camera, there may yet be another chapter in one of cinema's great creative partnerships.

Any time you need a shock to the system, remember that Paul Thomas Anderson made "Boogie Nights" when he was just 26. Most recently in the spotlight for finally winning Best Picture, Best Director, and Best Adapted Screenplay for "One Battle After Another," his freewheeling riff on Thomas Pynchon's "Vineland," Anderson has spent years as your dedicated cinephile's de facto favorite contemporary director.

With a career defined by such formal bravado, how could he not be? Nearly all his films have defenders who call them masterpieces, from the three-hour interconnected melodrama epic "Magnolia" to "Punch-Drunk Love," which proved Adam Sandler's capability as a dramatic lead. Of course, it's "There Will Be Blood," one of Daniel Day-Lewis' best films, that tops many best-of-the-century lists, but his subsequent work, "The Master," "Phantom Thread," and "Licorice Pizza," is imbued with his radiant sensibility just as well. Anderson makes movies that buzz with pure cinematic brilliance.

Nothing captures David Lynch's sensibility better than the clip of him being asked to elaborate on why "Eraserhead" is his most spiritual movie, and him curtly replying, "No, I won't." For as routine as the term "Lynchian" has become when describing movies that are any shade of strange or surreal, the true ethos of Lynch's movies is that intangible quality that's hard to explain in the first place and nearly impossible to replicate. Even still, Lynch's filmography is diverse: the tender, Oscar-nominated "The Elephant Man," the misfired blockbuster "Dune," the unsettling revelations of suburban secrets in "Blue Velvet," and the surprising warmth of his G-rated, Disney-produced road movie "The Straight Story."

His legacy will be remembered mostly for "Mulholland Drive," a project initially conceived as a spinoff of his groundbreaking television series "Twin Peaks," which later evolved into a standalone ABC pilot that Lynch reworked into a film after the network passed on it, as well as his return to "Peaks" with "The Return" in 2017, perhaps the boldest television has ever been. Lynch sadly passed away in 2025, but he leaves behind a legacy of unsettling dreams and devoted compassion toward the human experience. No other voice will ever be like his.

Martin Scorsese is cinema's most passionate student and, increasingly, its most devoted steward and custodian, through work such as his World Cinema Project, which preserves, restores, and showcases neglected and underseen films from around the world. Raised in Little Italy, he was an asthmatic kid who spent his childhood in movie theaters and nearly became a priest before NYU film school pointed him elsewhere. Sin, guilt, and the hunger for redemption would color so many of his works: the raw street poetry of "Mean Streets," the Palme d'Or-winning "Taxi Driver," the bruising "Raging Bull," and "Goodfellas," one of the defining landmarks of gangster cinema.

At 83, he's still making some of his best work. Take a look at movies like "The Wolf of Wall Street," "Silence," "The Irishman," and "Killers of the Flower Moon" to see a director who has never lost his touch, continually finding new ways to explore his perspectives on faith, morality, and humanity through his unmistakable cinematic style. There is indeed an argument that Scorsese is our greatest living filmmaker.

Stanley Kubrick's legendary attention to detail casts an imposing shadow across film history. Though he may never have won a Best Director Oscar, the skill he exhibited across a diverse slate of masterpieces is, in effect, one of the greatest influences on his contemporaries and those who followed in his wake.

His films have become synonymous with filmmaking mastery, and yet it still manages to stun that the same man made the likes of "Dr. Strangelove," "2001: A Space Odyssey," "A Clockwork Orange," "Barry Lyndon," "The Shining," "Full Metal Jacket," and "Eyes Wide Shut." That's not even counting his impressive early work, which included "The Killing," "Paths of Glory," "Spartacus," and "Lolita." He may not be the most prolific director on this list, but the caliber of his work has earned him enduring renown, plus a new tome-like brick from the Criterion Collection with 4K restorations of all his films.

No director has stared directly into the abyss quite like Ingmar Bergman. The son of a Lutheran pastor, he arrived at film after years in the theater, ruminating on guilt, faith, and dread, though he broke through with the bittersweet comedy "Smiles of a Summer Night." But his most revered works soon followed: the heavy gloom of "The Seventh Seal," the gentle "Wild Strawberries," and perhaps most notably the surreal, psychologically labyrinthine "Persona," a dreamlike investigation of identity.

Bergman built his vast filmography with trusted collaborators, including cinematographers Gunnar Fischer and Sven Nykvist and actors like Liv Ullmann, Max von Sydow, and Bibi Andersson, whose faces he observes with the same care as epic landscapes. "The Virgin Spring," "Through a Glass Darkly," and "Fanny and Alexander" each won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film, the last a warm, autobiographical epic he originally intended as his farewell to theatrical filmmaking.

John Ford made beautiful Westerns, but he also established much of the cinematic language the genre has followed ever since, all while demonstrating remarkable mastery across other genres. A veteran of the silent era, he directed more than 130 films between 1917 and 1970 and holds the record for Best Director Oscars with four — "The Informer," "The Grapes of Wrath," "How Green Was My Valley," and "The Quiet Man" — none of them Westerns. Two wartime Navy documentaries also won Oscars: "The Battle of Midway" and "December 7th." Ford personally filmed much of the former while under fire during the battle.

But the frontier was where Ford's poetry truly shines. "Stagecoach" turned John Wayne into a movie star, and Orson Welles reportedly studied it up to 40 times before making "Citizen Kane." His later Westerns interrogated the very mythologies he helped create: "The Searchers" cast a shadow of obsession and racism over Wayne's heroism, while "The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance" questioned the romanticized stories America tells about its own history. He's your favorite director's favorite director, from Scorsese to Spielberg, and his influence looms large in modern cinema.

Akira Kurosawa had a career that expanded the horizons of both Japanese and Western cinema: while his own films were masterpieces, the filmmakers he inspired would become mavericks. After debuting with "Sanshiro Sugata" in 1943, he impressed audiences abroad with "Rashomon," a film about a crime recounted in four contradictory ways, which won the Golden Lion at Venice in 1951 and an honorary Oscar. In the years that followed came "Ikiru" and, perhaps most notably to film fans, "Seven Samurai," whose team-assembling structure and staggering sense of craft became a blueprint for the action genre.

Kurosawa's echoes are everywhere in the movies you grew up loving: "The Magnificent Seven" remade "Seven Samurai," Sergio Leone's "A Fistful of Dollars" borrowed "Yojimbo," and George Lucas has cited "The Hidden Fortress" as an inspiration for "Star Wars." Yet no imitator can fully capture his signature style: telephoto compositions, multiple cameras, wind and rain as powerful reflections of his characters' emotional states, and precise editing. Trace the DNA of modern cinema, and you'll find Kurosawa somewhere in its lineage.

If anyone seems truly put on this Earth to entertain, Steven Spielberg may be the man. His name is both a brand and an adjective. He is an indispensable practitioner of moviemaking who completely changed the way Hollywood approached its business when he made "Jaws" before turning 30, the shark thriller that helped establish the modern summer blockbuster. He became the highest-grossing director in box-office history, with generational favorites like "Close Encounters of the Third Kind," "Raiders of the Lost Ark," and "E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial."

In 1993, he released both "Jurassic Park" and "Schindler's List," the latter winning him Oscars for Best Director and Best Picture,  and "Saving Private Ryan" brought him a second directing win. Critics call him sentimental, but "Munich" and "A.I." are darker and more ambiguous than his reputation suggests, and "The Fabelmans," his portrait of his parents' breakup and his own obsession with the camera, finally turned the lens on himself in stunning fashion. Across film history, it's hard to find a director who combines formal prowess with the ability to move and compel commercial audiences more effectively. He is the director for every flavor of film fan. His name is unmatched in film culture.

#3509. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Thankfully Resists FromSoftware’s Influence

Ocarina of Time sticks to the basics, and the remake is better for it

This year in video games, I’ve swung a digital sword more times than I can count. Thrilling action games like Onimusha: Way of the Sword and Phantom Blade Zero have gotten the feel of a sword fight down to a science, as steel clashes and sparks fly in spectacular fashion. But my favorite duels of the year aren’t in any of this year’s most razor-sharp action games; they’re all in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.

The Switch 2 remake builds on the combat of Link’s 1998 adventure in careful but effective fashion. The Master Sword feels more powerful than ever thanks to killer sound design and a bit of visual pizazz on impact. What the remake doesn’t do, however, is change Link’s moves to give him the most widely used trick in modern action games: the parry. There’s no deflection to be found in Ocarina of Time’s remake, and that makes a seemingly simple combat system stand out in an unexpectedly refreshing way.

Compared to many modern games, Ocarina of Time’s swordplay doesn’t require much mastery from players. Aside from a charged spin attack and a leaping slash, Link’s offensive options are limited. Lock on, swing the sword, hit the enemy, and that’s basically all you need to know. Sure, you can block attacks with your shield or use one of your items to switch it up, but you’re always going to follow the same motions to take out a Deku Baba with consistent strikes.

One of my questions heading into the remake was about how much Nintendo would modernize that approach. After all, lots of remakes and remasters these days make reworked combat a priority; just this year, we’ve seen that in projects like The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt Remastered and Assassin’s Creed Black Flag Resynced. Rather than following that wave, Nintendo chose to keep Link’s offense relatively unchanged. That can take some getting used to if you play a lot of modern action games that all seem to have some version of a parry, or at least some kind of counterattack.

The quicker you acclimate to Ocarina of Time’s throwback action, though, the quicker you’ll come to appreciate its elegance. Fights aren’t meant to be long duels against evenly-matched opponents; Link is a master of his craft and can dispatch virtually any enemy in a few hits. Precision and timing are key as you patiently wait for your opening before lunging forward with a strike. The same goes for Link’s evasive maneuvers, which allow him to sidestep and backflip away from incoming attacks. It only takes a few Stalfos encounters to learn their attacks and lock down the right dodge and attack follow-up timing to take one out quickly.

In my review, I compared that to the experience of playing Punch-Out!!. The classic NES game’s staying power comes from the fact that every fight hinges on you learning each enemy’s tells and reacting to them accordingly. Every boxing match is a dance, and you have to learn your half of it. Ocarina of Time functions the same way, pushing you to hit all your marks rather than rush through a careful fight.

There are several fights in Ocarina of Time that test your ability to follow that flow, especially the late-game Iron Knuckles who hit like a truck if you fail to dodge their attacks. The best skill check, though, comes during a clash with Dark Link in the Water Temple. It’s the one time where you find yourself up against a fighter who is as efficient and precise as you, because it is you. Patience is your greatest skill in a battle that will taunt you for swinging wildly while your shadowy foe seemingly has an answer to every mistake you make. It plays out like a theatrically staged fencing match. Once you feel that, every other fight clicks into place, too.

Though it may sound a little simple, Nintendo finds the right way to make every slash feel powerful. Every sword hit is accompanied by an impactful thwack and an explosion of colorful particles. Even slashing the weakest enemies as Young Link feels spectacular, as if your blade has busted them open like a pinata. Those small touches make every hit feel important and satisfying to execute, rather than futile hits against a sponge. I can’t say the same for something like GameFreak’s summer not-quite-a-Soulslike Beast of Reincarnation, where bosses fall to death by a thousand cuts.

It may sound strange to call a combat system rooted in 1998 design fresh, but it really is in a world where so many action games I play feel like variations on a theme. Ocarina of Time may not impress modern players who look for expression in their combat, but you won’t hear anyone labeling it a Soulslike or dubbing it “parryslop.” The battles have an unmistakable texture to them, born out of a focused design philosophy that suits an equally focused swordsman. Who needs a parry when no blade can cross you?

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

#3508. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.
