#3507. PlayStation 5 Gamers Can Free Up Storage Space Without Deleting Any Games

PlayStation 5 users now have the ability to free up a ton of storage space on their consoles without having to delete any games. While the PlayStation 4 offered an easy way to expand its available storage via external hard drives, things are a little more complicated this generation; only certain drives are compatible with the console, and you can't play games from an external drive — just store them.

So PS5 storage runs out fast, games just keep getting bigger, and deleting games to make room for new ones becomes a frequent ritual. Maybe you're making room for all 200+ GB of GTA 6, or this month's PS Plus games — regardless, you need to make room on your PS5, and you don't want to delete any games.

Now, according to Gaming Bible, there's a way to free up tons of space on your PS5 without having to delete a single game. Here's what you have to do:

A few caveats here: first, not every game will include a Customize option. Naturally, you have to have DLC for the game installed to use it.

In addition, you'll want to be careful not to delete anything that could mess with your ability to play the game. Cosmetic items should be fine, depending on how your chosen game handles cosmetics, but you might have to reinstall huge story DLC before loading your save file, so be mindful of what you're getting rid of.

Finally, a lot of video game DLC is too small to make a difference in your hard drive space when deleted individually. From the screenshot above, you can see that each piece of content for Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced takes up only a megabyte or two; I'd have to delete thousands like these to make a meaningful difference.

That said, there is bigger DLC out there; certain games in the notoriously storage-demanding Call of Duty series, for example, released with all their various game modes bundled in as DLC, so players wouldn't have to install the whole campaign if they just wanted to play Warzone, for example. These individual pieces of DLC are closer to 30–40 GB, so just by deleting a handful of those, you could free up more than 100 GB.

If you're looking to free up even more space, consider checking your Captures folder; by default, your PS5 saves a screenshot and a 15-second video whenever you get a Trophy. These can add up to occupy a ton of space.

And, if you're playing an RPG that includes story DLC you haven't started yet, you might be able to delete that, then reinstall it when it's time to move on to the next chapter. What works and what doesn't will vary greatly by the games you have installed on your PlayStation 5, but it's worth a shot.

#3506. Kristen Stewart's Family-Friendly Sci-Fi Box Office Bomb Is Worth Revisiting

While she's best known for a certain fantasy romance franchise (and has since gone on to do her best work in small indie dramas), Kristen Stewart is no stranger to genre filmmaking. In fact, she's amassed a nice little resume within the sci-fi genre, having acted in movies like "Jumper," "Crimes of the Future," and "Undersea."

Unfortunately, Stewart hasn't had much luck in the genre so far as the box office is concerned. But that doesn't mean you shouldn't seek out her various sci-fi projects. Quite the opposite: Her family-friendly 2005 bomb "Zathura: A Space Adventure" features a great cast of once and future franchise stars. It also marked an early directorial effort from the man who would eventually put Grogu and Martin Scorsese together on the big screen, and it boasts some pretty good practical effects to boot.

Yes, "Zathura" was Jon Favreau's third outing as a director and had a script credited to David Koepp and John Kramps, itself adapted from Chris Van Allsburg's book of the same name. "Zathura" is even technically part of the "Jumanji" movie franchise, as Allburg's original work takes place in the same universe as his classic fantasy adventure creation.

In "Zathura," Josh Hutcherson and Jonah Bobo play two brothers who constantly fight and are struggling with the recent divorce of their parents. Dealing with a workaholic dad and an older sister (Kristen Stewart) who couldn't care less what her siblings do, the pair find a magical board game that transports their house to outer space. From there, they're forced to survive various alien dangers and finish the game if they ever hope to get back safely home.

"Zathura," as mentioned earlier, features two then-future stars in the YA genre space, with Kristen Stewart becoming the face of the "Twilight" films and Josh Hutcherson co-leading the "Hunger Games" movies years later. The movie also co-stars Dax Shepard, Frank Oz as the voice of a defective robot, and Tim Robbins (decades out from his performance as the most underrated character on "Silo").

Admittedly, "Zathura" never really hides the fact that it really is just "Jumanji" in outer space, with a mysterious adult man chasing after the protagonists, huge special effects, and animalistic threats preying on the house where the story takes place. Yet, it mostly works, in no small part due to Stan Winston's contributions to the film's visual effects. Some of its CGI looks dated nowadays, sure, but the practical effects from Stan Winston Studios remain convincing and enhance the movie's sense of wonder. With its assorted fantastical creatures, "Zathura" helped to kickstart Jon Favreau's fascination with technology and effects as well — for better and for worse.

Sadly, Stewart doesn't have to do much in "Zathura," as her character ends up spending most of its runtime cryogenically frozen (with Stan Winston Studios having devised a life-size model of a frozen Stewart for the occasion). Of course, when she's not frozen, Stewart succeeds in giving her onscreen counterpart more than just the annoyed big sister who panics about her predicament. Her character gets some emotional moments with her brothers, too, along with some fun banter with Dax Shepard's Astronaut (who gets the film's best scene, in which we learn his true identity and tragic backstory).

"Zathura" has a 77% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, with the vast majority of the film's reviews being positive. Indeed, Roger Ebert was among those who praised the movie, writing that it works "gloriously as space opera" and commending Jon Favreau for bringing "a muscular solidity to his special effects" that infuses them with imperfections and personality (which, in turn, makes them feel more grounded and real).

Sorry to say, though, all that critical praise wasn't enough to make "Zathura" a hit. Instead, the film was overshadowed at the box office by Disney's "Chicken Little," which was the studio's first fully computer-animated movie. Making matters worse, "Zathura" was all but forgotten about a week later when "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" opened in theaters. In the end, the film barely matched its $65 million budget at the global box office. Still, it was nominated for several Saturn Awards, including Best Fantasy Film.

Some 14 years after its theatrical release, "Zathura" found its way back into the public consciousness when Jack Black, who was promoting "Jumanji: The Next Level" at the time, reminded audiences that "Zathura" is part of the same franchise (via Variety). Today, it remains a pleasant, family-friendly sci-fi flick that's worth your time, should you find yourself in the mood for some cosmic hijinks.

#3505. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.

#3503. This Canceled 2010s Fantasy Series Deserved More Time To Flesh Out Its Ambitious Premise

The supernatural TV series "The Secret Circle" debuted on The CW in 2011, falling squarely into the network's penchant for teen dramas and YA-inflected soaps. Sadly, it only lasted for one 22-episode season, ending its run in 2012. And like other TV shows that possess as much lore, backstory, and interpersonal relationships as this one, "The Secret Circle" needed to live a lot longer to fulfill its potential.

Based on the series of novels created by L.J. Smith (best known for writing "The Vampire Diaries"), "The Secret Circle" stars Britt Robertson (who also fronted the guilty pleasure that is Netflix's "Girlboss") as Cassie, a teenager who recently lost her mother in a fire and has since moved to Chance Harbor, Washington, to live with her grandmother, Jane (Ashley Crow). Cassie doesn't initially know this, but she's secretly a witch and has eerie magical powers. However, it doesn't take long for the other teen witches at her new high school to recognize that Cassie is a witch and invite her to be part of their Secret Circle.

Cassie isn't just a witch, she learns, her matronly lineage goes all the way back to the beginning of witchcraft. Cassie's father, it's revealed, is John Blackwell (Joe Lando), a mysterious dark warlock who lurks in the show's margins. Other members of the Secret Circle include Adam (Thomas Dekker), Faye (Phoebe Tonkin), Diana (Shelley Hennig), Melissa (Jessica Parker Kennedy), and Nick (Louis Hunter).

True to the soap opera spirit of The CW, there are romantic dealings between the Circle's members. For example, Nick and Melissa are dating, and Nick eventually has to learn to respect Melissa more. That is, in addition to being killed and resurrected (!). Cassie, meanwhile, instantly falls for Adam, which upsets Diana, who has always had a thing for Adam.

In addition to the kids in the Circle, Gale Harold plays Charles, Diana's father and a former Circle member. Elsewhere, Natasha Henstridge from "Species" plays Faye's mother, another former Circle member, and the principal of the high school where the show's action takes place.

"The Secret Circle" belongs to a vast and well-populated matrix of teen supernatural dramas that were very much in vogue on television in the 2000s and early 2010s (although L.J. Smith started publishing her "Secret Circle" novels in 1992). Indeed, it's worth recalling that The CW had already scored a hit when its TV adaptation of "The Vampire Diaries" began its run in 2009, to the point that the network would go on to develop multiple spin-offs (like the since-canceled "Legacies"). Clearly, "The Secret Circle" was an attempt to bottle the same lightning. Vampires, witches, teen drama, magic: It was all boiling together on The CW.

And "The Secret Circle" certainly doesn't lack conflict. It carefully balances the magic of a witch coven with the drama of being a regular high school student. As such, it features just as many stories about school dances and friend-group inter-flirting as ones about spell books and dark witchy forces that aim to attack the Circle for nefarious purposes. Case in point: The show includes three episodes that center on school dances, and its penultimate episode takes place at Prom. On the witch side of things, several plot lines focus on magic crystals that are coveted by various magical players for a variety of reasons.

Back in 2015, writer Gavin Hetherington penned a post-mortem on "The Secret Circle" for Spoiler TV, revisiting it three years after its cancelation. Hetherington noted that "The Secret Circle" actually began quite strong in the ratings, but it fell off quickly, falling far behind "The Vampire Diaries." For Hetherington, this was a tragedy, as he declared the show's finale to be its best episode up to that point, arguing that it only showed more potential going forward. In fact, four new characters arrive in that episode, with all of them being part of Cassie's witch ancestor's lineage. Sadly, though, the show ended before audiences could learn their whole story.

When "The Secret Circle" was canceled, its many fans tried to convince The CW to keep it going via a letter-writing campaign, but it was not successful. "The Vampire Diaries" simply left a deeper impact and is generally regarded as one of the best vampire shows of all time. Due to its truncated run, "The Secret Circle" just can't compete with that series.

It probably didn't help that critics were less impressed with "The Secret Circle" than its loyal fans. Reviewing the series for Variety in 2011, Brian Lowry even described it as "'One Tree Hill,' only with witchcraft," writing that "nothing in the pilot conjures any genuine magic, TV-wise." Still, it's a vestige of what the old CW used to be in all its glory.

#3502. Godzilla Minus Zero Opening Weekend Box Office Breaks A Foreign-Language Film Records

Godzilla Minus Zero had a great first weekend in theaters

Godzilla Minus Zero had a strong opening weekend, grossing more at the domestic box office than any live action foreign-language film before it. On top of that, a higher percentage of people sought out premium screens, like IMAX, to watch it even more than they did for The Odyssey earlier this year.

Deadline's reporting highlights that Godzilla Minus Zero is estimated to have grossed $32 million. Although American-made Godzilla movies have made more during their first weekend in theaters, this is a very impressive feat for a foreign-language film, as they rarely do this well at the domestic box office unless they're connected to an anime. As mentioned, this opening is record-breaking for a live-action one.

Godzilla Minus Zero's performance also shows the value of making movies that people want to see on the biggest screen possible, as around 74% of its gross came from IMAX or other premium large format screens. In comparison, The Odyssey got a lot of attention because around 54% of its opening weekend gross came from PLF screens. 2026 has certainly shown that there's demand for blockbusters that embrace that opulent style of filmmaking beyond a typical superhero movie.

Outside of Godzilla Minus Zero, the animated Cat in the Hat movie had a fairly underwhelming $20 million opening weekend, while You Can See Everything had an impressive hold week-over-week that makes a $100 million domestic gross more possible. That said, we do still seem to be in the quiet before the storm as new blockbuster Hunger Games, Avengers, and Dune movies hit theaters before the end of the year

#3501. Finally, CBS Confronts Painful Blue Bloods Truth With Boston Spinoff

Ana Dumaraog is a Writer and Editor at Screen Rant, where she expertly covers Network TV offerings, among other things She has spearheaded the effort to make the site an authority on broadcast shows, initially starting with The Big Bang Theory franchise, NCIS, and One Chicago before taking on the specialization in general. Warning! Spoilers ahead for Boston Blue season 2, episode 5, "Blood Diamond."Nearly two years after Blue Bloods ended its run, CBS finally confronts the painful truth about it with regard to Boston Blue. For a decade and a half, the Reagan family became a staple of the network's yearly slate, with the Tom Selleck-led series becoming a fan-favorite. Unlike the traditional police procedural, Blue Bloods differentiated itself by making it a family show first and foremost. The project dealt with a group of New York public officials, serving different agencies in the city.

After evading cancellation a couple of times, CBS officially cancelled the series in 2024, with Blue Bloods ending with season 14. The final stretch of the Reagans' run on TV was full of compelling cases and major personal milestones for the clan. It left viewers with the idea that while the series was wrapping, the Reagans' life in New York was going to continue. That was until it was announced that CBS was launching a spinoff with Donny Wahlberg's Danny spearheading Boston Blue. The offshoot has been a success thus far, and both Blue Bloods actors and their characters have been supportive of the expansion project. That said, it has always just been a matter of time before the long-ignored truth about Boston Blue comes to light.

Boston Blue has brought in multiple Reagans throughout the course of its run thus far. That said, its return during the CBS's fall 2026 slate marks the first time that it is featuring Will Estes as Jamie Reagan. The youngest of Frank's kids makes a trip up north to see how his older brother is doing after moving out of New York. Unlike Danny's interactions with Erin, Henry, and even Joe Hill, this latest reunion is tense, as Jamie finally confronts Wahlberg's character about leaving New York, and in effect, him.

Tackling this particularly difficult topic is long-overdue in Boston Blue. Granted that Sean's near-death experience was a justified reason for Danny to follow his son to Beantown, the offshoot arguably glossed over the specifics of his decision to not just stay with Sean temporarily, but uproot his whole life to be up north. For a clan that likes to discuss everything, Jamie reveals in his Boston Blue appearance that Danny barely talked to him about leaving. Blue Bloods was a family show; while the spinoff offered details about their conversations about the move, it didn't offer the whole picture, as it's difficult to imagine that it was an easy transition for the whole Regan clan. It took CBS a while, but thankfully, CBS finally addresses the matter.

It's no secret that Blue Bloods' cancellation was quite controversial. CBS had tried pulling the plug on the series a few times, but the cast and crew rallied to keep the series on the air. Despite the family procedural's popularity during its run, the network's budget cuts motivated them to cancel the series, which was expensive to make, considering that it was filming primarily on location in New York. Still, CBS recognized the popularity of the series and found a way to continue taking advantage of it, which resulted in Boston Blue.

The Raegans are preparing to say goodbye as Blue Bloods heads to its final episodes. Luckily, network TV already has a perfect 100% on Rotten Tomatoes

Considering the core message of Blue Bloods, splitting up the Reagans was the biggest hurdle when justifying the existence of Boston Blue. For over a decade and a half, the family came together every Sunday for family dinner, so seeing Danny leave would have been a major change for the clan. Jamie's debut in Boston Blue offers viewers an idea of how painful that transition was, even as the matter was originally ignored. That said, considering that his move was also for family, it's easier to accept it.

Blue Bloods follows the Reagan family, a multigenerational dynasty dedicated to law enforcement and public service in New York City. As Police Commissioner Frank Reagan and his children serve as a detective, patrol officer, prosecutor, and investigator, each episode balances the demands of policing with the family's personal lives.

Boston Blue follows NYPD officer Danny Reagan as he transitions to a role in the Boston Police Department. Partnered with detective Lena Peters, the eldest daughter of a notable law enforcement family, the series explores their collaboration within the dynamics of Boston's criminal landscape.

#3500. The Johnny Depp Comeback Hits Judgment Day with ‘Ebenezer’: How Paramount Is Carefully Reintroducing the Controversial Star

Hollywood studios turned away Johnny Depp eight years ago. With “Ebenezer,” Paramount Pictures is betting that audiences have not rejected him too. The “A Christmas Carol” adaptation, out November 13, marks a decisive moment for the studio, as it was one of the first films boarded by the company after its 2025 acquisition by Skydance.

Depp got some positive social media attention Monday evening when he was filmed “wyling out” and “wreaking havoc” in the Christmas Market of New York’s Bryant Park — as Scrooge, of course. In his first major pre-release promotional stop for “Ebenezer,” Depp donned a fright wig and make-up to enact some staged bah-humbugging, which included popping balloons, knocking over a Christmas tree, and playfully antagonizing an on-site Santa Claus. The stunt was Depp’s second in-character appearance as Scrooge, coming three months after a similarly interactive appearance at San Diego Comic-Con that also generated mounds of social media content from passerby. Later on at the event, Scrooge appeared onstage during Collider’s Directors on Directing panel to debut the first “Ebenezer” trailer. Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money The Bay Theater in Palisades Village, Closed Since the LA Wildfires, Will Reopen Thanks to Paramount and Rick Caruso

The approach leans into how audiences know Depp, who became one of the industry’s biggest stars in the aughts with his quirked-up performances in the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise and various Tim Burton joints. But several publicity veterans note that it’s also a strategy that helps the star skirt addressing himself: a typical component to the modern promotional gauntlet of podcast appearances and junketing. Paramount and representatives for Depp declined to comment for this story.

Indeed, the last time Depp was promoting a blockbuster in character was at Warner Bros.’ San Diego Comic-Con panel in 2018, where he appeared as Gellert Grindelwald, the seductively authoritarian wizard within J.K. Rowling’s world of “Harry Potter,” to promote the second “Fantastic Beasts” prequel. Depp was mired in controversy at the time, as his ex-wife, Amber Heard, alleged that he had been “physically abusive” in court documents filed in their divorce case. Depp denied the claims. Making things more awkward — Heard appeared at the same studio presentation, popping up an hour later for a panel hyping “Aquaman.”

Two years later, Depp departed from a third (and what ended up to be the final) “Fantastic Beasts” entry. On Instagram, the actor posted that he had been “asked to resign” by the studio. Depp had just lost a U.K. libel trial against The Sun, in which a judge ruled that an article reporting that the actor was a “wife beater” was found to be “substantially true.”

But Depp later claimed victory in a U.S. defamation trial against Heard herself. Heard had written a Washington Post op-ed in which she described herself as a survivor of domestic abuse. Depp claimed the article damaged his reputation and career; both parties argued the other was the aggressor through the grueling six-week spectacle. An initial jury ruling sided with Depp on three separate claims of defamation, ordering Heard pay him $10.35 million in damages. Heard won on one of her three counterclaims of defamation, ordering Depp to pay her $2 million. A later appeal by Heard ended with a settlement in which she agreed to pay $1 million to Depp.

The highly-gawked-at and internet-scrutinized trial reignited his fame and infamy, depending on your perspective. Once a big-screen titan, he was now ubiquitous on social media, particularly TikTok, emerging with an ardent online fanbase forged by a conviction that he was a man who had been rashly cast aside during the #MeToo movement’s prominence in the late 2010’s.

With “Ebenezer,” Paramount has the unique assignment of capitalizing on that celebrity, without inviting relitigation of an ugly legal battle that would cloud the sunny promotion of a family feature. Hence, the in-character appearances, along with underlining Depp’s penchant for transformative turns (though no further ones are planned). A promotional video featuring snippets of cast interviews, including the likes of Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Tramell Tillman, praise the actor as giving “a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before.”

“A less clever route would be turning the release into a ‘comeback’ victory lap. The result could be an unnecessary and noisy polarization of views, reviving the very controversy the studio would prefer to move beyond,” says media lawyer and crisis manager Amber Melville-Brown, who heads the media and reputation team at the law firm Withers. “A campaign built around vindication invites an argument about who, precisely, has been vindicated and for what — starting the debate over again. A campaign built around the performance sparks a different conversation.”

Meanwhile, Paramount has been careful to show “Ebenezer” to select audiences so far. The film was unveiled Sunday in New York City with a “special screening” at the Whitby Hotel’s 147-seat screening room — an intimate venue for the first unveiling of a studio feature. A handful of press outlets and more influencers were invited to a small carpet. One front-facing video posted by a guest featured her meeting Depp and calling the occasion “my sign from God that I chose the right path today.” A London premiere will take place at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Monday.

In another shrewd booking, Depp made a surprise onstage appearance during Aerosmith’s Hollywood Bowl concert on October 29. While other actors may tap in for a late-night spot or “Hot Ones” interview to mark the home stretch of film promotion, Depp instead let a guitar solo on “Train Kept A-Rollin'” do the talking.

Down the line, the “Ebenezer” review embargo will lift November 12, mere hours before public screenings begin — almost always a sign that a studio has little confidence in finding good PR from the critic class. The film’s director, Ti West, has usually drawn positive reviews through his career, mostly known as an indie horror darling until this first studio feature.

But most importantly for Paramount, “Ebenezer” doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to find success. The film’s production budget netted out to a rather modest $38 million, giving it a much easier pathway to theatrical profitability than Depp’s previous mega-budget tentpoles. Along with that comes hopes to leg out through the holiday season and a bank on grosses from overseas territories, where other older male movie stars like Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise have better retained their ability to sell tickets.

Rival studios are looking closely at whether audiences still see Depp as a big screen draw. Lionsgate is already in the Depp business for the revenge thriller “Day Drinker,” releasing in March. And at Disney’s D23 Expo in August, “Pirates of the Caribbean” producer Jerry Bruckheimer floated hopes to get the star on board for a sixth installment. That franchise has laid dormant for nearly a decade, despite numerous reports of development teams tinkering on a Depp-less take. In one of the more interesting quotes from the “Ebenezer” event in New York, Depp spoke with Entertainment Tonight and slid in a dig at the 2017 entry “Dead Men Tell No Tales,” saying he’d be open to a franchise return but noting that “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

But when Depp was first jettisoned from Hollywood’s A-list, major studios had begun to tire of his antics. There were reports of erratic on-set behavior, sky-high salary demands, and — in the true offender for studios — diminishing box office returns. The “Pirates” films still made money, but Depp headlined several costly bombs, including “Alice Through the Looking Glass” and “Mortdecai,” which had left companies less eager to write big checks, particularly given his public relations scandals.

But Depp’s absence may have not curbed his following. A National Research Group study from earlier this year found that he was the seventh-most cited name by people, especially in Europe, when they wre asked to name five actors or actresses that would motivate them to see “a new movie in a cinema,” even though he’s been away from the big screen for nearly a decade. Over those years, a growing refrain in the business has been that some movie stars have kneecapped their ability to open films by signing on to streaming productions, curbing consumers’ association of them with theaters. In that context, Depp may prove to be a unicorn, having essentially sat out years of the industry chasing Netflix — even if it wasn’t his choice to.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The process takes a few minutes, but it helps the soundbar perform better across different spaces rather than relying on a one-size-fits-all tuning profile. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

Its biggest compromise is bass—for a single soundbar, its low end is respectable, but it can't fully replace what a dedicated subwoofer brings to action movies, concerts, or bass-heavy music. The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3498. Was This Short-Lived '60s Sitcom Really The Worst Show To Ever Air On TV?

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The 1960s was truly a golden era for weird little shows that melded the quotidian and the fantastical. This was the decade that gave us the great fantasy sitcoms, in which some larger than life character with supernatural abilities would be slotted into a suburban setting for laughs. "Mister Ed" was one of the first, featuring a talking horse who could only be understood by his architect owner Wilbur Post (Alan Young). The much lesser-known "The Hathaways" was sort of in that vein as well. Rather than featuring an animal with fantastical powers, however, it featured three chimpanzees whose owners treated them as if they were actual children.

You might already be able to see why this series didn't last longer than a single season. But not only was "The Hathaways" short-lived, it seemed to stoke significant ire among certain critics. In "Watching TV: Four Decades of American Television," authors Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik outright described the show as "possibly the worst series ever to air on network TV."

Of course, such a claim is subjective. But there was an undeniably uncanny and slightly unsettling air to "The Hathaways," which saw Peggy Cass' Elinore Hathaway and Jack Weston's Walter Hathaway acting as "parents" to their three chimpanzees, referring to them as "the kids" and dressing them in human clothing. The suburban Los Angeles couple seemed to have completely lost the plot, yet it was all played for laughs. At least, it was for about 10 months. After that, ABC quite sensibly pulled the plug.

The sheer volume of failed shows in TV history is kind of breathtaking when you consider the amount of effort that goes into these things. Scripts are written, casts and production teams assembled, sets designed, and significant amounts of money are spent. (In the case of the swiftly-cancelled 1970s TV flop "Supertrain," we're talking major sums.) How many actors have been convinced that they were on the verge of their big break, only to become yet another footnote in TV history? It's weirdly tragic to think about. In the case of "The Hathaways," its chimpanzee stars were likely unfazed by the show's hasty cancellation, due to the fact they were in high demand elsewhere. That and they were literally animals.

Non-chimp leading man Jack Weston stars as Walter Hathaway, a real estate agent whose wife Elinore Hathaway acts as a mother to Candy, Charlie, and Enoch. These ape "kids" were part of the Marquis Chimps, a group of trained chimpanzees owned by Gene Detroy that were popular at the time. As the New York Times noted in a contemporaneous report ahead of the premiere of "The Hathaways," "The chimps got their new job through a TV guest appearance on 'The Jack Benny Show' [...] Robert Sparks, executive producer of the new series, saw them on the 'Benny' program and decided to develop a series."

That series saw Walter and Elinore taking care of their chimpanzee children while also booking them as a performing act, in which they would ride bicycles and build things. Otherwise, they would hang out at home, earning the Hathaways some strange looks from their neighbors. Other non-chimp cast members included Harvey Lembeck as talent agent Jerry Roper and Belle Montrose as neighbor Mrs. Harrison.

Was "The Hathaways" really one of the worst sitcoms of all time? Well, it was certainly strange. Perhaps, viewed in retrospect, the show feels a little too close to the unforgettable "Gordy" scene in Jordan Peele's "Nope," in which a chimpanzee mauls the entire cast and crew on the set of his sitcom. (Thankfully, nothing of the sort happened during filming on "The Hathaways.") But there's just something unsettling about the series, which seemed like a particularly cynical attempt at leveraging the chimps' popularity, even at a time when fantasy sitcoms featuring similarly unusual setups were coming to the fore. As Harry Castleman and Walter J. Podrazik write in their book, "The premise itself was utterly degrading to both the audience and the actors," adding that "The Hathaways" "stood as an embarrassing example of the depths programmers had reached in their desperate search for a chance hit in any format or premise."

Unsurprisingly, the sitcom didn't last long. "The Hathaways" debuted on ABC in October 1961 and was canceled by August 1962. A decade later, CBS tried its luck at a chimpanzee-led sitcom with "Me and the Chimp," which starred Ted Bessell as a dentist who lives with his family and a chimpanzee named Buttons. It, too, lasted one season. For some reason, NBC thought it could do better and unleashed "Mr. Smith" in 1983, a sitcom about a talking orangutan (played by the same ape who accompanied Clint Eastwood in his controversial project "Any Which Way But Loose") who becomes a political advisor after ingesting an experimental drug. Yep, one season. But "The Hathaways" remains the first and arguably the worst of these ape-led sitcoms.

#3497. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3496. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

#3495. Why Michael Stuhlbarg Left HBO's Boardwalk Empire

In "The Godfather Part II," Michael Corleone (Al Pacino) meets with the aged gangster Hyman Roth (Lee Strasberg) in his modest Florida home. Roth muses, "I've loved baseball ever since Arnold Rothstein fixed the World Series of 1919."

That reference isn't a movie embellishment. New York racketeer Arnold Rothstein really was alleged to have fixed the 1919 World Series in what's called "The Black Box Scandal," the blowback of which is explored in Season 1 of HBO's Prohibition period piece "Boardwalk Empire," featuring Michael Stuhlbarg as Rothstein. "AR," as his men often call him, remains a fixture of "Boardwalk Empire" during its first four seasons, and Stuhlbarg gives one of the show's standout performances.

Historians describe Rothstein as the one who put the "organized" in organized crime, thanks to a sharp knack for math and business. Stuhlbarg's Rothstein lives up to the history books. He's often shown playing pool or gambling and notes a great gambler never makes a bet without fixing the odds in his favor. He's extremely eloquent but only polite except in the most surface-level ways. Ice water runs in his veins.

So, it's a shame that he doesn't even get a real ending. History says that Rothstein died in 1928. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 ends in 1924, and then its fifth and final eight-episode season jumps ahead to 1931. That meant the show skips over lots of real history, including Rothstein's death. He simply disappears from the series, save for vague references to his demise in Season 5.

It's even more noticeable since his legacy hangs over the show's finale. "Boardwalk Empire" Season 5 includes a fictionalized account of how Rothstein's protégés "Lucky" Luciano (Vincent Piazza), Meyer Lansky (Anatol Yusef), and Benny "Bugsy" Siegel (Michael Zegen) took over the East Coast American mob.

Rothstein's death is a pretty big missing chapter in Season 5's story, but a consequence of the larger "Boardwalk Empire" production. Looking in from the outside, "Boardwalk Empire" appears to be a show that got cut short. A fifth and final season that's only two-thirds as long as the previous ones? And which leaps past several years of story? It's hard to believe that was always the intention. It really feels like a series that ran out of runway and jumped ahead to the intended ending to resolve itself as best it could. (Mind you, Season 5 still has some great episodes.)

The often repeated narrative is that "Boardwalk Empire" cost too much for HBO for too little a return, so it had to go. It was an unavoidably expensive show that came with a lot of homework for its cast (being a period piece), costing a reported $5 million per episode. The reported episode ratings do also show a consistent downward slump across seasons. From "Boardwalk Empire" Seasons 1-4, each successive season premiere and season finale was watched by fewer people than the previous one, and by Season 4, the show was slipping below even two million viewers an episode.

Nonetheless, "Boardwalk Empire" creator Terence Winter maintained back in 2014 that ending the series was a creative call. Speaking with Time and Hitflix, Winter said he and his writers felt series lead Nucky Thompson (Steve Buscemi) was already nearing his story's end by Season 4. 1931 was chosen as the most natural endpoint because it's when Al Capone (Stephen Graham) went to prison, Luciano and Lansky began the mafia's Commission, and Prohibition was winding down. The cost was skipping over major events like Rothstein's murder, which in real life remains shrouded in mystery.

Reportedly, Rothstein owed $300,000 after a poker loss and refused to pay up, earning him a bullet to the gut on November 4, 1928. But he took his killer's identity to the grave. Rothstein's real death being unsolved would give "Boardwalk Empire" dramatic license to fill in the details. I'm confident it would've pulled it off since whenever Rothstein was onscreen, "Boardwalk Empire" became a more compelling show.

The ending of "Boardwalk Empire" Season 4 even directly teases more to come from Rothstein. He enters a business alliance with Nucky's ex-wife, Margaret Thompson (a pre-"Lanterns" Kelly Macdonald), who is working as a secretary at a New York City investment firm and agrees to slip Rothstein insider information. Instead, nothing comes of that.

Stuhlbarg deserves a mountain's worth of credit. The actor studied his character, including how the real Rothstein thought of himself as a businessman and held his conduct to such a standard, and he's said the "Boardwalk Empire" writers' room was "amiable" about implementing his own research into his character. Stuhlbarg was similarly gracious about not returning for Season 5, especially considering it wasn't even his choice to leave the show, saying during a 2014 press junket that:

"They had to act fast, and they had a lot of ground to cover. It was amazing that we all got as much coverage as we did, considering how many characters they were juggling. I had so much fun doing the show, and I had no regrets. And yeah, sure it would've been fun to have shown [Rothstein's death], but I thought what they came up with was very cool, as it was. I think if they could have, they would've shown it, but they didn't have the time."

#3493. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3492. 36 Years Later, The Best Pennywise Line In IT Is Still The Creepiest In Horror TV History

Although Stephen King has written plenty of terrifying villains in his time, one standout quote from 1990’s IT miniseries has the unique distinction of remaining the single scariest line in the history of the medium. There are some heavy-hitting competitors when it comes crowning the creepiest single line of all time on TV. Littlefinger’s Game of Thrones speech about chaos is chilling, but hardly outright scary so much as it is enthralling.

Meanwhile, the creepiest line in Twin Peaks is unbelievably tragic in context, but it is delivered with a plaintive sadness entirely at odds with the panic-attack-inducing terror of what’s happening onscreen. This disconnect is typical of David Lynch and Mark Frost’s inimitable murde mystery masterpiece Twin Peaks, but it also means that the scariest line in the show is only scary in context.

In contrast, the true scariest line in TV history is one that can still send chills down the spine of viewers familiar with the series despite how comparatively tame the show itself is. 1990’s IT miniseries had to cut a lot out of Stephen King’s 1986 novel of the same name, both to conform to network TV censorship standards and to fit within a reasonable runtime. However, the show found room for Tim Curry to deliver the definitive version of Pennywise’s promise, and it is one that still haunts nightmares worldwide decades later.

In the very first scene of 1990's miniseries version of IT, as poor doomed Georgie attempts to retrieve his little paper boat from a flooded storm drain, Curry’s grinning clown welcomes him with a cryptic promise. He reassures George that “They float, Georgie... They float... and when you're down here with me... You’ll float too!” The line is delivered not with genuine malice, but rather a jarringly friendly glee that would fit a kid’s TV host.

The late, great Curry was a master of delivery, and his version of Pennywise arguably outdoes even the far gorier HBOMax prequel Welcome to Derry’s killer clown as he often seems like an actual real-life clown. A comedic veteran, Curry brings the same panache and charisma seen in everything from The Rocky Horror Picture Show to Muppet Treasure Island to the role of Pennywise and, unlike Bill Skarsgard’s more feral, animalistic Pennywise, he plays the clown as an actual children’s entertainer.

The result of this risky choice is a number of scenes, including the infamous "Prince Albert in a can" gag, that are simply genuinely funny instead of being scary. However, rather than ruining the character’s mystique, the comedy of these scenes only serves to make the moments where Pennywise becomes an inhuman monster all the more terrifying.

It is a delicate tonal tightrope, one that other King adaptations like versions of Carrie often have to tread when depicting characters who are both scary and potentially ludicrous, like Margaret White. However, Curry manages to not only nail the balance between Pennywise’s clowning and his evil, but also to encapsulate both contrasting versions of the character in this single line.

When Pennywise begins to tell Georgie about how they float down in his underground lair, he seems genuinely happy to be sharing a secret with the kid, and Curry’s giddy enthusiasm makes Georgie’s unfazed response feel believable. As his giddiness gives way to gleeful, deranged sadism, it feels horribly believable that Georgie might not notice what is so worryingly off about this clown until it is too late.

Over the years, later Stephen King shows and the increased prevalence of killer clowns in movies and TV have led new viewers to complain that no kid would go anywhere near Curry’s obviously evil monster in a million years. However, rewatching It’s opening scene without knowing where the story is going, what makes its most famous line so scary is how genuinely friendly the Stephen King villain seems to his utterly innocent, sheltered prey.

#3491. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3490. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3489. This X-Men-Esque '80s Sci-Fi Series Launched Courteney Cox's Career

The premise of James D. Parriott's 1985 superhero/comedy series "Misfits of Science," which featured a young Courteney Cox, will sound very familiar to fans of Marvel Comics' X-Men titles.

The series follows a human scientist named Dr. Billy Hayes (Dean Paul Martin), who has taken an interest in what he called "human anomalies," which are people who have been born with a variety of unpredictable superpowers. In the show's pilot episode, he assembles the main cast of powerful castoffs with the intention of studying them, but also helping them come to terms with their supernatural abilities.

The team was small but mighty. It included Dr. Hayes' lab partner, Dr. Lincoln (Kevin Peter Hall), who can shrink for a limited period. Additionally, Mark Thomas Miller plays "Johnny B" Bukowski, a rocker who can suck up electricity and who wears shades to cover his glowing eyes. He can throw lightning bolts.

Most strikingly, Courteney Cox, future star of "Friends" and "Scream," plays Gloria, a troubled teen with "Carrie"-like telekinetic powers. "Misfits of Science" wasn't Cox's first credit: She had appeared in an episode of "As the World Turns" back in 1975, when she was still a kid, and famously danced with Bruce Springsteen in the "Dancing in the Dark" music video in 1984. "Misfits of Science," though, was the first time Cox starred in a TV series.

"Misfits of Science" is not currently available to stream, but resourceful media hunters will be able to find episodes online easily enough. It's a whimsical, lighthearted show that prodded at the conventions of superheroes as much as it vaunted them. It's definitely worth a glance.

"Misfits of Science," it should be noted, only lasted for a single 16-episode season, so it's okay if you don't remember it.

The series does have something of a superhero legacy, as R. Timothy Kring, a.k.a. Tim Kring, wrote an episode of "Misfits of Science," and he would go on to create the hit series "Heroes," the first season of which remains a must-watch (the later seasons, though, less so). Kring's "Misfits" episode, called "Twin Engines," is about a young man (Joel Polis) who is plagued with uncontrollable visions. It's eventually revealed that he was sharing the visions of his long-lost twin brother.

Indeed, the entire show was based on a long series of super-powered shenanigans and investigations. Mostly, the protagonists get involved in run-of-the-mill spy plots. The main characters aren't costumed vigilantes, but they do seem to operate as freelance spies. Famed drummer Mikey Jones appears in the show's pilot as a character with freezing powers named Ice Man. According to Giant Freakin' Robot, that character was abandoned after Marvel Comics "raised objections" over its own Ice Man character. And speaking of Marvel, Courteney Cox's character was very similar to the X-Men's Jean Gray.

Some fun trivia: Shortly after the time "Misfits of Science" was being made, Dr. Lincoln actor Kevin Peter Hall (who played the original Predator in John McTiernan's sci-fi action classic) was in contention to play either Data or Geordi La Forge on "Star Trek: The Next Generation." /Film has previously talked about all the finalists for the roles, and Hall eventually lost the roles to Brent Spiner and LeVar Burton, respectively.

As mentioned, "Misfits of Science" was not successful. Thanks to low ratings, the series was canceled before all of its episodes could even air, leaving one of them unaired in the United States.

Courteney Cox continued to work undeterred, of course. In 1987, she appeared in the low-budget, high-profile Cannon adaptation of "Masters of the Universe," a movie so goofy, it has been subjected to a "How Did This Get Made" oral history. That same year, she began playing the recurring role of Lauren Miller on the hit sitcom "Family Ties." By 1994, she was appearing in the comedy "Ace Ventura: Pet Detective" and began playing one of the six lead roles on "Friends." "Misfits of Science" was her first starring role, but it certainly wasn't her last.
