#3486. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3485. This Handheld Vacuum Fixed My Biggest Problem With Cleaning

We're highlighting the small changes—from useful new gadgets, to fresh productivity techniques, to efficient hacks—that are improving our lives on a weekly basis.

I may not be “messy,” exactly, but no one would describe me as “neat,” either. One of my biggest issues is that I tend to wait for a mess to get big enough to justify dragging out a full-size vacuum before I deal with it, because a full-size vacuum means finding the cord or the charger, wrestling it out of the closet, going room to room, and then putting it all away again. When the mess in question is still only a few cracker crumbs? Forget it—I'm just too lazy.

The solution to my laziness has been removing all the friction and hassle of my full-size vacuum, and instead keeping a handheld vacuum always within reach.

Though there are many handheld vacuums out there, I use the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, which I got from Target. It's great for quickly sucking up crumbs and everyday messes, and that's exactly the job I need it to handle. The "dual air" part is what makes it more interesting than your average handheld: It's both a vacuum and a blower, so it can pull debris in or push it out, depending on what you're dealing with. I didn’t expect to need the blower at all, but I’m surprised how handy it is for blasting crumbs out of keyboard keys or loosening up stubborn debris before I suck it up.

The result is that my apartment is simply cleaner. Not because I'm spending more time cleaning overall, but because I'm no longer letting small messes pile up into big ones. When my monthly (or quarterly) deep clean does roll around, it's far less painful, because there's so much less to deal with. Perhaps this is the real upgrade: cleaning up messes the moment they happen instead of saving them up.

I love the Sharper Image Dual Air Slim, but there are plenty of similar cordless handheld vacuum and air duster combos out there, and they tend to land in a pretty similar price range. If another one catches your eye, or goes on sale, or has a design you prefer, go for it.

When comparing models, here are my handheld vacuum musts:

It should offer both vacuum and blower modes.

It should be both cordless and rechargeable. If it needs an outlet, you'll have another barrier to using it, and that defeats the purpose.

It should be lightweight and slim. You want something you can grab and use one-handed without thinking about it.

The dust cup should be easy to empty. If emptying it is a hassle, you'll use it less.

You should be able to keep it in plain sight. The closer it lives to where messes happen (the kitchen, the entryway), the more you'll use it.

I used to think a clean apartment meant big, scheduled cleaning sessions. Now I think it's mostly about making the small stuff effortless. A handheld vacuum and blower won't replace your regular vacuum, but it will make you far less likely to need it as often. If you've been waiting for the next big mess, or the next big clean, to get things tidy, consider changing the system instead.

#3484. This Chilling Japanese Folk Horror Series Is One Of Hulu's Best Hidden Gems

If you're in the mood for a discrete dose of folk horror, Hulu recently added Adam Scott's terrifying horror "Hokum." But if you'd like to extend your trauma over, say two seasons of sheer terror, then "Gannibal" is for you. The show stars Yuya Yagira as a police officer who leaves the city to start over in a remote village. Here, he quickly discovers things aren't quite as idyllic as they seem.

"Gannibal" premiered in December 2022 but has failed to make much of an impact outside of Japan, despite arguably being one of the best horror series of the 2020s. Thus far, two seasons of "Gannibal" have been released, and had they hit Netflix in the United States, the show may well have become a big hit stateside. As it stands, this is one of Japan's best kept secrets and it's waiting to be discovered on Hulu.

Masaaki Ninomiya's "Gannibal" manga was originally serialized across thirteen volumes from October 2018 to November 2021. In October of that year, it was announced that "Gannibal" would be adapted as a TV series, with Shinzo Katayama directing from teleplays by Takamasa Oe.Thankfully, it turned out to be a worthy adaptation.

One of the best foreign horror shows streaming right now, "Gannibal" shares much in common with the South Korean horror movie with a 99% Rotten Tomatoes score "The Wailing." Both are set in remote villages and follow a police officer who becomes increasingly menaced by some terrifying ancient evil. But "Gannibal" departs from the movie with its tale of a cannibal conspiracy.

Yuya Yagira plays police officer Daigo Agawa, who after an unfortunate ordeal in Tokyo moves to the small mountain village of Kuge with his wife Yuki Agawa (Riho Yoshioka) and daughter Mashiro Agawa (Kokone Shimizu). At first, this secluded hamlet seems like the ideal refuge from the city and Agawa's fraught past. But things get off to an eerie start as Kuge's previous police officer has mysteriously vanished.

As Agawa and his family become more acquainted with the village and its people they discover the Goto family essentially run the town, and they don't seem like the most charming bunch. Meanwhile, a woman's body is found on the mountain, and while the Gotos claim she was killed by a bear, Agawa notices a human bite mark. Soon, his family's escape starts to turn into a nightmare. As such, this is not a horror TV show you can watch with the whole family. But it definitely deserves your attention regardless.

While you may never have heard of "Gannibal," the series has become a sensation in its native Japan. In April 2025, The Hollywood Reporter reported that "Gannibal" had become the most-viewed title in the country on Disney+ since its second season debuted in March of that year. The show also set new records for the streamer, solidifying its status as a bonafide mega-hit in Japan. In the United States, however, "Gannibal" mostly flew under the radar.

There are no "top critic" reviews for the series on Rotten Tomatoes, and it hasn't shown up on any "best horror series" lists since its 2022 debut. But it has managed to generate a small amount of buzz among non-Japanese viewers. One Redditor described the series as "grim folk horror" and was evidently left "completely wrecked" by it. Elsewhere on Reddit, another user described the series as "like 'Midsommar' meets 'Resident Evil 7'" and praised the "amazing actors, great cinematography, chilling and memorable soundtrack, and an absurdly dark story."

Letterboxd users are similarly impressed. "I just love it," writes one, who goes on to commend the series for its "sharp plot," "creepy characters," and "unsettling vibes," as well as the "splendid cinematography." Another also highlighted how the show is "beautifully shot and incredibly well-acted." Unfortunately, it seems unlikely there will be more to come. "Gannibal" Season 2 was released on March 19, 2025 and that wrapped up the story told in Masaaki Ninomiya's manga. Thankfully, if you are able to binge your way through both seasons of the series, there are plenty of great folk horror movies to tide you over.

#3483. Recasting Sabrina The Teenage Witch In 2026: All 9 Main Roles

In 1996, Melissa Joan Hart perfectly embodied the titular star of the magical coming-of-age sitcom, Sabrina the Teenage Witch, but 30 years on, a reboot could have a very different cast. The show was a massive success, and as such, it ended up running for seven seasons from 1996 until 2003.

Beyond that, the series also ended up with an animated spin-off and sequel, a reimagined revival in 2018 which took a much darker approach to the narrative, and a handful of feature films, including the 1996 movie starring Hart and Ryan Reynolds that kicked it all off.

But, if TV executives wanted to bring the series back today, and stick more closely to the light-hearted comedy roots of the 1996 series, there are only a handful of actors who could really excel at playing the parts that brought this series to life in the first place.

First up, we need a loud, boisterous, and versatile actor who can bring the humor, enthusiasm, and depth to the character of Sabrina that this role deserves. And with that in mind, there is no one better suited to playing this part than Ruby Stokes. Stokes has been steadily building out her credits since 2010, with a major turn in 2016 when she played a central role in the film Una.

Since then, Stokes has tackled a variety of performances, from the stage to the screen, and performed in period dramas, dark comedies, and captivating dramas, all of which have given her both the experience to play the role and more than qualified her to take the lead as a mischievous young witch discovering her powers.

While Gillian Jacobs played the uptight and anxious Britta in Community, the role that she is currently best known for, she also has the capacity to play much more laid-back and fun-loving roles. And considering Hilda Spellman, one of Sabrina's aunts who is also a full witch, is prone to act on impulse and take things less seriously than her sister Zelda, it would make a lot of sense to cast Jacobs as Hilda.

Hilda is the younger sister who loves to have fun and is willing to play along with Sabrina's ideas, often getting herself in trouble with her sister along with their niece. Jacobs brings humor, vibrancy, and warmth to her roles that allows her to deliver characters who may not be the most practical, but they are certainly endearing.

Meanwhile, Zelda Spellman is frequently the voice of reason, and the most level-headed witch in the room. In order to bring this part to life, someone like Ayo Edebiri, who recently came off her turn in the incredible series, The Bear, would be an ideal choice to play the person keeping everything together while everyone else is chasing their own directions.

In many ways, this is exactly how her character, Sydney, ended her run in The Bear, having learned valuable lessons through her challenging work with the team at The Bear restaurant, before taking the reins and becoming the Head Chef and co-owner. So, in a sense, playing Zelda could help to see that type of character evolve even further in Edebiri's capable hands.

Bill Hader is an accomplished comedy actor whose deadpan delivery style has made him a fan favorite throughout his career, from his time as a regular cast member on SNL to a series of roles in TV and film over the last decade or so. Hader has also taken to voice acting in recent years with a growing list of credits for major roles in projects such as The Cat in The Hat, Inside Out, and many more.

With all of that preparation, Hader is easily the strongest candidate to tackle the sarcastic and snappy wizard who was turned into a cat as a punishment for attempting to take over the world, Salem.

Harvey Winkle is the awkward but lovable, goofy and endearing love interest that Sabrina Spellman finds herself fawning over. While the character in the 1996 series was popular thanks to his status as an athlete, times have moved on, and there are many other qualities that earn people a stamp of popularity and approval in high school settings, which opens the door for an updated take on Harvey, played by Jack Martin.

Martin has only recently started to land credited roles on the screen with his career taking off in 2020. Since then, he has tackled a number of small parts in TV and film, before landing a central role in the 2026 comedy series, Not Suitable For Work. It's here that Martin proved himself as the perfect cast for a part like Harvey Kinkle, and with that series getting axed after its debut season, Martin has some space on his schedule.

Libby Chessler is the quintessentially popular girl in a high school setting who is the head of the cheerleading squad, and who is frequently seen belittling and mocking other girls for being weird, or as Libby liberally refers to her classmates such as Sabrina, "freaks."

As an athlete, it makes sense to cast a performer like Maddie Ziegler who can bring the physicality to the role to convincingly play this part, while also having a cold and intense outward face that could inspire fear in others and establish her as a dominant force.

On the back of his performance as Phil Dunphy in Modern Family, Ty Burrell is an outstanding actor who brings so much physicality, personality, and incredible humor to his roles. All of that would go a long way to depicting one of the most fascinating mainstays of the original show, Principal Willard Kraft.

Principal Kraft is a bit of a bumbling buffoon who has an intense crush on Sabrina's aunt Hilda, but throughout the show's run ends up sparking relationships with both aunts at different points. Burrell would be an incredible addition to the lineup, and one that could reasonably juggle all of the different facets of the character that becomes so integral throughout the show's run.

In season 1 of Sabrina the Teenage Witch, Sabrina has a best friend by the name of Jenny Kelley. Jenny is quirky, studious, and eccentric, which means she matches Sabrina's energy as a young witch without knowing her friend's newfound secret. Together, the pair get up to all sorts of misadventures, and they appear to have a powerful bond that brings them together.

However, the series mysteriously replaced the character from season 2 onward. Regardless, a reboot could bring Jenny Kelley back into the story with an actor like Anna Cathcart who delivered an outstanding performance in To All the Boys and XO, Kitty, making her a more central and enduring part of the narrative. Cathcart perfectly embodies the traits of this character, and would make a great contrast to the energy that Ruby Stokes could bring to Sabrina.

In seasons 2 and 3, Valerie Birkhead takes Jenny's place as Sabrina's best friend, and the show avoids referencing Jenny ever again. Valerie then asserts herself as the new best friend, though the energy she brings to the part is much more self-conscious, shy, and awkward. And in a reboot, it would be great to have Sabrina matched up with both Jenny and Valerie to flesh out the cast and give the character more to bounce off.

So, to tackle this role, an experienced comedy actor with a talent for playing more reserved and quiet roles makes the most sense, which is why Iris Apatow is a perfect fit. Apatow has perfected the portrayal of teenage neuroticism that is central to playing the role of Valerie, and her presence opposite Ruby Stokes would be a pleasure to watch unfold.

All in all, while an updated take on Sabrina the Teenage Witch would no doubt look very different to what came before, the talent to pull off such a reboot is perfectly positioned to make an updated version of the series that captures the magic of the original.

#3482. ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

For one of the most important screenings of “To Hold a Mountain,” the filmmakers had to bring their own electricity. In July, co-directors Biljana Tutorov and Petar Glomazić hauled a tent, a generator, and a DCP up to the Montenegrin highlands where they had spent years filming.

The creative couple, also partnered in life, wanted the shepherds who lived and worked in Sinjajevina to see the movie they had made possible. But by then, Montenegro had already resolved their story’s central conflict — scrapping the government’s plan to turn these people’s ancestral pastures into a military training ground after joining NATO in 2017. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“To Hold a Mountain” won the World Cinema Grand Jury Prize for documentary at Sundance, and Montenegro’s prime minister and president even showed up to the shepherds’ screening with their families, unannounced. When the film opens at New York’s Film Forum on December 16, American audiences will see the feature’s updated conclusion.

“We reopened the film to continue shooting and then a second end happened that was very empowering and powerful,” Tutorov said at IndieWire’s Art of the Doc series.

During our conversation, the filmmaker recalled arriving in Sinjajevina with Glomazić on the first day of protest. They wanted to help the community and make a movie, and agreed early on that those were two different jobs.

“We will separate our activist mission from our filmmaker’s mission,” she said. “That was a very good decision because it allowed us to be very bold in both roles.”

Onscreen, the fight over who would get to lay claim to the mountain centered on two people who already did: Gara, a shepherd and community leader, and Nada, the young girl she was raising. As the threat to their home brought a history of violence in their own family to the surface, the directors had to reckon with how much of Nada’s private life might become public.

“We really wanted it to be an empowering experience for [her],” Tutorov said.

Nada was twelve and a half when the filmmakers began to understand what the story would ask of her, and Tutorov said they decided to keep filming until she turned eighteen — precisely so Nada could decide for herself whether she wanted to be part of it. The crew logged more than 230 shooting days, though some yielded only half an hour of footage.

Gara and Nada had work to do, too. The directors and cinematographer Eva Kraljević shared a small shepherd’s shed, assisting with various chores including cows that had to be milked twice a day. Over successive summers, their routine became a framing device. Tutorov, who studied art history, thinks of the mountain as a kind of chorus bearing witness to living things on it.

Last July, just as the filmmakers were wrapping up, Montenegro’s government canceled the training-ground plan. Tutorov believes “To Hold a Mountain” and how it told the existing community’s story influenced that decision. She also pointed out that a different government was in power by 2025, following years of organizing by Sinjajevina locals.

At the shepherd’s screening a year later, Prime Minister Milojko Spajić said the film reinforced his view that canceling the plan had been the right call. Then Montenegro chose “To Hold a Mountain” as its official submission for the international feature Oscar. Tutorov said there was irony in realizing that, after years of fighting the government, she and Glomazić would be proudly representing the country on a global stage.

“It feels like they really kind of destroyed our strategy,” she said, warmly.

It’s a good joke, and an even better reason to remember that rough-and-tumble showing. For an evening, the people who’d spent years making their case to the government got to host its leaders on the very land they’d fought to keep. Tutorov recalled what Montenegro’s president told the filmmakers after seeing the movie: “Thank you guys for teaching us democracy.”

You can get thousands of free e-books over the course of 2026 if you know where—and when—to look. All year long, Amazon is offering free Kindle e-books to readers, with new opportunities popping up every month. In November, Prime members can get two free Kindle e-books from Amazon's First Reads program.

Amazon First Reads is a program aimed at Prime members that offers early access to new e-books across many genres, as curated by First Reads editors (one of many Prime Member benefits). Prime members can choose to download one free e-book every month from a rotating list—though some months that number is bumped up to two, usually with a free short novel—and non-members get them for a discounted price. These e-books can be read on any compatible Kindle device or via the free Kindle app.

Go to the First Reads landing page to see the full list of e-books available this month. Once you find a book that seems interesting, click the "Shop Now" button from the First Reads landing page. Make sure you’re not being redirected to the Kindle or Amazon mobile application, because you won't see the free book option there; instead, use your internet browser on your phone or computer.

Make sure you’re not clicking the ”Pre-order for...” button, as that will direct you to pay. Instead, click the “Read for Free” or the "Buy Now with 1-Click" button under the "First Reads" banner on the book's Amazon page (don't worry, you won't be charged). This will send the e-book directly to the Kindle linked to your Amazon account. You can see what it should look like from the screenshot below.

You’ll know you did it right when you see a “Thanks, [your name]!” order summary indicating the e-book is being auto-delivered to the Kindle Cloud Reader.

#3478. ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases “Zi” in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

A Hong Kong violinist who’s losing her grip on reality, young Zi (Michelle Mao) is haunted by visions of her future self. The doctors at the local neurology center suspect that she might be suffering from the early symptoms of a brain tumor, but Zi — a being of pure cinema, cobbled together from the half-formed memories of films like “La Jetée” and “Cléo from 5 to 7” — will have to wait a long and lonely 24 hours for the test results to come back.  Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

Well, maybe not so lonely. Crying on one of the innumerable concrete steps that climb Lantau Island, Zi is consoled by a sweet American expat with a strangely familiar face (and an aggressively unnatural blonde wig). Her name is L, she’s a disillusioned former dancer played by the luminous Haley Lu Richardson, and she can’t help but reciprocate the inexplicable closeness that Zi feels towards her. Over the course of a single night together, these two lost souls will help to relocate each other in time — to resynchronize with the world around them, reconnect with the infinite potential of the present, and return themselves to the creative purpose that once anchored them to it.

Even if seen without a shred of context, it would be obvious to anyone that “Zi” was made by someone who is — or hopefully was — desperate to spark a realignment of his own. To steal himself away from regret and anxiety and tether his perspective back to the now. Shot without a script or a budget in the immediate aftermath of Kogonada’s ill-received “A Big Bold Beautiful Journey” (the “After Yang” auteur’s studio debut, by all indications a soul-crushing experience for an artist whose two previous features retained the delicate grace of the video essays that he used to make), this searching and unformed wisp of an experiment hardly represents the first time that an ascendent director has scaled down after a misstep, but “Zi” takes the notion of “one for me” to much greater and more galvanizing extremes than usual.

This isn’t just a filmmaker trying to get back on track, it’s a filmmaker desperately, nakedly searching for a way to fall back in love with filmmaking itself. A way to prove that it might still love him back. (Kogonada described the project to IndieWire as “A retreat, as well as a pursuit.”)

While the prospect of watching Kogonada do that will naturally be of greater interest to those who have watched him get to this point, this movie’s palpably improvised nature — its stolen shots and recursive shape lend the impression of someone trying to cut their ultra-evocative vacation footage into a coherent narrative — would force anyone to wonder about the meta-textual aspects of its creation. “You feel like your sole purpose in life is something, and it doesn’t choose you back,” L sputters out at one point. “What do you do with that? I had to get away from it all. That’s why I came here. Wandering.”

Since arriving in Hong Kong, she’s made a habit of collecting sounds in much the same way as Kogonada has come there on the hunt for images. They both find a dissonance around Victoria Harbor that reflects their internal feelings of otherness and self-alienation. It’s China, but not. It’s a single city, but one split across two main areas by a stretch of the sea that some people never cross. It’s among the world’s most densely populated metropolises, but the vertical terrain seems fundamentally inhospitable to human civilization, and nature continues to assert itself between every skyscraper, shopping mansion, and crack in the sidewalk. Zi is the only native character in the film, but the history and design of Hong Kong reflects her disassociation as well — like her, the former British colony’s experience of the present is delayed.

That’s the closest thing to a diagnosis we get for what ails her, though it’s clear that Kogonada is leaning more towards soft science-fiction than the stuff of hard medicine. “Temoral relativism” is how L’s ex-fiancé Min (Jin Ha) describes it, though he’s slow to reveal how much he knows about Zi’s condition. Everything she perceives is already in the past. I suppose that’s true for all of us to some degree, if you factor in the nanoseconds that elapse between stimuli and our ability to perceive it, but the situation is more pronounced for Zi (who Mao plays with the effervescent helplessness of a paper airplane). Of course, that doesn’t explain why she believes she’s bearing witness to visions of her future self, but that confusion only exacerbates her feelings of distance from the present.

Even in its more platonic dimensions, the threadbare story that gradually allows Zi to close that gap is awash with the romance of loss, reconciliation, and belonging. Kogonada is falling back in love with the movies right before our eyes, and yet,  in characteristic fashion, that process isn’t garish or forced. His is a vision that is revealed through careful subtraction — by clearing away all of the dust and smudges that came to obscure it.

While Kogonada indulges in a few legible winks to his cinematic forebears (the most obvious of those being a step-printed homage to Wong Kar Wai, and my most far-fetched being a disoriented nod to José Luis Guerín’s “In the City of Sylvia”), he and cinematographer Benjamin Loeb almost completely eschew the neon exoticism that foreigners tend to look for in Hong Kong, with the vast majority of the film being captured in unfussy handheld shots that accentuate its here-and-now anxiety and delegate the emotional heavy lifting to an impeccably curated soundtrack of Ryuichi Sakamoto remixes and originals.

By the end, “Zi” engenders a certain emotional attachment toward and between its characters, all of it building to a gently unexpected gutpunch of a final minute. But even that last-minute reveal — not a plot twist so much as a sudden change in perspective — is rooted more in the movie’s form than its plot, as Kogonada’s characters remain largely symbolic of their function in the writer-director’s journey back to himself.

It’s a testament to Mao, Ha, and especially Richardson — who continues to be so good at grounding Kogonada’s most abstract ideas in a tender human place — that “Zi” retains even a soft dramatic pull as it searches for the present, though its recursive nature certainly wasn’t conceived with a casual audience in mind. If you’re hooked, which I wasn’t, or haunted by it, which I was, that will likely have less to do with an acute emotional connection to these characters than with the overflowing rewards of watching someone rediscover the sound of their own voice, and hear a way forward into the future in its echoes.

“Zi” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Grasshopper Film releases it in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3477. 10 Brilliant Sci-Fi Books You Can Finish in One Day

Time is finite, and reading takes it. Further, reading takes up more time than certain other forms of entertainment, because if you're sufficiently dedicated (and not being employed helps), a couple of movies a day, on average, is doable. Depending on what games you like, maybe you can get through those within a day or two (not all games), and then… okay, TV shows take a while, but again, not all shows. Getting through a miniseries might not be that much more of a time commitment than your average epic film.

With books, though, unless you're skim-reading, or maybe listening to audiobooks with the speed way up, you're generally not going to be able to get through as many. Of course, one other strategy is targeting shorter books, especially if you want to keep reading but don’t feel like you have a great deal of free time. These are all sci-fi books that can be read in a day, generally not topping 200 pages and therefore being completable within a matter of hours, rather than a matter of days or weeks. They're also high-quality books, so that helps make them easy to digest rather speedily, too.

The Running Man was written by Richard Bachman, at least according to the cover, but Richard Bachman is Stephen King, and The Running Man wasn’t released too far back in time from the point that the truth came out. Anyway, it is worth reading if you’ve generally liked all the “official” Stephen King books, but The Running Man stands out for being particularly fast-paced, even compared to some of King’s slimmer and speedier novels.

The Running Man does not take very much time to read at all, and then, according to King, it also took very little time to write.

It definitely earns its title, with the main character being on the run the whole time, taking part in a dangerous high-risk/high-reward game show, and it’s all done in a way to make you feel like you're there alongside him, needing to sprint much of the time as well. The Running Man does not take very much time to read at all, and then, according to King, it also took very little time to write, as he wrote the first draft in about a week. Truly breathless writing and reading here, nice and in-sync and all.

So you “can” finish Burning Chrome in a day, but whether you “should” finish Burning Chrome in a day… maybe not. It’s quite dense, because it’s written by William Gibson, and that is his style, more or less. It’s just that it’s a bit more digestible than most of his novels, since this short story collection is slimmer in terms of pages, and then the stories don’t really unravel (or Sprawl, ha) as much as his longer works, so you ultimately don’t get as lost.

If you don’t read it in one day, you'll probably burn through Burning Chrome in maybe a couple of days. Most of the stories here are pretty strong, and if you're a big cyberpunk fan who’s somehow not read this particular collection yet, then it feels logical to make doing that a priority.

Don’t enter into Slaughterhouse-Five expecting a ton of science fiction elements, since this is a slim book and it only has so much room to operate within all the different genres it chooses to tackle. And there are a lot, since this takes place during World War II, kind of, and also after the war (again, kind of), with it being dramatic, sometimes satirical, and also generally quite confounding.

It’s equal parts effective and unique as an anti-war novel, and it’s also interesting in how it chooses to (once more, kind of) incorporate a sort of time travel into the whole mind-bending nightmare that it is. Emotionally, it’s not an easy read, though Slaughterhouse-Five is always quite gripping and engaging, and then if you have an afternoon or evening free, you will likely be able to (and probably even want to) get through it in a single sitting.

Graphic novels or volumes of an ongoing manga series are usually comparable to “ordinary” novels if you just look at the number of pages, but when the story’s being told with images alongside text, it’s inevitably only going to be particularly text-heavy graphic novels (or comic/manga-like works) that take a similar amount of time to read as novels that are just text.

With Akira, it’s an especially visual manga series, so if you just tackled all 2000-ish pages of it, spread out across six main volumes, it might take about a week, or even a little less. And so take Vol. 1, for instance, which is the one to start with for hopefully very, very obvious reasons, and you can blast through it in probably an hour or two, though if you want to spend a bit more time with it marveling at the impressive and seriously detailed artwork, then honestly, fair enough!

The movie version of A Clockwork Orange is probably more famous than the book, but it’s worth mentioning because you could probably get through the book in only a little more time than it would take to watch the film. It’s a 136-minute-long movie made from a book that’s under 200 pages, and sure, reading speeds vary, but four or five hours at the most is probably enough for most readers to digest this one.

Oh, unless you're struggling with the slang, wanting to understand every word, perhaps by checking a guide or something. That would slow you down. Otherwise, A Clockwork Orange is not a huge time commitment, and it’s packed with stuff to think about (and feel unsettled by), so it certainly lingers in the mind for a great deal longer than it takes to actually read.

This one’s here for similar reasons to Burning Chrome, because I, Robot is a collection of short stories by a legendary sci-fi author (if that’s not underselling him), Isaac Asimov. So, it being split up like that makes chomping through all those stories a little like getting really into a TV show and potentially watching an entire season of it in one day.

Sure, it takes time, but when you can break things up like that, it feels more manageable from a psychological perspective than taking in one whole work of similar length that doesn’t really have breaks or some kind of episodic structure. As for the content of I, Robot, it’s nine fairly short stories written by Asimov largely in the 1940s, and when you take them all together, it makes for an important and undeniably influential piece of sci-fi literature.

Imagine not putting Fahrenheit 451 here? Admittedly, apologies are in order if you’ve been going over a fair few rankings concerning books in recent days/weeks/months and have seen Fahrenheit 451 mentioned a great many times, but it is pretty fantastic. It’s aged extremely well and much of what it has to say still feels relevant, but then beyond that, the entertainment it offers also feels quite timeless.

You can be a bit lukewarm on the whole activity of reading and still likely get through Fahrenheit 451 quite easily, and in a fairly short amount of time, too. If it were much shorter, it’d probably be a novella rather than a novel, and the entire thing is paced incredibly well, with a whole lot packed into a little over 150 pages (even with the brief length, it has proven difficult to adapt into a film, but maybe it’s best that the book about books remains, like, a book).

While it is part of a series of the same name, it’s 1979’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy that feels like the most important and worth reading of the bunch, and it’s also probably the most entertaining. It could well be one of the funniest books of all time, and its status in such a category is helped by the fact that it’s comedic throughout, with there being something laugh-worthy on almost every page.

With the science fiction stuff, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy is also interesting and sometimes even thought-provoking, not to mention undoubtedly unique, just with the way it works some big philosophical ideas in with all the weirdness and absurdity. It’s a fairly effortless book to get through in a short amount of time, thanks to not being all that long and being one of the more broadly enjoyable books not just of its era/genre, but maybe even of all time, and of any genre, really.

Entirely on the other end of things to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy if you're talking about tone, here’s I Who Have Never Known Men, which is harrowing enough to feel like something of a horror novel while also being a piece of science fiction. Oh, and regarding it being sci-fi, it’s not entirely. Like, maybe it’s a bit easier to describe as dystopian or post-apocalyptic, with the horror coming in because of how little is explained, and just how few things the narrator really seems to know.

So, maybe call it a mystery novel as well, albeit one without answers. But I Who Have Never Known Men is skillfully written enough that this doesn’t feel frustrating, and it also doesn’t stop the novel as a whole from feeling compelling. The unease and uncertainty are the point, and that point is conveyed artfully, with the whole thing being undeniably haunting to let linger in your mind and look back on.

It’s hard to truly emphasize how important the whole The Dark Tower series is within the Stephen King multiverse, but it would be even harder to suggest anyone try reading most of the books within a single day. The second is about twice as long as the first, and then from three onwards, they don’t necessarily get bigger in a linear way, but they all get pretty chunky, and a few on their own can be counted among King’s longest books overall.

So, back to book #1: The Gunslinger. The first one. This is a dense read, but it is very short for a Stephen King book, and you could technically digest all those pages in just a sitting or two. It’s a strange yet intriguing prologue for the larger series, and its relative brevity and that sense of it being a taste of things to come is why it’s here. For the record, though, it’s more than “just” sci-fi, since The Dark Tower is very much a dark fantasy/adventure/Western series at the same time, and since it’s Stephen King, it does get a little horror-heavy at times as well.

#3476. NBC Has No Choice But To Break One Chicago's 10-Year Tradition In 2026

Few shows reach a triple-digit episode run; even reaching 100 episodes is a cause for celebration. Chicago Fire has gone two steps further, celebrating its 300th episode, aptly titled "Three Hundred," with a beautiful goodbye to Cruz. After his life-changing injury was revealed in the Chicago Fire season 15 premiere, Cruz found a reason to work through rehab before realizing that his family needs him more than his firehouse crew.

As bittersweet as that arc was, something within Chicago Fire season 15's milestone episode fell flat. The series had to break a trend it had followed in previous milestone episodes, and it shows that the series' heart has been missing for a while.

Several notable characters were absent in this important episode, including Boden, whose absence hurt Chicago Fire's legacy. The other glaringly absent character was Severide's best friend at Firehouse 51, Matt Casey (Jesse Spencer).

In previous milestone episodes of Chicago Fire, Casey was always at the center. The 100th episode included Casey and Dawson applying to adopt Louie, while the 200th episode focused on Casey's exit from the firehouse.

This tradition made sense; from the beginning of the series, Casey has been one of the most central and well-developed characters. Casey took Andrew Darden's loss hard in the series premiere, and the 200th episode featured the perfect connection back to him.

Chicago Fire season 15 had no choice but to move on from the Casey-focused story trend in episode 300. Spencer has moved on from the series. While he has returned for small storylines here and there, they have always been connected to Brett, who he was in a relationship with when he left Chicago for Portland. With Brett now gone and Dawson on missions helping people around the world, he has no major ties left at the firehouse.

Whenever a character returns, there needs to be a meaningful story behind it. Coming back just because it was Episode 300 isn't enough. With Cruz's exit set up, there wasn't room for Casey. Of all Chicago Fire's characters, Otis and Severide were the closest to Cruz, and only one could realistically be included in person.

Casey's absence was certainly felt, along with Boden's. A milestone episode is usually a chance to look back at how far a series has come. The 300th episode should be a monumental moment, as so few shows get to reach this point. Even before streaming, it was rare for a series to reach 300 episodes. It's a testament to how viewers have connected to the characters.

Casey's arcs were always meaningful to the firehouse as a whole. His decision to leave during the 200th episode connected back to the show's opening in a way nobody could have predicted. He stepped up as a father figure, sacrificing everything for someone he still missed and felt guilty about losing. Everyone felt that loss, while Cruz's exit really only affects Severide and Squad 3.

Chicago Fire's key changes for season 15 amount to a soft reboot this fall, but the changes won't fix the issues with the cast size in recent years.

While Chicago Fire season 15, episode 5 delivered some poignant and meaningful moments for Cruz, the rest of the hour fell flat. It largely focused on the new probies, and while it was great to see Kidd step up more as a leader, the arc seemed more about getting Marcus to fit in with Firehouse 51 and want that family. Severide's arc shows him floundering a little as captain, and he could use someone like Chicago Fire's Boden to step in and help guide him.

Even the humorous photo plot didn't quite capture the heart of other fun moments from previous milestone episodes. The only benefit this time was that Herrmann already had a photographer to capture that beautiful ending. Chicago Fire has lost a bit of its spark, and this 300th milestone episode proves it.

New episodes of Chicago Fire season 15 air Wednesdays at 9 pm ET on NBC.

Chicago Fire follows the lives of firefighters, rescue squad members, and paramedics of Firehouse 51 in Chicago as they face professional and personal challenges, showcasing their dedication, teamwork, and resilience.

#3475. All the Health and Fitness Products You Didn't Realize You Could Buy With HSA Funds

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), it's that time of year: Use those funds, or you'll lose them. Luckily, there are plenty of clever ways to spend your remaining FSA funds on qualifying healthcare costs—some that you may never have considered as "qualifying."

For instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch (even the latest Fitbit Air). At least, that's what plenty of brands like Whoop, Oura, and even Nike want you to think. Is the process really as straightforward as the marketing suggests? Here's what to know about all the unexpected ways you can spend your FSA funds before the end of the year.

Right off the bat, when it comes to most of these fitness trackers and smartwatches, your HSA/FSA dollars won't be able to cover the entire purchase; instead, you'll save an average of 30% on eligible health purchases.

There is some more fine print, although it’s not as tricky as you might think. For the most part, if a device is necessary for treating or monitoring a specific medical condition—and not just “general wellness”—it could be eligible to purchase with those pre-tax health dollars.

The main “catch” here (as I’ve previously explained) is proving that device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN). Your LMN is basically a doctor's note required to classify certain purchases as qualified medical expenses under IRS guidelines, proving that the device will be used to treat a legitimate medical condition, such as obesity or a heart condition. Let’s take a look at what you can actually expect if you want to get a fitness wearable approved as a medical necessity.

When it comes to securing your LMN, you might not even need to make a doctor's appointment, thanks to third-party players like Truemed. When you browse sites like Coros, Amazfit, and more, you'll see the option to “Pay With Truemed” at checkout. From there, you'll be asked a few questions about your health circumstances, and you’ll be matched with a provider to determine your eligibility. If you qualify, you’ll get an LMN that will allow you to use your HSA or FSA funds to complete your purchase—all without ever having to meet with your primary doctor.

Truemed is one of the most popular payment platforms in this space, with the company claiming on its site that “90% of LMNs are issued within seven hours.” I spoke with Truemed’s co-founder and CEO Justin Mares to find out how it works behind the scenes. After you take that short survey about your health, an independent licensed provider reviews your answers before deciding whether the purchase looks medically necessary. If it doesn't, Truemed won't bother forwarding the request at all. Because Truemed screens your case before it has a chance of getting denied, those approval numbers get to stay mighty high. And the reality is, most Americans will have at least one health marker—like weight or cholesterol levels—that they can self-report to prove that, say, a Fitbit Air is necessary tool for prevention and maintenance.

For the purchases that do go through to a medical professional, approval turns out to be surprisingly straightforward. It comes down to the idea of "standard of care" in general. “If you go into a doctor's office and say your family has a history of high blood pressure,” Mares says, “your doctor probably is not going to ask for lab work before they'll talk to you about it. They simply take you at your word and help you manage the risk.” Proving HSA/FSA eligibility works on that same standard fairly often, according to Mares. You're not submitting a stack of medical records; you're answering a simple intake form about your health history, and a licensed clinician uses that, plus their own judgment, to decide whether a given product is appropriate for you.

Before you get your hopes up too high, FSA/HSA eligibility for wearables is still far from a free-for-all. An LMN only covers you, personally, for a specific product from a specific merchant, and it's usually tied to a specific condition, like cardiovascular risk, pre-diabetes, sleep issues, chronic pain, and so on. Some employers' FSA administrators scrutinize wearable purchases more closely than others, and even a fully compliant LMN doesn't guarantee your plan will approve the claim. Some companies (like Coros, for one) are more transparent about walking customers through the required medical consultation at checkout, while other brands market "HSA/FSA eligible" prominently without explaining that the LMN step is what actually makes that true. Luckily, I’ve saved you some time and rounded up some of the major wearables—and other unexpected items—that you might be able to prove as FSA/HSA eligible.

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. These tend to draw more scrutiny from plan administrators simply because they're marketed as lifestyle products first, so the strength of your intake answers matters more here than it does for something obviously medical, like a blood pressure cuff.

If cardiovascular monitoring, training load tracking, or heart rate accuracy is relevant to a documented health concern, these watches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches. Sadly, no Garmin watches are HSA/FSA-eligible. Still, the following Garmin-brand products are eligible for an HSA/FSA purchase:

You can filter by HSA/FSA eligibility and browse all eligible Garmin items here.

Think adjustable dumbbells, rowing machines, and connected bikes. It's the same logic doctors use when they tell a patient with pre-diabetes or high cholesterol to start exercising regularly; if a clinician is willing to attest that structured exercise is part of your treatment plan, equipment that enables that can qualify. For instance, here are some HSA/FSA eligible products from Nike Strength:

The common thread across all of these is that the product itself doesn't determine eligibility—your health history does. A Whoop band might be an easy approval for someone managing a cardiac condition, but it'll get more pushback for someone with no relevant health history at all. If you're curious whether something on your wish list might qualify, it's worth filling out the intake process just to see how creatively you can spend those pre-tax health dollars. However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste.

#3474. How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying

No one is doing monster movies quite like director Takashi Yamazaki and his team — who not once but twice now, with “Godzilla Minus One” and “Godzilla Minus Zero,” have made Godzilla feel both bigger than Tokyo Bay and extremely emotional and personal, even handcrafted. Much of that comes down to the narrative balance between our human heroes and the King of the Monsters, of course. But it’s also about the grounded, physical ways the monsters are brought to life.

Much has already been made of the fact that both Godzilla’s and King Ghidorah’s roars were recorded by blasting the sound effects against real physical spaces (and probably scaring some hikers in the process) so we wouldn’t just hear something otherworldly. We’d hear the texture of the loudspeakers, the reverberation of the sound on the concrete of a dam (for Ghidorah) or a dome (for Godzilla) — the unreal brought into a real, physical space. Related Stories ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson ‘To Hold a Mountain’ Took on the Government — Now It’s Montenegro’s Oscar Submission

But that is only the light-up blue tip of the kaiju for the work done by the “Godzilla Minus Zero” sound design team. Sound designer Natsuko Inoue and production and post-production sound mixer Hisafumi Takeuchi constantly found ways to tie the most fantastical moments back to Earth, because that sonic believability keeps the audience invested in the action.

“ When audiences hear sounds that they’ve never heard before too frequently, I think it removes you from the world because it’s too foreign and it’ll stand out,” Inoue told IndieWire. “Once a fantasy-like or fictitious sound goes through the sort of real-world echo, then it becomes a lot more palatable, or we become more receptive to how it sounds because it’s echoing in a way that we recognize. So that was a way that we really tied the visuals to the sound and made it feel more grounded.”

This grounding process is especially important, and especially challenging, when things that should be on the ground take to the air as a part of Ghidorah’s gravity beam. Inoue did an initial pass of the sound effect for the beam that allows Ghidorah to throw whole houses up in the air high enough for our favorite eternally tormented, former Kamikaze pilot Kôichi Skikishima (Ryûnosuke Kamiki) to fly past them. But it wasn’t quite right.

“So I went back into the Foley studio, and I wanted to capture that feeling of something being lifted and rising. I took this very small speaker, and I placed it right next to a bunch of different objects — a sheet of metal or some wood or a water tank — to capture a sound that almost felt distorted,” Inoue said.

That distortion, bounced off different types of objects, captured the sensation Inoue was after: the sonic equivalent of your stomach lifting into your mouth.

“Oftentimes in sound design, when you layer too many sounds or put too much processing on it, it starts to ruin the original material or the original sound that you’ve captured. So this distortion became a very strong foundation. I didn’t add too much post-processing on it,” Inoue said.

What she did do was hand it over to Takeuchi to create the sense of whole blocks caught up in Ghidorah’s gravity beam and preserve the dialogue and add background dialogue, so that we’re always afraid for the human beings in danger during Ghidorah’s rampages.

When Shikishima first flies through Ghidorah’s gravity beam, the sound team really wanted to lean into the character’s emotional response to something that’s mindbendingly horrible. “I added a Doppler effect — so like when an ambulance or a police car drives by and the sound shifts slightly — [to give] the sensation that you’re passing through,” Takeuchi told IndieWire.

It’s that shifting of sound, more than any one particular sound, that adds a scale to the horror beyond what Shikishima or what we can see. “We wanted to be very mindful of the balance and what it was doing and what it was supposed to do for each scene,” Takeuchi said.

“What we were trying to do is take sounds that you would hear in nature and then design and add to it in almost like an extension type of way, and that’s how we make the Kaiju as well as the gravity beam feel more real,” Inoue added.

“Godzilla Minus Zero” is now playing in theaters.

#3473. 25 Years Later, ‘Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s Best Quote Is Still the Most Inspiring Line in TV History

Buffy’s story has always revolved around death. Throughout its seven-season run, Buffy Summers (Sarah Michelle Gellar) has wanted to escape from it or, boldly, return to it. Upon a rewatch, death is one of the clearest themes of the series — this wasn’t the case on my first time watching, when I reacted in disbelief every time the series brought up the possibility of Buffy dying. Surely, they wouldn’t go there. But they did.

In the Buffy the Vampire Slayer season 5 finale, Sunnydale is collapsing, and Buffy’s allies have nowhere to go. Her little sister, Dawn (Michelle Trachtenberg), is the reason why a dangerous portal has opened, and she tries to jump in to close it. But Buffy stops her. “The hardest thing in this world is to live in it,” she tells her. “Be brave. Live. For me.”

The hardest thing in this world is to live in it.

The two share the same blood, so Buffy is capable of closing the portal on her own. She jumps in and dies. It’s a moment that closes out an arc that had been teased since season 1.

Season 5 is one of Buffy’s most emotional seasons. It’s also one of its boldest, committing to a new central dynamic: Buffy and Dawn. Maligned series creator Joss Whedon shared that he introduced Dawn as a way of giving Buffy an intense dynamic that wasn’t based in romance. After seasons of Angel, Riley, and hints of Spike, it feels like a breath of fresh air to see Buffy get mad, angry, happy, and distraught over a different type of relationship.

One of the show’s biggest twists was the introduction of Dawn. Buffy, a notorious single child for most of the show, suddenly has a sister, introduced in a throwaway moment that made me think I had skipped a few episodes. But Dawn’s introduction is not a plot hole. The season spends the rest of its runtime deconstructing this, revealing that Dawn is a Key made up of ancient energy that was put into the body of a girl, with monks giving Buffy and her friends memories of her.

With Dawn’s arrival, Buffy’s era as a teenager is officially over. The season is all about making her grow up fast, stripping her of almost everything that gave her a sense of safety, including her human boyfriend Riley and her mother Joyce. It’s the end of Buffy the Vampire Slayer’s lighter era. From then on, you can’t say that the series is about a scrappy group of teens trying to save the world.

“The Gift,” written by and directed by Whedon, neatly closes all of the storylines that it introduced in its first episode. Throughout the season Buffy and Dawn’s dynamic morphs, from annoying siblings to Buffy becoming Dawn’s caregiver. Buffy learns that Dawn isn’t real early on, but the discovery changes nothing. To Buffy, Dawn is the most important person in her life and only family left. In the finale, when Giles brings up the possibility of sacrificing Dawn to stop a ritual, Buffy immediately shuts him down.

“The Gift” takes its title from a line in “Intervention,” where Buffy goes on a vision quest to meet the First Slayer, a prehistoric girl who tells her: “Death is your gift.” The line reinforces one of Buffy’s biggest fears: that she’s a killing machine, closer to the vampires and demons she hunts than to the human world she’s so desperate to belong to. But Buffy’s words to Dawn show what her gift really means. For Buffy, being the Slayer has never been about strength or power; it’s about sacrifice. With her death, Buffy tasks her sister with living, no matter how difficult and lonely it gets. Those words will haunt her in season 6, finding Buffy at her most anguished and destructive after being ripped out of heaven and coming back to life.

While we now know that Buffy the Vampire Slayer continued for two more seasons and that it ended on a relatively happy note (at least she’s alive), the writers didn’t know that. Season 5 was the last to air on The WB, before the series found its final home on UPN. That uncertainty is why Whedon and company treated “The Gift” as a series finale, wrapping up Buffy’s story while engaging in a conversation with “Prophecy Girl,” the season 1 finale. That episode shows a younger Buffy, one who’s so afraid of dying that she can barely face the Master. This time around, Buffy chooses death calmly, because it means saving her sister.

“The Gift” ends with an indelible image. As Buffy’s friends mourn her and Dawn remembers her sister’s final words, we pan over Buffy’s body over a pile of rubble. We cut to her tombstone: “Buffy Anne Summers. Beloved sister. Devoted friend. She saved the world a lot.”

#3472. Letterboxd’s Sale to the New York Times: 9 Pros, Cons, and Big Questions from the $330 Million Deal

After several months of business talks and speculation, Letterboxd is about to have new owners. The New York Times is closing in on deal to acquire the film-logging social media platform, which values the company at $330 million. It’s an eye-popping increase from 2023, when the Canadian holding company Tiny bought a majority stake at a $50 million valuation.

Far beyond the film industry, there is a dismal track record and daunting uncertainty when it comes to companies’ ability to maintain their identities after being acquired. Social media reception to the pending New York Times deal generally peaked at resigned relief (“the best case scenario” was a common refrain) while also drawing more cynical, even existential responses about the future of Letterboxd. As the website’s user base holds its breath over the future, these are some pros, cons, and big unknowns to consider about where Letterboxd is going. Related Stories Letterboxd Finalizing $330 Million Sale to The New York Times ‘The Weed Eaters’ Lands Expanded Release from Yellow Veil Pictures: New Zealand Cannibal Movie Sets Winter Rollout

There’s understandably a lot of negative social chatter about the news of Letterboxd’s looming acquisition, but let’s rest assured that it’s at least not a studio taking ownership of the wildly popular cinephile engagement platform. A24, Sony, Netflix, and Skydance were all reported to have registered talks about an acquisition. Whether or not this new iteration of Letterboxd will exist behind a paywall is one matter, but that’s not the worst thing compared to the potential studio-ification (i.e. A24-ification, as they were in talks for the sale) of the brand. Compare it to studios running an exhibition chain — not just Sony purchasing Alamo Drafthouse, but all the way back to the days before the Paramount Decrees, which legislatively blocked studios from having a monopoly on theaters. (Decrees that are no longer in effect.) In that situation, there’s more potential for marketing nepotism and favoritism to titles and properties in-house. A media company taking over Letterboxd should, in theory, prevent the kind of self-interest that threatens independence. —Ryan Lattanzio

A deal would bring two unusually loaded cultural conversations under one roof. The movie-logging platform has helped reshape the world’s repertory film scene — effectively gamifying the enjoyment of archival art — while debates about the Times often wind their way back to the paper’s coverage of Palestine and trans rights. For Letterboxd users who see that coverage as having real consequences for whose lives and experiences are taken seriously by mainstream journalistic institutions, the prospect of the Times owning a community they helped build raises questions of trust. A bigger audience would be a genuine upside, but for some users, who owns the room is an existential issue. —Alison Foreman

While some users might not even know about Letterboxd’s digital magazine, the Journal has been a growing presence on the platform, with a staffed editorial team regularly publishing interviews, retrospective considerations, film festival coverage, and other longform articles. The question remains on how, or if, those writers and editors will be integrated into the New York Times newsroom. A shuttering of the Journal would wreck yet another publication for professional film coverage and freelance opportunities, of which there are fewer and fewer. On the other hand, when the New York Times bought The Athletic in 2022 for a whopping $550 million, the banner initially continued as a semi-independent banner. But a year later, the Times dissolved its existing sports department, laying off or reassigning staff, and positioned The Athletic as a replacement. The New York Times’ culture desk has not been immune to shake-ups over recent years; the potential addition of Letterboxd begs the question of whether further changes are in store. —J. Kim Murphy

As the number of Letterboxd accounts has skyrocketed over the past few years, navigating the platform has become a bumpier experience for users. Pop-up Cloudflare turnstiles reading “Verifying you are human. This may take a few seconds” make frequent interruptions clicking from page to page, while Gremlins-centric error messages signaling server crashes are semi-regular occurrences. The New York Times draws much more web traffic than Letterboxd and such technical hiccups are essentially anomalous. The company certainly has the resources to bolster the strength of Letterboxd’s servers. —JKM

Letterboxd users have historically been an extremely discerning audience, sensitive to changes that might be seen as minute or inconsequential for other websites. A memorable hiccup from recent years came when the platform abruptly removed an option to list out all star-ratings given by the accounts one follows on a single web page. After some backlash from users (like myself) who noticed the feature’s disappearance, Letterboxd was swift in reintegrating the tool. It was a small crisis with a happy ending, but it speaks to how quickly UI changes can dishearten the platform’s users. If the New York Times wants to make even small tweaks to the platform, or heavily integrate it into its digital ecosystem, it will face an audience that’s quick to rally against such changes. —JKM

The New York Times Company is the poster child for brand elasticity in the digital media age. America’s newspaper of record didn’t just adapt to the Internet; it built an empire of games, recipes, and sports that a sizable chunk of the world needs to engage with in a daily basis. But it’s less apparent how Letterboxd fits into the strategy. The social network exists somewhere between an editorial product and a game and doesn’t have a clear comp within the NYT organization. Is the plan to simply move the entire Letterboxd infrastructure behind the NYT paywall, making the $30 monthly subscription tier even more unavoidable for cinephiles? Draw on users’ data to bolster revenue opportunities for streaming promotions and the Times’ product recommendation banner Wirecutter? The answer might be some combination of the above, but the Times is entering uncharted territory. —Christian Zilko

Plenty of filmmakers IndieWire has spoken to are concerned about the widening gap between what defines film criticism and what defines a hot-take social media sound-off, i.e., the “instant reaction.” Reviews on Letterboxd can range from the thoughtful and long-form to the pithy and snarky. As film critic jobs evaporate globally, what happens when you merge Letterboxd closer to the purview of established, institutional film writing, the kind that’s hard, that demands a chunk of your soul? Letterboxd has further democratized criticism, no question, and while many of us argue that we need an elevated discourse, what happens if more people start to think… we don’t? Will the fusion of the Times and Letterboxd stoke that debate, or create harmony? Will this only fuel the growing primacy of influencers over critics and journalists as an authority on a film’s quality? Either way, cantankerous conversation will abound. —RL

It follows then that if enough Letterboxd users distrust the Times, they might log fewer movies, post fewer reviews, or exit the app altogether. From a web-development perspective, the basic mechanics of a movie diary are incredibly easy to replicate. (Hell, AI just cloned Adobe Photoshop.) The hard part is getting the consumers whose aggregate taste is a cultural bellwether to once again show up in the same place. It wouldn’t take a mass exodus for Letterboxd to feel fundamentally different, and if the core group of people who reliably made consumers laugh or put weird repertory picks on your radar stop contributing, there will be fewer reasons to engage. The community could splinter across new competitor sites — which, yes, opens up potential opportunities for aspiring critics to gain exposure and find their followings. But we can’t know if any of that would be as big as the OG Letterboxd. —AF

#3471. Apple Is About to Release a Touchscreen MacBook Pro (Plus Four More Devices)

Apple has had a busy fall. Head to the company's website, and you'll immediately be greeted by a sea of new products: the foldable iPhone Duo; the iPhone 18 Pro; HomePod mini 2; Apple Watch Series 12; the list goes on. It seems, under new Apple CEO Jon Ternus, the company is ready for a refresh of just about every product it sells. To that point, the company seems far from finished. Just this week, Apple is planning to release five brand new products, each launching on Friday. While four of these are Macs, Apple does have a new iPad in the works, as well. Here's everything new Apple is releasing this week.

Finally. For the first time, the iPad mini is about to ship with an OLED display. Apple's smallest tablet has always come with a standard screen. Despite its price tag, the iPad mini has never come with an OLED display, or even a mini-LED screen, until now. With this new model, there is no backlight. As such, each individual pixel on the iPad's display will be able to shut itself off when displaying dark content. That will benefit the content you watch on this device, as well as the overall contrast of the screen.

Beyond the new OLED panel, the new iPad mini is thinner and lighter than the previous model. It also comes with Apple's newest A20 Pro chip, the same processor the company put in its iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo smartphones. The new device starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, though there are various upgrades, including nano-texture glass (add $100) and cellular (add $150).

Good news: There's a new iMac. Bad news: Not much is different here from the previous model. The biggest change here is the new M6 chip, which Apple says is up to five times faster than the iMac with M4 and up to 12 times faster than the iMac with M1. With that M6 chip, the iMac now supports Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6. Other than that, this is the same iMac you may already know: It comes with a 24-inch LED display (no OLED, unfortunately), two or four USB-C ports (depending on the configuration), and a built-in 12MP webcam. If you're looking for a new all-in-one computer, or you've been considering upgrading your older iMac, this is likely a great choice. But if you already have an M-series iMac, it's not such an obvious upgrade. (My M1 iMac may be up to 12 times slower, but it's still plenty fast for me.) Apple didn't change the price here: The M6 iMac still starts at $1,499 for two ports, 16GB of RAM, and 256GB of storage.

Similarly, Apple's newest 14-inch MacBook Pro isn't much different from the previous model—save for the new processor. This model also comes with Apple's M6 chip, which Apple says is up to 13 times faster for AI processing than the M1 MacBook Pro. (Apple seems keen on convincing stubborn M1 users to upgrade this cycle.) Now, the company is offering this model of MacBook Pro in three chipsets, depending on use case: M6 for "entry-level" pro work; M5 Pro for mid-tier pro work; and M5 Max for the most demanding situations.

But, like the M6 iMac, this is the same MacBook Pro Apple sold before. It has a 14-inch mini-LED display with a refresh rate up to 120Hz. It comes with three Thunderbolt 4 (USB-C) ports, an HDMI port, and an SDXC card slot. It, too, has a 12MP webcam for video calls. Apple's newest MacBook Pro starts at $1,999, but you can quickly ramp up that price tag with screen, chip, memory, or storage upgrades.

Apple's most exciting product launch this week is undoubtedly the new touchscreen MacBook Pros. Unlike the M6 MacBook Pro, which only comes in the 14-inch variant, Apple's first touchscreen laptop comes in both 14- and 16-inch options. Apple says this touchscreen lets you scroll, zoom, or draw on the display. That works with basic functions, like web browsing or selecting files, but also with specific workflows, like playing virtual instruments in Logic Pro, or manipulating an object in a 3D modeling app. Like the iPad mini, this laptop comes with an OLED display (Apple calls it PROLED XDR), with up to 1,000 nits of typical brightness and 2,000 nits of HDR brightness. It also brings back the backlit Apple logo, something I've missed on my last two MacBooks.

This MacBook Pro also comes with the iPhone's Dynamic Island for the first time. This replaces the "notch" that other MacBook Pros and MacBook Airs currently ship with. It can function as a basic webcam, but also as a dedicated zone for Spotlight, Live Activities, and Siri AI. This machine comes in either M5 Pro or M5 Max variants—no M6 for this model—as Apple seems to be positioning it exclusively for the most taxing situations (particularly AI). The company says the new MacBook Pro has up to 13 more hours of battery life than Intel-based MacBook Pros, and can fast charge up to 50% in 30 minutes. It's essentially a supercharged version of the existing MacBook Pro.

As such, this is Apple's most expensive laptop. The 14-inch M5 Pro version starts at $2,899, while the 16-inch starts at $3,399. However, you can configure these machines to have outrageous price tags. The maxed-out 16-inch MacBook Pro is $14,549, roughly half of which is the 16TB of RAM.
